## Abstract

We prove that the empirical law of eigenvalues of Brownian motion on the Lie Group $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ converges almost surely to a deterministic probability measure, characterized by a free stochastic differential equation. This fully resolves a conjecture made by Philippe Biane in 1997. Our analysis includes a family $\{B=B_{\varrho,\zeta}\colon\varrho>0,|\zeta|\leq\varrho\}$ of diffusion processes on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ whose laws are invariant under unitary conjugation.

The crux of our analysis is a strong quantitative approximation of Brownian motion $B(t)$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ for small $t$ by a single increment $I+W(t)$ , where $W=W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ is an elliptical Brownian motion in the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}(N,\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ . Specifically, for any $t\in[0,1]$ and $\delta>0$ ,

for a constant $C=C_{\varrho}$ . Leveraging independence of multiplicative increments of the Brownian motion then allows us to use powerful (anti-)concentration tools for Gaussian matrices to complete the Hermitization procedure for convergence of eigenvalues.

## 1. Introduction

In this paper, we answer the longstanding question of convergence of eigenvalues of Brownian motions on the Lie group $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ of complex invertible $N\times N$ matrices.

Brownian motion and heat kernel analysis on Lie groups have been studied extensively since the 1970s; see the survey [108] and especially [106, 57, 64, 49] for perspective relevant to the present work. One effective construction of Lie group Brownian motion is through a stochastic differential equation driven by “flat” Brownian motion on the Lie algebra; see (1.3). This provides a direct connection to the classical ensembles of random matrix theory. The unitary group $\mathrm{U}(N)$ has, as Lie algebra, the space of skew-Hermitian matrices in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ ; the “flat” Brownian motion on this space is $\mathbf{i}X(t)$ where, for each $t\geq 0$ , the Hermitian matrix $X(t)$ is a Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (scaled by $\sqrt{t}$ ). Meanwhile, the general linear group $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ has as Lie algebra the full space $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ ; the standard “flat” Brownian motion $W(t)$ here is, for each $t\geq 0$ , a matrix of all i.i.d. complex Gaussian random variables, i.e. a Ginibre Ensemble (scaled by $\sqrt{t}$ ).

These ensembles comprise two of the most well-known settings for large- $N$ limits of eigenvalue distributions: Wigner [114, 115] proved the density of eigenvalues of $X(1)$ converges to the semicircle law, while Ginibre [53] proved that $W(1)$ ’s eigenvalues converge to the circular law, as $N\to\infty$ . Wigner’s semicircle law was extended to matrices with i.i.d. entries above the diagonal under the optimal finite second moment hypothesis within a decade; cf. [8, 7, 56]. On the other hand, the analogous extension of the circular law was not accomplished until 45 years after Ginibre’s work in [104], following incremental progress by several authors – see the survey [21]. This is a testament to the vastly greater difficulty working with eigenvalues of non-normal matrices than with selfadjoint matrices.

As curved-space complements to these classical theorems, it is very natural therefore to study large- $N$ limits of eigenvalues of Brownian motions on $\mathrm{U}(N)$ and $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ . The unitary case was initiated by Philippe Biane in [19, 20], with some related work by Eric Rains around the same time [97]. Inspired by earlier work of Applebaum, Hudson, and Parthasarathy [6, 71] and especially Bożejko, Kümmerer, and Speicher [24, 78], Biane set the framework for free stochastic calculus, and used it to construct a noncommutatve process $(u(t))_{t\geq 0}$ he called free unitary Brownian motion as a solution to a free SDE (the free version of (1.9)). He then proved that, with the correct scaling of the metrics on the groups $\mathrm{U}(N)$ , the unitary Brownian motion $U(t)\in\mathrm{U}(N)$ converges to $u(t)$ as $N\to\infty$ in $\ast$ -distribution: convergence of traces of polynomial functions of the process at different times. Given that both $U(t)$ and $u(t)$ are unitary operators, this sufficed to prove convergence of the density of eigenvalues of $U(t)$ to a probability measure determined by $u(t)$ . This convergence result, and the free unitary Brownian motion process, found many uses in the theory of free entropy (e.g. [112, 34]). Many more refined convergence results were explored in the ensuing two decades, including concentration at the edge and absence of outliers [36], strong metric convergence and mesoscopic scale analysis of eigenvalue evolution [84], linear fluctuations [79, 31], applications to Yang–Mills theory [46, 43], and connections with non-intersecting Brownian motions [80].

In parallel, Biane introduced the free multiplicative Brownian motion $(b(t))_{t\geq 0}$ – another non-commutative stochastic process that satisfies a free SDE (a special case of (1.20)). In [20], it played a central role in constructing a free version of the Segal–Bargmann–Hall transform – a unitary isomorphism in geometric quantization theory that concretely implements wave-particle duality. The transform intertwines heat kernels (i.e. marginal distributions of Brownian motions) on $\mathrm{U}(N)$ and its complexification $\mathrm{U}(N)_{\mathbb{C}}=\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ . While connected by analogy with Brownian motion $B(t)$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , Biane wrote [19, p. 19] “It is very likely that the [free multiplicative Brownian motion] process is the limit in distribution…of the Brownian motion with values in $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ …but we have not proved this.” The functional calculus and Fourier analytic methods Biane invented to prove convergence of eigenvalues in the unitary setting are unavailable for $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , making the problem much harder for the same reason the circular law is much harder than its semicircular cousin: most matrices in $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ are non-normal, so the spectral theorem is no use. (Indeed, in [76, Prop. 4.15], it was shown that, with probability $1$ , $B(t)$ is not normal at any time $t>0$ for $N>1$ .)

*Figure 1. Eigenvalues and limit support set of the Brownian motion $B(t)$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , with $N=2000$ and $t=3,4,4.5$ left to right. These figures closely match the plots in [20] of the region Biane denoted $\Sigma_{t}$ (herein denoted $\Sigma(1,t)$ , see Section 2), instigating the work that has culminated in this paper.*

The framework to begin understanding the large- $N$ limit of the Brownian motion $(B(t))_{t\geq 0}$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ was created independently in [32] and [45]. The processes $(W(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(B(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , along with their Hermitian and unitary cousins, have Markov generators that are Laplacians on different spaces (see Section 1.1 for details). Careful analysis of the associated Markov semigroups yields explicit covariance estimates, e.g. $\mathrm{Cov}[P(B(t),B(t)^{\ast}),Q(B(t),B(t)^{\ast})]=\mathcal{O}_{t,P,Q}(\frac{1}{N^{2}})$ for any $t\geq 0$ and non-commutative polynomials $P,Q$ . In [76, 77], these results were generalized to multiple times and to a two-parameter family of diffusion processes on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , all Brownian motions with respect to invariant metrics, which includes the unitary Brownian motion as a boundary case. Meanwhile, the original Segal–Bargmann–Hall transform was extended to allow for complexified time [47], and this gave rise to a third (and final, in a sense explained at the end of Section 1.2 below) parameter for invariant metrics. Very recently [11] upgraded these convergence results to this $3$ -parameter “elliptical” setting, and moreover upgraded the convergence from traces to norms of polynomial functions (i.e. strong convergence).

All that being said, the spectrum is discontinuous in the topology of convergence in $\ast$ -distribution. For example [21, Example 1.2] the permutation matrix $Q$ of a full $N$ -cycle and the unilateral shift $S$ on $\mathbb{C}^{N}$ have the same limit $\ast$ -distribution (being bounded rank- $1$ perturbations of each other); but the spectrum of $Q$ consists of the $N$ th roots of unity, while the spectrum of $S$ is $\{0\}$ for all $N$ . In general, convergence of eigenvalues is much harder to establish than convergence in $\ast$ -distribution. For example, in the case of polynomials in independent Ginibre random matrices, the convergence in $\ast$ -distribution has been known since the early nineties, see [110], but the convergence of the empirical eigenvalue distribution remains a currently active problem – see the 2022 paper [38] for partial results, and the very recent preprint [66] for a proposed full solution.

The challenges presented by the gap between $\ast$ -distribution and eigenvalue convergence left Biane’s original conjecture about convergence of eigenvalues of Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ open. Until now. Our main Theorem 1.2 proves convergence of the density of eigenvalues for all invariant $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ processes that deserve the title “Brownian motion”.

To set the stage for this main result, we step back briefly to concretely describe Brownian motions on fairly general Lie groups.

### 1.1. Brownian Motion on Lie Groups

Generally, a Brownian motion is any Feller–Markov process whose generator is ( $\frac{1}{2}$ of) a Laplace operator. What is meant by a Laplace operator may depend on the precise geometric context; it is an elliptic second-order linear differential operator that resembles the classical Laplacian $\sum_{j}\partial_{j}^{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . On manifolds, this form can be precisely mirrored by sums of squares of vector fields; on Lie groups, the group structure begs for the vector fields to be left- (or right-)invariant.

Let $\mathfrak{G}$ be a Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}=T_{I}G$ , the tangent space at the identity $I\in\mathfrak{G}$ . For any vector $\xi\in\mathfrak{g}$ , the vector field $\partial_{\xi}$ (often denoted $\tilde{\xi}$ ) is defined by $(\partial_{\xi}f)(A)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(A\exp(t\xi))\right|_{t=0}$ for $f\in C^{\infty}(\mathfrak{G})$ . Here, $\exp\colon\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{G}$ is the exponential map which is a local diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of $0\in\mathfrak{g}$ onto a neighborhood of $I\in\mathfrak{G}$ ; if $\mathfrak{G}$ is a matrix Lie group, $\exp$ is simply the matrix exponential. The vector field $\partial_{\xi}$ is left-invariant, meaning that $\partial_{\xi}(f\circ L_{A})=(\partial_{\xi}f)\circ L_{A}$ where $L_{A}(B)=A^{-1}B$ , and every left-invariant vector field on $\mathfrak{G}$ has this form (if $\tilde{X}$ is left-invariant then $\tilde{X}=\partial_{\xi}$ where $\xi=\tilde{X}|_{I}$ ).

Given a finite collection of vectors $\beta\subset\mathfrak{g}$ , we may consider the associated sum-of-squares operator

$$ \Delta_{\beta}=\sum_{\xi\in\beta}\partial_{\xi}^{2}. $$

If $\beta$ is a vector space basis of $\mathfrak{g}$ , then $\Delta_{\beta}$ is an elliptic operator. If $\mathfrak{G}$ is unimodular, $\Delta_{\beta}$ coincides with the the Laplace–Beltrami operator for the left-invariant Riemannian metric on $\mathfrak{G}$ induced by the inner product on $\mathfrak{g}$ for which $\beta$ is an orthonormal basis. (It is then a standard calculus exercise that the operator $\Delta_{\beta}$ does not depend on which orthonormal basis $\beta$ is used.)

If $\beta$ is not a vector space basis for $\mathfrak{g}$ , the operator $\Delta_{\beta}$ is degenerate, but it may still have nice properties. Hörmander’s theorem [70] asserts that if $\beta$ generates $\mathfrak{g}$ as a Lie algebra (under vector space operations and Lie brackets) then $\Delta_{\beta}$ is hypoelliptic, meaning in particular that the associated heat kernel (the fundamental solution $u=u(t,\cdot)$ to the heat equation $\partial_{t}u=\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\beta}u$ , which is the marginal distribution of the Brownian motion at time $t$ ) is a smooth function on $\mathfrak{G}$ , strictly positive if $\mathfrak{G}$ is connected. Feller–Markov processes with hypoelliptic generators retain many of the robust properties imbued by ellipticity (such as neighborhood recurrence and unique stationary distributions when $\mathfrak{G}$ is connected), and hence also deserve to be called Brownian motions.

The sum-of-squares form (1.1) for the Laplacian allows for a simple description of Brownian motion in $\mathfrak{G}$ in terms of a stochastic differential equation driven by standard Brownian motion $W$ in (a subspace of) the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ . Specifically: for a given linearly independent set $\beta\subset\mathfrak{g}$ , let $\{W_{\xi}\colon\xi\in\beta\}$ be independent standard Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$ , and define

$$ W(t)=W_{\beta}(t):=\sum_{\xi\in\beta}W_{\xi}(t)\,\xi. $$

The process $W$ is determined by the inner product on $\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\,\beta$ for which $\beta$ is orthonormal; if $\beta^{\prime}$ is any other orthonormal basis with respect to this inner product, $W_{\beta}$ and $W_{\beta^{\prime}}$ have the same law. We therefore think of $W$ associated to an inner product on (a subspace of) $\mathfrak{g}$ .

The diffusion process $B$ on $\mathfrak{G}$ whose generator is $\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\beta}$ (and is rightfully called a Brownian motion provided $\beta$ satisfies Hörmander’s condition) can equivalently be described as the strong solution to the Stratonovich SDE

$$ B(t)=B(0)+\int_{0}^{t}B(s)\circ dW(s). $$

In the case that $\mathfrak{G}$ is a matrix Lie group, there is a simple conversion of (1.3) to an Itô integral:

$$ B(t)=B(0)+\int_{0}^{t}B(s)\,dW(s)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B(s)\Xi\,ds $$

where $\Xi=\sum_{\xi\in\beta}\xi^{2}$ [83, p. 116]. (The Itô correction term is $\frac{1}{2}$ the quadtratic covariation of $B$ and $W$ .) If $\beta$ satisfies Hörmander’s condition (i.e. generates $\mathfrak{g}$ as a Lie algebra), the sum-of-squares matrix $\Xi$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{g}$ . Note that $\Xi$ can be computed directly from the given $\mathfrak{g}$ -valued diffusion $W$ (1.2) by

$$ \mathbb{E}[W(t)^{2}]=\sum_{\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\in\beta}\mathbb{E}[W_{\xi_{1}}(t)W_{\xi_{2}}(t)]\xi_{1}\xi_{2}=\sum_{\xi\in\beta}t\xi^{2}=t\Xi. $$

If $B_{I}$ denotes the solution to (1.4) with $B(0)=I$ and if $B_{0}$ is any random matrix independent from the process $B_{I}$ , the process $B=(B_{0}B_{I}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ satisfies (1.4) with $B(0)=B_{0}$ ; hence, Brownian motion with any given initial distribution $B_{0}$ can equivalently be constructed this way, and we generally restrict the SDE to $B(0)=I$ . Similar considerations show that $B$ has independent multiplicative increments: for $0\leq s<t$ , $B(s)^{-1}B(t)$ is independent from $\{B(r)\colon r\leq s\}$ . Moreover, the inverse is itself an Itô process: a stochastic calculus exercise shows that the process $\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}=(\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ defined by

$$ \rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)=I-\int_{0}^{t}dW(s)\circ\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(s)=I-\int_{0}^{t}dW(s)\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(s)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\Xi\,\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(s)\,ds $$

is the inverse of $B(t)$ for each $t$ ; i.e. $B(t)\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)=I$ . That is: since $-W$ has the same law as $W$ , the inverse $B(t)^{-1}=\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)$ is a right-invariant Brownian motion on $\mathfrak{G}$ , driven by $W$ . See [76, Section 4.2] for further discussion.

### 1.2. Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$

Now, let us specialize to the case $\mathfrak{G}=\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , in which case the Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{gl}(N,\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , the algebra of all $N\times N$ complex matrices. The above constructions are determined by a choice of a linearly independent set $\beta\subset\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , or equivalently a choice of a possibly degenerate inner product on $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ . Consider the (rescaled) Pauli spin matrices

$$ \displaystyle\mathscr{S}_{N}=\Big\{\textstyle{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}}E_{i,i}\colon 1\leq i\leq N\Big\} \displaystyle\sqcup\;\Big\{\textstyle{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2N}}}(E_{i,j}+E_{j,i})\colon 1\leq i<j\leq N\Big\} \displaystyle\sqcup\;\Big\{\textstyle{\frac{\mathbf{i}}{\sqrt{2N}}}(E_{i,j}-E_{j,i})\colon 1\leq i<j\leq N\Big\} $$

where $E_{i,j}\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ has a $1$ in the $(i,j)$ -entry and $0$ elsewhere. The set $\mathscr{S}_{N}$ is orthonormal with respect to the scaled Hilbert–Schmidt inner product

$$ \langle A,B\rangle_{N}:=N\,\mathrm{Re}\,\mathrm{Tr}(B^{\ast}A) $$

where $\mathrm{Tr}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}A_{jj}$ is the trace. We denote the associated process (1.2) as $W=X=(X(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , a Hermitian Brownian motion. The joint law of entries of $t^{-1/2}X$ is a Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE): $\{X_{ij}\colon i\leq j\}$ are independent, with diagonal entries real Gaussians of variance $t/N$ and upper-triangular entries complex Gaussians with independent real and imaginary parts of variance $t/2N$ . This is the variance scaling that Biane considered in [19, 20], ergo the $N^{-1/2}$ scaling of $\mathscr{S}_{N}$ and associated scaling up of the inner product in (1.8). See further discussion below in Definition 3.7.

#### Remark 1.1 (Unitary case).

The span $\mathbf{i}\mathscr{S}_{N}$ of skew-Hermitian matrices is the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{u}(N)$ of the compact Lie group $\mathrm{U}(N)$ of unitary matrices. In particular, $\mathbf{i}\mathscr{S}_{N}$ does not satisfy Hörmander’s condition for all of $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ . The sum of squares $\Xi$ of matrices in $\mathbf{i}\mathscr{S}_{N}$ is equal to $-I$ , and so in this context (1.4) becomes

$$ U(t)=I+\mathbf{i}\int_{0}^{t}U(s)\,dX(s)-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}U(s)\,ds $$

where we have renamed $B=U$ here as it is Brownian motion on $\mathrm{U}(N)$ . Note that $U(t)^{\ast}$ then satisfies (1.6), showing directly that $U(t)^{\ast}=U(t)^{-1}$ , i.e. $U$ takes values in $\mathrm{U}(N)$ . Indeed, with the present scaling, $U$ is the unitary Brownian motion whose large- $N$ limit was studied by Biane [19].

In this paper, we consider the general class of Brownian motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ driven by elliptical Brownian motions on $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ : i.e.

$$ W=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(aX+\mathbf{i}bY) $$

where $X$ and $Y$ are independent Hermitian Brownian motions, $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ (not both $0$ ), and $\theta\in[-\pi,\pi)$ . If $ab\neq 0$ , $e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}W$ corresponds to (1.2) with a spanning set consisting of positive scalar multiples of all the matrices in $\mathscr{S}_{N}\sqcup\mathbf{i}\mathscr{S}_{N}$ , and so the associated Laplacian is elliptic; it then follows that $W$ has an elliptic generator as well. If either $a=0$ or $b=0$ , the Laplacian is degenerate. However, straightforward computations show that $\mathbf{i}\mathscr{S}_{N}\subset[\mathscr{S}_{N},\mathscr{S}_{N}]$ , and this shows that the Hörmander condition holds except in the cases that $W$ reduces to a real multiple of $\mathbf{i}X$ or $\mathbf{i}Y$ — which yield the unitary Brownian motion (Remark 1.1).

It is useful to make the following change of variables:

$$ \displaystyle\varrho: \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathrm{tr}[|W(1)|^{2}]=a^{2}+b^{2} \displaystyle\zeta: \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\mathrm{tr}[W(1)^{2}]=e^{2\mathbf{i}\theta}(a^{2}-b^{2}) $$

where $\mathrm{tr}=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}$ is the normalized trace on $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ and, for any matrix $A$ , $|A|^{2}:=A^{\ast}A$ . The parameters $(\varrho,\zeta)$ satisfy $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ . Conversely, for any pair $(\varrho,\zeta)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ , all the elliptical Brownian motions (1.2) with $(a,b,\theta)$ satisfying (1.11) have the same law. Ergo the pairs $(\varrho,\zeta)$ parametrize all elliptical Brownian motions (in law); we henceforth denote $W=W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ . Note that:

- $\bullet$ $W_{1,0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X+\mathbf{i}Y)$ is the full Ginibre Brownian motion. All its entries are i.i.d. complex Brownian motions. When $\zeta=0$ , the process is invariant under left (or right) multiplication by any deterministic unitary matrix; in particular, multiplying by $e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}$ does not change the distribution in this case.

- $\bullet$ The ellipticity condition $ab\neq 0$ exactly corresponds to $|\zeta|<\varrho$ .

- $\bullet$ When $|\zeta|=\varrho$ , $W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ is hypoelliptic except in the particular case $\zeta=-\varrho$ which yields time rescaled Unitary Brownian motion – see Remark 1.1.

See Section 3.2 for more detail on the relationship between $(a,b,\theta)$ and $(\varrho,\zeta)$ .

We can now fully describe the group Brownian motions of (1.4) corresponding to the elliptical driving processes $W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ . Since $\Xi$ is in the center of $\mathfrak{gl}(N,\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ which consists of scalar multiples of $I$ , it follows from (1.5) and (1.11) that $\Xi=\mathbb{E}[W(1)^{2}]=\zeta I$ . Hence, the main objects of study in the present work are Brownian motions $B_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ where

$$ B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)=I+\int_{0}^{t}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)\,dW_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)\,ds. $$

The standard Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ is the specal case $B_{1,0}$ , driven by the Ginibre Brownian motion $W_{1,0}$ on $\mathfrak{gl}(N,\mathbb{C})$ .

Note that all the elliptical Brownian motions (1.10) are invariant under unitary conjugation: if $U\in\mathrm{U}(N)$ is a deterministic unitary matrix then $UW_{\varrho,\zeta}U^{\ast}$ is equal in distribution to $W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ . It follows from (1.12) that the Brownian motions $B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ are similarly invariant; see (3.7). Unitary conjugation invariance is a historically useful property for connecting random matrices to large- $N$ limits with free probability, see Proposition 3.5. In [47, Theorem 3.3, Proposition 3.7], the authors characterized all inner products, and hence all Brownian motion processes $W$ (1.2), on $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ that are $\mathrm{U}(N)$ -conjugation invariant; they are all of the form $W_{\varrho,\zeta}+cZI$ where $c\in\mathbb{R}$ and $Z$ is a (scalar) complex Brownian motion independent from $W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ . (The proof assumes strict positivity of the inner product, but a simple modification shows that the characterization also applies to the degenerate case $|\zeta|=\varrho$ .) Since $ZI$ commutes with $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , it follows that the most general $\mathrm{U}(N)$ -conjugation invariant Brownian motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ have the form $e^{cZ(t)}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ . As the spectral distribution of $e^{cZ(t)}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ is obtained from that of $B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ by multiplying each eigenvalue by the independent scalar random variable $e^{cZ(t)}$ , we henceforth treat only the case $c=0$ .

### 1.3. Main Result

Given a matrix $A\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , denote its $N$ complex eigenvalues by $\{\lambda_{j}(A)\}_{j=1}^{N}$ (counted with multiplicity and labeled arbitrarily). The empirical law of eigenvalues of $A$ , denoted $\mu_{A}$ , is the random probability distribution with equal masses at all eigenvalues of $A$ :

$$ \mu_{A}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{\lambda_{j}(A)}. $$

Our main theorem asserts that, almost surely, the empirical law of eigenvalues $\mu_{B(t)}$ converges weakly to a deterministic measure as $N\to\infty$ . In fact, we prove this more generally for the Brownian motion $B_{0}B(t)$ for any initial distribution $B_{0}$ that has a large- $N$ limit of its own.

#### Theorem 1.2.

Let $\varrho>0$ , $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ , and let $B=B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ denote a Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , see (1.12). Let $B_{0}$ be a random matrix in $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ independent from the process $B$ and suppose that $B_{0}$ converges a.s. in $\ast$ -distribution (see Definition 3.2) to an operator $b_{0}$ as $N\to\infty$ .

Then for fixed $t>0$ , a.s. as $N\to\infty$ , the empirical law $\mu_{B_{0}B(t)}$ of eigenvalues of the Brownian motion $B_{0}B(t)$ converges weakly to a deterministic measure $\mu_{b_{0},t}$ (see Definition 1.7 and Section 2 below).

If $B_{0}$ is a normal matrix, the $\ast$ -distribution convergence criterion simply means that the empirical eigenvalue distribution of $B_{0}$ converges weakly a.s. to some deterministic probability measure on $\mathbb{C}$ .

When $B_{0}$ is not normal, as discussed in the last two paragraphs before Subsection 1.1, convergence in $\ast$ -distribution does not generally imply convergence of eigenvalues. Thus, our theorem implies that multiplying a matrix by a multiplicative Brownian (at any time $t>0$ ) has a regularizing effect on its empirical measure which simplifies considerably the proof of its convergence. Theorem 1.2 thus provides a multiplicative analogue of a well-known result of Sniady [101]; see Section 1.7 for further discussion.

### 1.4. Ideas of the Proof

In this work we develop a robust approach to convergence of the spectrum of non-normal matrix diffusions based on strong quantitative approximation by multiplicative random walks. Potential future applications of this strategy are discussed in Section 1.7.

As in most works on the spectrum of non-normal random matrices, we apply Girko’s Hermitization framework, reviewed in Section 1.6, which reduces our task to establishing sufficient control on small-to-mesoscopic scale singular values of $B_{0}B(t)-zI$ , for a.e. $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , to guarantee convergence of the log potential. This is often the most challenging step for proofs of convergence of the spectrum of non-normal matrices, and amounts to proving stability of the spectrum under small perturbations. Recall that the singular values of an $N\times N$ matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{\ast}A$ , or equivalently the eigenvalues of $|A|=\sqrt{A^{\ast}A}$ ; they are denoted

$$ \|A\|=\sigma_{1}(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{N}(A)\geq 0. $$

Note that $\sigma_{N}(A)=\|A^{-1}\|^{-1}$ if $A$ is invertible and $\sigma_{N}(A)=0$ otherwise, so bounding small singular values of $B_{0}B(t)-zI$ from below is equivalent to bounding large singular values of the resolvent $(B_{0}B(t)-zI)^{-1}$ from above.

Perhaps the most well-known quantification of spectral (in)stability of a matrix is by its pseudospectrum. Recall that the $\varepsilon$ -pseudospectrum of $A\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ is the set of points $z\in\mathbb{C}$ at which the resolvent has norm at least $1/\varepsilon$ , or equivalently $\sigma_{N}(A-zI)\leq\varepsilon$ . We refer to the beautiful text [107] for a comprehensive review of pseudospectrum and its relevance for numerical analysis. Implementing Girko’s framework requires showing that (almost) any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ is unlikely to be in the $\varepsilon$ -pseudospectrum of $B_{0}B(t)$ for $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{N}$ not shrinking too fast (a polynomial decay will suffice); but further requires strong lower bounds on the $k$ th smallest singular value of $B_{0}B(t)$ for all $k=o(N)$ .

The key tool we develop for these tasks is a small-time affine approximation of the process $B$ , given in Theorem 1.3, which in turn is established using an approximation of the process $B(t)$ by a discrete-time multiplicative random walk.

#### 1.4.1. Random walk approximation

As shown by Berger in [16], Brownian motion $B$ (1.4) on a matrix Lie group is well approximated by a Donsker-like multiplicative random walk:

$$ B(t)\approx B_{n}(t):=\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\left(I+W(\textstyle{\frac{i}{2^{n}}})-W(\textstyle{\frac{i-1}{2^{n}}})+\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\Xi\right). $$

We prove (in the case of interest, $B=B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ where $\Xi=\zeta I$ ) a quantitative $L^{p}$ version of Berger’s theorem: for any fixed $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \|B(t)-B_{n}(t)\|_{p}:=(\mathbb{E}\ts(|B(t)-B_{n}(t)|^{p}))^{1/p}\leq C_{n,t,p}2^{-n/2p} $$

where the constant $C_{n,t,p}$ is independent of $N$ and locally uniform in $t$ (see Proposition 4.1). Here, the trace is normalized to take value 1 at the identity, and for a matrix $A$ we write $|A|:=(A^{*}A)^{1/2}$ . The main step for (1.14) is to show $B_{n}(t)$ is Cauchy in $L^{2}$ , which we do using Gaussian integration by parts (also known in this context as the Schwinger–Dyson equation – see Proposition 3.16).

#### 1.4.2. Affine approximation

The following is the core technical result of the paper, and our main tool for controlling small singular values of scalar shifts $B(t)-zI$ of the process $B$ . It shows that over a small time increment, the multiplicative process $B$ is well approximated by an additive Gaussian elliptical perturbation of the identity.

#### Theorem 1.3 (Small-time affine approximation).

For any finite $T$ there exists $C=C_{\varrho,T}<\infty$ so that, for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $\delta>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\left\|B(t)-I-W(t)\right\|\geq\delta\right)\leq\left(\frac{Ct}{\delta}\right)^{N^{2/3}}. $$

In other words, we have $B(t)=I+W(t)+E(t)$ , for an error $E(t)$ bounded in operator norm by $\mathcal{O}(t)$ with overwhelming probability for any fixed $t\leq 1$ , say. For comparison, note that $W(t)$ typically has norm of order $\sqrt{t}$ . For the purposes of proving Theorem 1.2 a bound $\|E(t)\|=\mathcal{O}(t^{1/2+c})$ would suffice for any positive constant $c$ , but Theorem 1.3 captures the correct order in $t$ of the norm (as can be seen by computing the expected squared Frobenius norm of $B(t)-I-W(t)$ ). Note that from (1.3) it is intuitive that $B(t)\approx I+W(t)$ for small $t$ ; the point of Theorem 1.3 is get an effective bound that is independent of $N$ .

By the moment method, to establish Theorem 1.3 it suffices to show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{tr}\left(|B(t)-I-W(t)|^{2k}\right)\right]\leq\mathcal{O}(t)^{2k} $$

for $k$ of order $N^{2/3}$ , where the implicit constant depends only on $\varrho,T$ . From the $L^{p}$ approximation (1.14) with $p=2k$ we can replace $B(t)$ with $B_{n}(t)$ in (1.15). As $B_{n}(t)$ is a polynomial in the increments $W(\frac{i}{2^{n}})-W(\frac{i-1}{2^{n}})$ , which in turn are combinations of GUE matrices (see (1.10)), the problem is reduced to bounding

$$ \mathbb{E}\ts Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N})\leq\mathcal{O}(t)^{2k} $$

where $\boldsymbol{X}^{N}=(X^{N}_{i})_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N}=(Y^{N}_{i})_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}$ are independent sequences of independent GUE matrices, and $Q$ is a non-commutative polynomial of degree $2k\times\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor$ .

To bound the left hand side of (1.16), we use a quantitative expansion of the expected trace in powers of $\frac{1}{N^{2}}$ :

$$ \mathbb{E}\ts Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N})=\sum_{q=0}^{r-1}\frac{\alpha_{q}}{N^{2q}}+\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{r}^{N}}{N^{2r}}. $$

In the case that $Q$ is a monomial, this expansion coincides with the genus expansion which appeared first in [25]. In that case, $\alpha_{q}$ is a positive integer, and represents a count of certain colored maps on a surface of genus $2q$ ; see [60] for more general development. This combinatorial description is not very useful for quantitative computations: beyond $r=1$ there are are no known formulas or even reasonable bounds. Recently, a more analytic approach to the expansion was introduced in [37] (in the case $r=1$ ) and fully developed in [94]. The core idea is to work in a space where the GUE matrices $\boldsymbol{X}^{N},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N}$ and their free probability limit operators $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}$ coexist, and then interpolate between them using Ornstein–Uhlenbeck type processes. By differentiating along two subsequent interpolations, using the Schwinger–Dyson equations and Gaussian integration by parts, the $r=1$ term appears; the procedure can be iterated $r$ times to achieve the full expansion. See Section 3.3 for a more detailed explanation of the method.

Following this approach, the coefficients $\alpha_{q}$ have explicit (though complicated) expressions in terms of iterated applications of a certain differential operator $L$ (the composition of the generators of the two interpolations) to the polynomial $Q$ , evaluated at the limit semicircular variables; the remainder coefficient $\tilde{\alpha}_{r}^{N}$ is similar, involving an extended system of GUE matrices. See Lemma 3.21 for the full technical result, which allows for effective estimation. In our setting, we will use Lemma 3.21 to show $\mathbb{E}\tr Q(X^{N},Y^{N})=\mathcal{O}(t)^{2k}\exp(\mathcal{O}(k^{4}/N^{2}))$ with implicit constants depending only on $\varrho,T$ , giving the desired estimate (1.16) for $k\sim N^{2/3}$ .

We note that a different matrix-to-free interpolation was also used in the recent paper [11] to study $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motions; this approach does not allow simultaneous consideration of $B(t)$ and $W(t)$ and therefore does not suit our needs. Moreover, the overarching strategy used in [11] (i.e. studying the expectation of traces of a smooth function evaluated in random matrices to deduce $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{N^{2}})$ fluctuations), while effective to prove strong convergence, is not sufficiently sharp to obtain the fine-scale concentration estimates on the norm that are needed for our main results. We believe our strategy of expressing $B(t)$ and $W(t)$ jointly in terms of small increments of the driving process $W$ provides a general approach for analyzing the spectrum of matrix SDE – see Section 1.7 for further discussion.

#### 1.4.3. Application to small singular values

To control the small singular values of scalar shifts $B_{0}B(t)-zI$ we use Theorem 1.3 in conjunction with the following observation. If $B$ and $\widetilde{B}$ are independent $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motions then, for any $t>0$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,t)$ , $B(t-\varepsilon)\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)$ has the same law as $B(t)$ . From Theorem 1.3,

$$ \widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)\approx I+W(\varepsilon) $$

for small $\varepsilon$ , and hence $B(t)\approx B(t-\varepsilon)(I+W(\varepsilon))$ . The robust behavior of singular values of the elliptical Ginibre matrix $W(\varepsilon)$ can thence be parlayed into good behavior of singular values for $B_{0}B(t)-zI$ . We note that the basic strategy of exploiting more tractable randomness in the Lie algebra was brilliantly used in [98] to bound the smallest singular value of Haar unitary/orthogonal perturbations of arbitrary matrices. In that argument the analogue of the step (1.18) is elementary, whereas here we rely on Theorem 1.3, the key technical innovation of this work.

Apart from a lower bound on the smallest singular value $\sigma_{N}(B_{0}B(t)-zI)$ , we need lower bounds on “mesoscopic” singular values $\sigma_{N-k}(B_{0}B(t)-zI)$ for $k\in[N^{1-c},\kappa N]$ for some small fixed $c,\kappa>0$ . The most common approach in the literature is to deduce these from upper bounds on the Stieltjes transform of the empirical singular value distribution $\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-zI|}$ ; see for instance [9, 61, 103, 58, 38]. Indeed, this was the route taken in [58] for the proof of the Single Ring Theorem, where bounds on the Stieltjes transform were obtained via a quantitative analysis of the Schwinger–Dyson loop equations. Here we take a more flexible approach pioneered by Tao and Vu in their proof of the Circular Law under the optimal finite second moment hypothesis [104]. The argument makes use of the inverse second moment identity (see (A.12)) to pass to a problem on the concentration of distances of columns to the span of remaining columns for arbitrary shifts $M+W(\varepsilon)$ of the elliptical Gaussian matrix $W(\varepsilon)$ . While such estimates are standard for the case that $W$ is real or complex Ginibre, or $W$ is GO/UE and $M$ is Hermitian (see Appendix A for review of the literature), the case that $W$ is GUE and $M$ is arbitrary (and possibly non-normal) appears to be new – see Lemmas A.1, A.6.

We use this framework to prove Propositions 5.1 and 5.2, which give quantitative lower bounds on the singular values of arbitrary shifts of $B(t)$ , holding with high probability.

In Section 6 we provide an alternative argument to bound mesoscopic singular values by the Stieltjes transform approach, which may be of independent interest. Using the interpolation method of Section 4 we can pass to the Stieltjes transform of the $*$ -distribution limit $|b(t)-z|$ (see Section 1.5) to which we can apply the delicate SDE and PDE methods developed in [48], whereby regularity properties for the Stieltjes transform are obtained from analysis of characteristic curves for a Hamilton–Jacobi-type PDE for a regularization of the log-potential. The resulting Corollary 6.2 is incomparable to Proposition 5.2: the former controls $\sigma_{N-k}(B(t)-zI)$ for $k$ of order at least $N^{9/11}$ , whereas the latter permits $k$ of order $\log N$ . On the other hand, Corollary 6.2 gives lower bounds of the correct shape $\sigma_{N-k}(B(t)-zI)\gtrsim k/N$ , whereas the bound $\gtrsim(k/N)^{2}$ of Proposition 5.2, while sufficient to establish Theorem 1.2, is not sharp.

Finally, in Section 7 we use our regularity estimates on small and mesoscopic shifted singular values to prove the requisite convergence in Theorem 1.2; see also Section 1.6 for a bigger picture discussion of the Hermitization method.

### 1.5. Free Multiplicative Brownian Motions

To fully describe the deterministic limit density of eigenvalues in Theorem 1.2, we need some constructs and tools from free probability theory; see Section 3.1 for a brief primer and references.

The Brownian motion $B=B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ (1.12) on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ is driven by the elliptical Brownian motion $W=W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ (1.10), which is constructed from a pair $X,Y$ of independent Hermitian Brownian motions in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ (Definition 3.7). These processes have a large- $N$ limit. Let $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ be a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space that supports two freely independent free semicircular Brownian motions $x,y$ (Definitions 3.3 and 3.6). Voiculescu showed [111] that $\left(X,Y\right)$ converges a.s. in finite dimensional $\ast$ -distributions to $(x,y)$ as $N\to\infty$ . In particular,

$$ w_{\varrho,\zeta}=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(ax+\mathbf{i}by) $$

is a free stochastic process in $\mathscr{A}$ that is the a.s. large- $N$ limit in finite dimensional $\ast$ -distributions of $W_{\varrho,\zeta}=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(aX+\mathbf{i}bY)$ ; here $(\varrho,\zeta)\leftrightsquigarrow(\theta,a,b)$ as in (1.11). The process $w_{\varrho,\zeta}$ is a non-commutative martingale [72],so stochastic integrals and quadratic covariation may be treated analogously to the classical setting. In particular, the free Itô equation

$$ b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)=1+\int_{0}^{t}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)\,dw_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)\,ds $$

has a unique solution in $\mathscr{A}$ for all $t\geq 0$ , see [18, 74]. The original free multiplicative Brownian motion introduced by Biane in [19, 20] is the special case $(\varrho,\zeta)=(1,0)$ , while the free unitary Brownian motion is the edge case $(\varrho,\zeta)=(1,-1)$ . The two-parameter family introduced in [76] corresponds to $b_{\varrho,\zeta}$ with $\zeta\in(-\varrho,\varrho)$ (i.e. real $\zeta$ ). The fully complex parameter $\zeta$ with $|\zeta|<\varrho$ was later introduced in [47] in the context of heat kernel analysis on compact type Lie groups (notably the question of when the heat kernel can be complexified in both space and time). The three-parameter families of free stochastic processes $w_{\varrho,\zeta}$ and $b_{\varrho,\zeta}$ , including the degenerate cases $|\zeta|=\varrho$ , were studied extensively in [63, 62], as strong limits in [11], and most recently in terms of general additive perturbations of $w_{\varrho,\zeta}$ in [116].

#### Notation 1.4.

As with the matrix-valued processes $W=W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ and $B=B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ , we generally suppress the explicit dependence of the notation for the Brownian motion processes on the parameters $(\varrho,\zeta)$ , and define

$$ \displaystyle w_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)=:w(t)\qquad\;\;b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)=:b(t). $$

The following lemma guides our aim to describe the large- $N$ limit distribution $\mu_{b_{0},t}$ of eigenvalues of $B(t)$ in Theorem 1.2.

#### Lemma 1.5.

Let $\varrho>0$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ , and let $B$ be a $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ . Let $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ be a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space that contains a free multiplicative $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motion $b$ , and let $b_{0}$ be an operator in $\mathscr{A}$ that is freely independent from $b$ .

Let $B_{0}=B_{0}^{N}$ be a sequence of random matrices in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ independent from the process $B$ such that $B_{0}$ converges a.s. in $\ast$ -distribution to $b_{0}$ as $N\to\infty$ .

Then for any $t\geq 0$ , $B_{0}B(t)$ converges in $\ast$ -distribution to $b_{0}b(t)$ a.s.

Under the additional assumption that $B_{0}$ converges strongly to $b_{0}$ (see Definition 3.2), the recent paper [11] proved Lemma 1.5 with the stronger conclusion of strong convergence. Lemma 1.5 is proved in Section 3.2.

### 1.6. Singular Values, Eigenvalues, and Hermitization

Lemma 1.5 suggests that the large- $N$ limit $\mu_{b_{0},t}$ of the empirical law of eigenvalues of $B_{0}B(t)$ is connected to the free multiplicative Brownian motion $b_{0}b(t)$ . That connection is through Brown measure.

#### Definition 1.6.

Let $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ be a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space, and let $a\in\mathscr{A}$ (just $L^{2}(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ suffices). Then $a^{\ast}a=|a|^{2}$ is selfadjoint, and so has a spectral measure $\mu_{|a|^{2}}$ : the unique compactly-supported probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ whose moments are given by $\int x^{k}\mu_{|a|^{2}}(dx)=\tau[(a^{\ast}a)^{k}]$ (see (3.1)). Denote by $\nu_{a}$ the push-forward of $\mu_{|a|^{2}}$ under $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$ ; in other words, $\nu_{a}$ is the spectral measure of $|a|:=\sqrt{a^{\ast}a}$ .

For $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , define the log potential $U_{a}\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ by

$$ U_{a}(z):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\log(x)\,\nu_{a-z}(dx). $$

It is a subharmonic function, and so its (weak) Laplacian is a positive Radon measure. In this case it is a probability measure: the Brown measure of $a$

$$ \mu_{a}:=\Delta U_{a}\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\int_{\mathbb{C}}\psi\,d\mu_{a}=\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta\psi(z)\,U_{a}(z)\,dz\qquad\forall\,\psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{C}). $$

The Brown measure is then also uniquely defined by

$$ \int_{\mathbb{C}}\log|\lambda-z|\,\mu_{a}(d\lambda)=U_{a}(z). $$

The measure $\mu_{a}$ was introduced by Brown in [26]. We use the same notation $\mu_{a}$ for Brown measure as for spectral measure because if $a$ is normal then its Brown measure is its spectral measure.

Brown measure is closely related to the Hermitization procedure invented by Girko [54] for studying eigenvalues of non-normal random matrices. Indeed, in the $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}),\ts)$ , the Brown measure is exactly the empirical law of eigenvalues. To see why, note that for $A\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , the eigenvalues of $|A|=\sqrt{A^{\ast}A}$ are the singular values $\sigma_{j}(A)$ of $A$ , and hence $\nu_{A}$ is the empirical law of singular values. But then

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}\log(x)\,\nu_{A-zI}(dx)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\log\sigma_{j}(A-zI)=\frac{1}{N}\log\det[|A-zI|]. $$

But $\log\det[|A-zI|]=\frac{1}{2}\log\det[|A-zI|^{2}]=\log|\det[A-zI]|$ , and hence

$$ \frac{1}{N}\log\det[|A-zI|]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\log|z-\lambda_{j}(A)| $$

where $\lambda_{j}(A)$ are the eigenvalues of $A$ . The (weak) Laplacian of this is indeed the empirical law of eigenvalues (1.13).

The log potential $U_{A}$ is locally uniformly integrable in $z$ , with universal bounds independent of $A$ ; hence, proving a sequence of Brown measures $\mu_{A^{N}}$ converges weakly to a Brown measure $\mu_{a}$ is tantamount to proving pointwise convergence of the log potentials: $U_{A^{N}}(z)\to U_{a}(z)$ for a.e. $z\in\mathbb{C}$ . From Definition 1.6, this means the goal is to prove

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\log\,d\nu_{A^{N}-zI}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\log\,d\nu_{a-z}\quad\text{for a.e. }z\in\mathbb{C}. $$

Equation (1.21) had the flavor of weak convergence, but the test function $\log$ is neither bounded nor continuous near $0$ and $\infty$ . Hence, to prove convergence of the ESD (i.e. Brown measure) of a random matrix ensemble $A^{N}\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ to the Brown measure of an operator $a\in\mathscr{A}$ , it is necessary to show not only that the the measure $\nu_{A^{N}-zI}$ (empirical law of singular values of $A-zI$ ) converges weakly to $\nu_{a-z}$ ; one must also show that mass does not escape at $0$ or $\infty$ – i.e. uniform integrability of $\log$ with respect to the measures $\{\nu_{A^{N}-zI}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ . Proving small singular values of $A-zI$ don’t concentrate and decay too fast can be quite subtle, and can fail even in some simple examples, cf. [21, Example 1.2].

After Girko [54] presented the above method for handling eigenvalues of non-normal random matrix ensembles (in particular i.i.d. matrices and the circular law), it took more than 25 years for his program to reach full fruition, with the first major breakthrough by Bai [9] requiring the law of each entry of $A^{N}$ to have a bounded density on $\mathbb{C}$ and more than $6$ finite moments. Numerous improvements over the following decade culminated with Tao and Vu’s full proof [104].

The same Hermitization roadmap has been used for various generalizations of the Circular Law (see the excellent survey [21] for an extensive summary of work up to $\sim$ 2011), the much larger class of “Single Ring” ensembles (that are unitarily bi-invariant) [58, 14] and generalizations, e.g. [15, 12, 69], the elliptic law [85], inhomogeneous circular laws [39, 40, 2, 3], local circular laws [22], polynomials of independent matrices [90, 89, 55, 38, 66], sparse directed graphs [41, 13, 81, 99] and (related to the present work) very general matrix random walks with unitarily bi-invariant increments [44].

Our present interest is in Brownian motion $B_{0}B(t)$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ . For these ensembles, weak convergence of empirical singular values $\nu_{B_{0}B(t)-zI}$ to $\nu_{b_{0}b(t)-z}$ follows directly from Lemma 1.5. Theorem 1.2, via Theorem 1.3, completes the rest of the Hermitization procedure. In particular, we can now clarify:

#### Definition 1.7.

The deterministic measure $\mu_{b_{0},t}$ in Theorem 1.2 is the Brown measure of the operator $b_{0}b(t)$ . In particular: Theorem 1.2 asserts that the empirical spectral distribution of $B_{0}B(t)$ converges weakly a.s. to the Brown measure of $b_{0}b(t)$ .

### 1.7. Directions for Future Work

The tools developed in this paper open the door to a more general study of the spectrum of continuous-time non-normal matrix processes and refined properties of the spectrum.

#### 1.7.1. Other matrix diffusion processes

The methods we develop for Theorem 1.2 are not intrinsically tied to diffusion processes on Lie groups. Consider a general matrix diffusion processes of the form $dM(t)=\sigma(M(t))dW(t)+b(M(t))dt$ for sufficiently nice matrix-valued drift and diffusion functions $\sigma,b$ , or more generally

$$ dM(t)=\sigma(M(t))\#dW(t)+b(M(t))\,dt $$

where $\sigma\colon\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ and $(A\otimes B)\#X=AXB$ . Under appropriate regularity assumptions, we may seek a version of Theorem 1.3 to locally approximate the process in terms of an increment of the standard Brownian motion $W(t)\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , which is enough to regularize the spectrum and establish convergence to the Brown measure.

#### 1.7.2. Regularization of Brown’s spectral measure

A well-known result of Sniady (see [101, Theorem 6]) states that if $B_{0}=B_{0}^{N}$ is a sequence of random matrices converging almost surely in $*$ -distribution to an operator $b_{0}$ , and $W(t)=W^{N}(t)$ is (additive) Ginibre Brownian motion independent from $B_{0}$ , then for every fixed $t>0$ , $\mu_{B_{0}+W(t)}$ converges weakly to the Brown measure $\mu_{b_{0}+w(t)}$ , and moreover, there exists a sequence $t_{N}\to 0$ such that $\mu_{B_{0}+W(t_{N})}\to\mu_{b_{0}}$ weakly almost surely. The speed at which $t_{N}$ may vanish and its dependence on the initial condition $B_{0}$ was investigated in [59, 52]. Our main result Theorem 1.2 establishes a multiplicative version of the first half of Sniady’s result concerning fixed $t>0$ . It is natural to pursue an analogue of the second half: Does there exist a sequence $t_{N}\to 0$ such that $\mu_{B_{0}B(t_{N})}\to\mu_{b_{0}}$ weakly almost surely? How does the allowable speed of vanishing of $t_{N}$ depend on the initial condition?

#### 1.7.3. Path properties

Consider the empirical laws $\mu_{t}^{N}=\mu_{B_{0}B(t)}$ as a stochastic process $(\mu_{t}^{N})_{t\geq 0}$ taking values in the Polish space $\mathcal{M}_{1}(\mathbb{C})$ of probability measures on $\mathbb{C}$ with the topology of weak convergence. Theorem 1.2 immediately implies a.s. convergence of finite dimensional marginals of this process, i.e. for fixed times $0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}$ , $(\mu^{N}_{t_{1}},\dots,\mu^{N}_{t_{n}})$ converges almost surely in the product weak topology on $\mathcal{M}_{1}(\mathbb{C})^{n}$ to the deterministic vector $(\mu_{b_{0}b(t_{1})},\dots,\mu_{b_{0}b(t_{n})})$ . (In fact we can take any countable sequence of times.) Does the random curve $(\mu_{t}^{N})_{t>0}$ in $\mathcal{M}_{1}(\mathbb{C})$ almost surely converge locally uniformly to the deterministic curve $(\mu_{b_{0}b(t)})_{t>0}$ ?

#### 1.7.4. Local universality

Beyond the limiting law for the global spectral distribution, the Hermitization approach and control of the pseudospectrum provides a route to prove universality at mesoscopic and local spectral scales. In particular, a local law should hold, showing the empirical law $\mu_{B_{0}B(t)}$ is well approximated by the limit $\mu_{b_{0},t}$ at scales down to $N^{o(1)-\frac{1}{2}}$ ; such a result was established for matrices with i.i.d. entries in [105, 22]. At the scale $N^{-1/2}$ of the typical separation of eigenvalues we expect rescaled correlation functions to converge to universal determinantal point processes, with Ginibre kernel in the bulk and Faddeeva kernel at smooth points of the boundary of the support; for related results see [105, 29, 88, 50] for i.i.d. matrices and [17, 67] for normal matrix ensembles. The current understanding of point processes of eigenvalues in the vicinity of singular boundary points – such as at $z=-1$ for the Lima Bean Law at time $t=4$ (see middle of Figure 1) – is incomplete even for additive Ginibre Brownian motion $B_{0}+W(t)$ . The possible behaviors of the limiting spectral density of $B_{0}+W(t)$ near singular boundary points was classified in [51, 4], and universality (allowing $W$ to have non-Gaussian entries) for local eigenvalue statistics near such points was established in [33], assuming $B_{0}$ is normal; the correlation functions themselves have only been computed for certain initial conditions $B_{0}$ [27, 82]. See also recent works [5, 28] on lemniscate-type normal matrix ensembles. Whether the classification of singular boundary points and universal correlation functions carry over to multiplicative Brownian motion $B_{0}B(t)$ , with $B_{0}$ possibly non-normal, are open questions.

## 2. The Brown(ian) Measure

In studying the bulk limits of eigenvalues of non-normal random matrix ensembles, there are two fundamental (challenging) problems: identifying the (putative) limit measure, and proving convergence to it. In this paper, we solve the convergence problem: Theorem 1.2 proves that the empirical law of eigenvalues of Brownian motion $B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ with any initial state $B_{0}$ possessing a large- $N$ limit $b_{0}$ converges to an identifiable deterministic measure: the Brown measure of the operator $b_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ . The former problem of identifying those Brown measures has been well studied in the past five years, see [48, 68, 63, 42, 65, 62]. These papers succeeded in computing the Brown measure precisely for general $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ and any unitary $b_{0}$ , along with some partial results for positive definite $b_{0}$ , using stochastic, complex analytic, and PDE methods.

In this section, we briefly summarize known results about these Brown measures (all from 2022 or later), with some pictures of their support sets with simulations of eigenvalues of the associated Brownian motions for fairly large $N$ . Given the now known (thanks to Theorem 1.2) robust connection to the eigenvalues, the simulations are suggestive of the more general picture of the support of the Brown measure for general initial conditions.

We begin with the case of the “standard” free multiplicative Brownian motion $b_{1,0}$ , with unitary initial condition $b_{0}=u_{0}$ . The computation of the Brown measure with $b_{0}=1$ was initially accomplished by Driver–Hall–Kemp in [48], and then extended to include unitary initial conditions by Ho–Zhong in [68].

#### Theorem 2.1 ([48],[68]).

Let $b_{0,1}(t)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion, and let $u_{0}$ be a unitary operator freely independent from $b_{0,1}$ . Denote by $\mu_{u_{0}}$ the spectral measure of $u_{0}$ , a probability measure on the unit circle $\mathbb{T}$ .

Define $T(u_{0},\cdot)\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ by

$$ T(u_{0},z)=\frac{\log|z|^{2}}{|z|^{2}-1}\left(\int_{\mathbb{T}}\frac{\mu_{u_{0}}(d\xi)}{|\xi-z|^{2}}\right)^{-1}. $$

Also, for each $t>0$ , define the open precompact set $\Sigma(u_{0},t)$ by

$$ \Sigma(u_{0},t)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\colon T(u_{0},z)<t\}. $$

The Brown measure $\mu_{u_{0}b_{1,0}(t)}$ has support equal to $\overline{\Sigma(u_{0},t)}$ . The Brown measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and has density on $\overline{\Sigma(u_{0},t)}$ that is real analytic in $\Sigma(u_{0},t)$ . The density has the form $z=re^{i\theta}\mapsto w_{t}(\theta)/r^{2}$ , with the radial function $w_{t}$ bounded by $w_{t}(\theta)<\frac{1}{\pi t}$ .

Following this, in [63] Hall–Ho refined the PDE analysis from the above-mentioned papers to allow the Brownian motions $b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ from the full parameter range $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ .

#### Notation 2.2.

The laws of the random matrices $W_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ and $B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ are overparametrized. Since $(W(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is the same as the law of the process $(W(rt)/\sqrt{r})_{t\geq 0}$ for any $r>0$ , it follows that $W_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ (and consequently $B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ ) satisfy

$$ \displaystyle W_{\varrho,\zeta}(t) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}W_{t\varrho,t\zeta}(1)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}W_{1,\zeta/\varrho}(\varrho t) \displaystyle B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}B_{t\varrho,t\zeta}(1)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}B_{1,\zeta/\varrho}(\varrho t). $$

The same applies to the free limits $w_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ and $b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ .

[63, 62] elected to simplify parameters and only work with $b_{\varrho,\zeta}(1)$ ; we do the same for the remainder of this section. We also follow [63]’s convention and, in this parameter reduction, let $t$ play the role of $\varrho$ . Hence we treat the operators

$$ \displaystyle W(t,\zeta) \displaystyle:=W_{t,\zeta}(1)\qquad \displaystyle\qquad B(t,\zeta) \displaystyle:=B_{t,\zeta}(1) \displaystyle w(t,\zeta) \displaystyle:=w_{t,\zeta}(1)\qquad \displaystyle\qquad b(t,\zeta) \displaystyle:=b_{t,\zeta}(1). $$

Then the Brownian motion $u_{0}b_{1,0}(t)$ in Theorem 2.1 has the same law as

$$ u_{0}b_{1,0}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}u_{0}b(t,0). $$

For each $t>0$ and any $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq t$ , the Brown measure $\mu_{u_{0}b(t,\zeta)}$ is a push-forward of the Brown measure $\mu_{u_{0}b(t,0)}$ from Theorem 2.1 under a continuous map that is a diffeomorphism in the interior $\Sigma(u_{0},t)$ and a homeomorphism on the closure. To properly define this map, we introduce the following analytic transform: for any operator $a$ in a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space, define

$$ J_{a}(z)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\frac{\xi+z}{\xi-z}\,\mu_{a}(\xi) $$

where $\mu_{a}$ is the Brown measure of $a$ . This integral defines a conformal map on the complement of $\supp\mu_{a}$ ; on this region, it can be written in the form $J_{a}(z)=\frac{1}{2}\tau[(a+z)(a-z)^{-1}]$ . The integral (2.4) may be well defined for (some) $z$ in the support of $\mu_{a}$ , as will be the case relevant to the following theorem.

#### Theorem 2.3 ([63, 62]).

Let $t>0$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq t$ (but $\zeta\neq-t$ , which is the unitary Brownian motion). Let $b(t,\zeta)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion (see Notation 2.2) and let $u_{0}$ be a unitary operator freely independent from $b(t,\zeta)$ . Define the map $\Psi^{u_{0}}_{t,\zeta}$ by

$$ \Psi^{u_{0}}_{t,\zeta}(z)=z\exp\{\zeta J_{u_{0}b(t,0)}(z)\}. $$

This map is continuous on $\mathbb{C}$ . Restricted to $\Sigma(u_{0},t)$ , it is a diffeomorphism onto its image, an open set we denote $\Sigma(u_{0},t,\zeta)$ . The map $\Psi^{u_{0}}_{t,\zeta}$ is a homeomorphism from the closure of $\Sigma(u_{0},t)$ onto the closure of $\Sigma(u_{0},t,\zeta)$ , and is a conformal map between the complements of these closures.

The Brown measure of $u_{0}b(t,\zeta)$ is the push-forward under $\Psi^{u_{0}}_{t,\zeta}$ of the Brown measure of $u_{0}b(t,0)$ (from Theorem 2.1). Its support is $\overline{\Sigma(u_{0},t,\zeta)}$ , and it has a smooth density on its support.

One key feature of Theorem 2.3 which explains the parameter choices is that, for fixed $t>0$ , the support regions $\{\Sigma(u_{0},t,\zeta)\colon|\zeta|\leq t\}$ are all diffeomorphic to the region $\Sigma(u_{0},t)$ from the standard Brownian motion $u_{0}b(t,0)$ . I.e. the topology of the domain where the eigenvalues cluster can change with $t$ , while $\zeta$ is a deformation parameter that does not change the topology of the support set.

Finally, moving beyond the case of unitary initial conditions, the papers [42, 65] use a related but qualitatively different PDE approach to analyze the support of the Brown measure of $b_{0}b(t,\zeta)$ in the case that $b_{0}$ is a positive definite operator. In [42], Demni–Hamdi considered the case $\zeta=0$ and restricted $b_{0}$ to be a projection; refining those ideas, Eaknipitsari–Hall [65] considered general $b(t,\zeta)$ and general positive definite $b_{0}$ . The formulas and techniques in the latter paper are not particularly specific to the positive case, and so we state the results as a special case of a conjecture.

#### Conjecture 2.4 ([65]).

Let $b_{0}$ be an invertible operator in a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ . Define

$$ \tilde{p}_{0}(z)=\tau[|b_{0}-z|^{-2}]\qquad\&\qquad\tilde{p}_{2}(z)=\tau[b_{0}^{\ast}b_{0}|b_{0}-z|^{-2}] $$

where, as usual, for any operator $a\in\mathscr{A}$ , $|a|^{2}:=a^{\ast}a$ . Define $T(b_{0},\cdot)\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ by

$$ T(b_{0},z)=\frac{\log(\tilde{p}_{2}(z))-\log(|z|^{2}\tilde{p}_{0}(z))}{\tilde{p}_{2}(z)-|z|^{2}\tilde{p}_{0}(z)}. $$

For each $t>0$ , define the open precompact set $\Sigma(b_{0},t)$ by

$$ \Sigma(b_{0},t)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\colon T(b_{0},z)<t\}. $$

Let $b(t,\zeta)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion (see Notation 2.2) freely independent from $b_{0}$ . Then the support of the Brown measure of $b_{0}b(t,\zeta)$ is equal to the image $\overline{\Sigma(b_{0},t,\zeta)}$ of $\overline{\Sigma(b_{0},t)}$ under the map $\Psi^{b_{0}}_{t,\zeta}$ of (2.5).

The expression 2.7 is defined by limits if any of the terms diverge. The quantities $\tilde{p}_{0}(z)$ and $\tilde{p}_{2}(z)$ are positive but possibly infinite; if one is infinite, a calculus exercise shows that $T(b_{0},z)=0$ , meaning that $z\in\Sigma(b_{0},t)$ for all $t>0$ .

If $b_{0}$ is unitary then $\tilde{p}_{2}(z)=\tilde{p}_{0}(z)$ , and (2.6) reduces (2.1); so Conjecture 2.4 follows from Theorem 2.3 in the case of a unitary initial condition. In [65], the authors considered the case that $b_{0}>0$ (i.e. positive definite), and the conjecture was half proved in that case: $\supp\mu_{b_{0}b(\varrho,\zeta)}$ was shown to be contained in $\overline{\Sigma(b_{0},\varrho,\zeta)}$ (with an exception at $0$ ). The obstructions to extending this containment to more general initial conditions were technical, and it is natural to expect it to hold true in full generality.
