## 3. Preliminaries and Background

### 3.1. Basic Constructions from Free Probability

We begin by reviewing the following definitions and basic results from non-commutative (and especially free) probability.

The basic arena is a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space: a pair $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ consisting of a von Neumann algebra $\mathscr{A}$ (a $\ast$ -algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space, that is closed under the weak operator topology), and $\tau\colon\mathscr{A}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a tracial ( $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ ) state ( $\tau(1_{\mathscr{A}})=1$ ) that is faithful ( $\tau(a^{\ast}a)=0$ iff $a=0$ ) and $\sigma$ -weakly continuous. The core motivating example is $\mathscr{A}=L^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\mathbb{P})$ , the algebra of bounded random variables on a probability space, with $\tau=\mathbb{E}$ the expectation with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ . Indeed, all commutative $W^{\ast}$ -probability spaces have this form; the general $\sigma$ -weak continuity assumption is in place precisely to verify the Dominated Convergence Theorem in general.

More relevant to us presently is the example $(\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}),\ts_{N})$ : the algebra of $N\times N$ complex matrices equipped with the normalized trace $\ts_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\tr_{N}$ , with the usual matrix trace $\tr_{N}[A]=\sum_{j=1}^{N}A_{jj}$ . We will also frequently consider the “product” of these two examples: the algebra $L^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\mathbb{P};\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}))$ of random matrices (with bounded entries), equipped with the expected normalized trace $\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}$ – or, when relevant, we use only the trace $\ts_{N}$ (in which case $\ts_{N}[A]$ is $\mathbb{C}$ -valued random variable rather than just a scalar).

Not content to always insist on bounded random variables, we can generally extend a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space to include random variables with $p$ finite moments. For any $a\in\mathscr{A}$ , $a^{\ast}a$ is positive semidefinite and so the Spectral Theorem can be used to define $|a|^{p}:=(a^{\ast}a)^{p/2}$ . The $L^{p}$ -norm is then defined

$$ \left\|a\right\|_{p}:=\left(\tau[|a|^{p}]\right)^{1/p},\qquad 1\leq p<\infty. $$

The usual convexity proof demonstrates the triangle inequality, and the faithfulness of $\tau$ means it is a genuine norm. The trace property implies that $\left\|a\right\|_{p}=\left\|a^{\ast}\right\|_{p}$ .

The non-commutative $L^{p}$ -space $L^{p}(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ is defined to be the closure of $\mathscr{A}$ in the norm $\left\|\,\cdot\,\right\|_{p}$ . The state $\tau$ satisfies $|\tau[a]|\leq\tau[|a|]$ , which means that it extends to a linear functional on $L^{1}(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ (which we also denote $\tau$ ). The $L^{p}$ -norms satisfy Hölder’s inequality: if $1<p<\infty$ and $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{\prime}}=1$ , then for $a\in L^{p}(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ and $b\in L^{p^{\prime}}(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ ,

$$ |\tau(ab)|\leq\|ab\|_{1}\leq\|a\|_{p}\|b\|_{p^{\prime}}. $$

In particular, since $\|1_{\mathscr{A}}\|_{p}=1$ for all $p$ , it follows that $\|a\|_{p}^{p}=\tau[|a|^{p}\cdot 1_{\mathscr{A}}]\leq\||a|^{p}\|_{r}\|1_{\mathscr{A}}\|_{r^{\prime}}=\|a\|_{pr}^{p}$ for $r\geq 1$ ; i.e. $p\mapsto\|a\|_{p}$ is increasing, so that $L^{p}(\mathscr{A},\tau)\subseteq L^{q}(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ for $q\leq p$ . Because $\tau$ is faithful, it follows that the operator norm on $\mathscr{A}$ satisfies $\|a\|=\lim_{p\to\infty}\|a\|_{p}$ ; so we may set $\|a\|_{\infty}:=\|a\|$ and extend Hölder’s inequality fully to $1\leq p\leq\infty$ , identifying $L^{\infty}(\mathscr{A},\tau)=\mathscr{A}$ .

We regard the elements of a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space as (generalized) random variables; as such, we must define their distributions. Classically, a (joint) probability distribution of random variables is determined by testing expectations of functions on them. Owing to the non-commutativity, the natural class of test functions readily available is non-commutative polynomials.

#### Notation 3.1.

We denote $\mathcal{P}_{d}=\mathbb{C}\langle X_{1},\dots,X_{d}\rangle$ the set of non-commutative polynomials in $d$ variables. In this paper, $X_{i}$ denote generic non-commuting indeterminates for polynomials. A given $P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ may be evaluated at a $d$ -duple $\boldsymbol{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{d})\in\mathscr{A}^{d}$ in $W^{*}$ -probability space $\mathscr{A}$ to produce a new element $P(\boldsymbol{a})\in\mathscr{A}$ .

#### Definition 3.2.

Let $\boldsymbol{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{d})$ be a $d$ -tuple of non-commutative random variables in some $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ . The $\ast$ -distribution of $\boldsymbol{a}$ is the linear functional $\mu_{\boldsymbol{a}}\colon\mathcal{P}_{2d}\to\mathbb{C}$ given by $P\mapsto\tau\left[P(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a}^{\ast})\right]$ .

If $(\mathscr{A}_{N},\tau_{N})$ is a sequence of $W^{\ast}$ -probability spaces for $N\geq 1$ , and $\boldsymbol{a}_{N}\in\mathscr{A}_{N}$ are $d$ -tuples, we say $\boldsymbol{a}_{N}$ converges in $\ast$ -distribution to $\boldsymbol{a}$ if the $\ast$ -distributions $\mu_{\boldsymbol{a}_{N}}$ converges pointwise to $\mu_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ ; i.e. if, for all $P\in\mathcal{P}_{2d}$

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\tau_{N}[P(\boldsymbol{a}_{N},\boldsymbol{a}_{N}^{\ast})]=\tau[P(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a}^{\ast})]. $$

We say that $\boldsymbol{a}_{N}$ converges strongly to $\boldsymbol{a}$ if, in addition to converging in $\ast$ -distribution, also

$$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\|P(\boldsymbol{a}_{N},\boldsymbol{a}_{N}^{\ast})\|=\|P(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{a}^{\ast})\|. $$

In this paper, Definition 3.2 will be used for the sequence of matrix $W^{\ast}$ -probability spaces, i.e. $(\mathscr{A}_{N},\tau_{N})=(\mathbb{M}_{N},\ts_{N})$ , typically with random elements. As such, the above notions of convergence must be applied randomly as well – in expectation, in probability, or almost surely (with the latter requiring that we sample all entries of all matrices in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ for all $N$ from a single probability space).

If $a\in\mathscr{A}$ is a single normal element, $aa^{\ast}=a^{\ast}a$ , and if $P\in\mathcal{P}_{2}$ , then $P(a,a^{\ast})$ reduces to a linear combination of monomials of the form $a^{n}a^{\ast m}$ . Since $a$ is bounded, there is a unique compactly-supported Borel probability measure $\mu_{a}$ on $\mathbb{C}$ determined by

$$ \tau[a^{n}a^{\ast m}]=\int\lambda^{n}\bar{\lambda}^{m}\,\mu_{a}(d\lambda). $$

The support of $\mu_{a}$ is precisely the spectrum $\sigma(a)$ , and thence the $\ast$ -distribution of $a$ is determined entirely by $\mu_{a}$ in the classical fashion:

$$ \tau[P(a,a^{\ast})]=\int_{\mathbb{C}}P(\lambda,\bar{\lambda})\,\mu_{a}(d\lambda). $$

This measure is called the spectral distribution of $a$ . In the particular case of a normal matrix $A\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , the spectral distribution is none other than the empirical law of eigenvalues

$$ \mu_{A}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{\lambda_{j}(A)}. $$

Note, however, that for non-normal $a$ , the $\ast$ -distribution is no longer encoded by a probability measure; similarly, for a tuple $\boldsymbol{a}$ of $\geq 2$ random variables that do not commute with each other, there is no reduction of the $\ast$ -distribution to a measure on $\mathbb{C}^{d}$ as occurs in the classical (commutative) case. The ESD (3.2) of course always exists, and more generally so does the Brown measure (also denoted $\mu_{a}$ ) introduced in Section 1.6. But the connections between $\mu_{a}$ and the $\ast$ -distribution of $a$ is tenuous at best when $a$ is not normal.

We now come to the framework that gives free probability its name.

#### Definition 3.3.

Let $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ be a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space, and let $\mathscr{A}_{1},\dots,\mathscr{A}_{n}$ be $*$ -subalgebras of $\mathscr{A}$ , sharing the same unit $1_{\mathscr{A}}$ . They are said to be freely independent or just free if, for all $k$ , for all $a_{i}\in\mathscr{A}_{j_{i}}$ such that $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$ , $j_{2}\neq j_{3}$ , …, $j_{k-1}\neq j_{k}$ :

$$ \tau\Big((a_{1}-\tau(a_{1}))(a_{2}-\tau(a_{2}))\dots(a_{k}-\tau(a_{k}))\Big)=0. $$

I.e. products of centered elements from adjacent-alternating algebras have trace $0$ . Families of non-commutative random variables are said to be free if the $*$ -subalgebras they generate are free.

Freeness does not occur in finite-dimensional matrix algebras, or classical $L^{\infty}$ probability settings, except in fairly degenerate settings (e.g. constants are always freely independent from all other random variables). However, a plethora of examples from random matrix theory exhibit asymptotic freeness, i.e. as dimensions of the matrices tend to $\infty$ , they become free. We state a classical example of this phenomenon below.

#### Definition 3.4.

A Haar Unitary Ensemble $U^{N}$ is a random $N\times N$ matrix whose distribution is the Haar measure on $\mathrm{U}(N)$ . In a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ , a Haar unitary operator $u\in\mathscr{A}$ is a unitary operator whose $\ast$ -distribution is determined by $\tau[u^{n}]=\tau[u^{\ast\,n}]=\delta_{n0}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ .

#### Proposition 3.5 ([110]; [102]).

Let $A_{0}^{N},A_{1}^{N}$ be random matrix ensembles, i.e. random elements in the $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}),\ts_{N})$ . Let $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ be a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space, with elements $a_{0},a_{1}\in\mathscr{A}$ such that $A_{0}^{N}\to a_{0}$ a.s. in $\ast$ -distribution and $A_{1}^{N}\to a_{1}$ a.s. in $\ast$ -distribution. For each $N\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $U^{N}$ be a Haar Unitary Ensemble independent from $\{A_{0}^{N},A_{1}^{N}\}$ , and let $u$ be a Haar unitary operator in $\mathscr{A}$ freely independent from $\{a_{0},a_{1}\}$ . Then $(A_{0}^{N},U^{N}A_{1}^{N}U^{N\,\ast})$ converges a.s. in joint $\ast$ -distribution to $(a_{0},ua_{1}u^{\ast})$ ; $ua_{1}u^{\ast}$ has the same distribution as $a_{1}$ ; and $a_{0},ua_{1}u^{\ast}$ are freeely independent. I.e. $A_{0}^{N}$ and $U^{N}A_{1}^{N}U^{N\,\ast}$ are a.s. asymptotically free.

Now we introduce important families of free random variables that are large- $N$ limits of Gaussian random matrix ensembles and stochastic processes.

#### Definition 3.6.

A family of non-commutative random variables $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})$ in a $W^{*}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ is called a free semicircular system if $x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}$ are freely independent, selfadjoint ( $x_{i}=x_{i}^{*}$ , $i=1\dots m$ ), and for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $i=1,\dots,m$ one has

$$ \tau(x_{i}^{k})=\int t^{k}\,\varsigma(dt), $$

with $\varsigma(dt)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-t^{2}}\ \mathbbm{1}_{|t|\leq 2}\,dt$ the semicircle distribution. For an explicit construction of such operators, we refer to [87, Lecture 7].

A free semicircular Brownian motion $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is a family of semicircular variables such that $x(t)/\sqrt{t}$ has the semicircle distribution for each $t>0$ , and the additive increments of $x$ are stationary and freely independent: for $0\leq t_{1}<t_{2}<\infty$ , $x(t_{2})-x(t_{1})$ has the same law as $x(t_{2}-t_{1})$ , and $x(t_{2})-x(t_{1})$ is freely independent from $(x(t))_{0\leq t\leq t_{1}}$ . See [18] for a detailed construction and properties.

We also review relevant classical random matrix models.

#### Definition 3.7.

A Hermitian Brownian motion $(X^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ of size $N$ is the Brownian motion on the vector space of Hermitian matrices in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , with respect to the scaled Hilbert–Schmidt inner product (1.8). Entry-wise, it can be described as follows:

- $\bullet$ For $1\leq i\leq N$ , the random variables $\{\sqrt{N}[X^{N}(t)]_{i,i}\}_{t\geq 0}$ are independent standard Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$ .

- $\bullet$ For $1\leq i<j\leq N$ , the random variables $\{\sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Re}[X^{N}(t)]_{i,j}\}_{t\geq 0}$ and $\{\sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Im}[X^{N}_{t}]_{i,j}\}_{t\geq 0}$ are independent standard Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$ , independent from $\{[X^{N}(t)]_{i,i}]\}_{t\geq 0}$ .

A random matrix $Y^{N}$ whose law is equal to that of $X^{N}(1)$ is called a Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, or $\mathrm{GUE}$ for short; its law can be described by its density with respect to Lebesgue measure on Hermitian matrices, which is proportional to $X\mapsto\exp(-N\mathrm{Tr}_{N}[X^{2}])$ . This density is invariant under unitary conjugation, hence the name. The process $(X^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is sometimes called a $\mathrm{GUE}$ Brownian motion.

#### Definition 3.8.

A Ginibre Brownian motion of size $N$ is an $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ -valued diffusion process $Z^{N}(\cdot)$ of the form

$$ Z^{N}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X^{N}(t)+\mathbf{i}Y^{N}(t)) $$

where $X^{N},Y^{N}$ are independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$ . Entrywise, this can be described simply: for $1\leq i,j\leq N$ , $\{\sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Re}Z_{i,j}^{N},\sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Im}Z_{i,j}^{N}\}_{t\geq 0}$ are all independent standard Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$ .

The random matrix $Z^{N}(1)$ , whose entries are all i.i.d. complex normal random variables, is called a Ginibre Ensemble first introduced in [53]. Equivalently, the law of $Z$ has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ which is proportional to $Z\mapsto\exp(-N\mathrm{Tr}_{N}[Z^{\ast}Z])$ . Note that this density is invariant under $Z\mapsto UZV^{\ast}$ for any deterministic unitary matrices $U,V\in\mathrm{U}(N)$ ; thus, the law of the Ginibre ensemble is unitarily bi-invariant.

We will often need to consider free semicircular variables and matrices in the same space. To do so, let $(x_{u,v})_{1\leq u\leq v\leq N}$ and $(y_{u,v})_{1\leq u<v\leq N}$ be free semicircular variables in a $W^{*}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ , and set

$$ x^{N}_{u,v}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\displaystyle{\frac{x_{u,v}+\mathbf{i}y_{u,v}}{\sqrt{2N}}}&\text{ if }u<v\\
\displaystyle{\frac{x_{u,v}}{\sqrt{N}}}&\text{ if }u=v\\
\displaystyle{\frac{x_{v,u}-\mathbf{i}y_{v,u}}{\sqrt{2N}}}&\text{ else.}\end{array}\right. $$

Then if we set $\tau_{N}\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\tau\circ\ts_{N}$ , one has that the trace of the $k$ -th moment of $x^{N}$ is equal to the right hand side of Equation (3.4). Thus $x^{N}$ is a free semicircular variable. Let us now define $x_{i}^{N}$ just like $x^{N}$ but where each $x_{i}^{N}$ is generated with freely independent semicircular systems. Next, we set $\mathscr{A}_{N}$ to be the $W^{*}$ -subalgebra of $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathscr{A})$ generated by $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ and $(x_{i}^{N})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ and we endow $\mathscr{A}_{N}$ with $\tau_{N}$ . We then have the following lemma.

#### Lemma 3.9.

With $(\mathscr{A}_{N},\tau_{N})$ built as above, we have that $(x_{i}^{N})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ is a free semicircular system, free from $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ .

Thus one can view $(\mathscr{A}_{N},\tau_{N})$ as the free product of $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ with the $W^{\ast}$ -algebra generated by a free semicircular system. For the proof see [91, Proposition 2.3].

In particular, since the law of $(x_{i}^{N})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ does not depend on $N$ , we will often simply denote it $(x_{i})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ . Note that when restricted to $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , $\tau_{N}$ is just the regular normalized trace on matrices. Similarly, the restriction of $\tau_{N}$ to the $W^{\ast}$ -algebra generated by $(x_{i}^{N})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ does not depends on $N$ and hence will simply be denoted by $\tau$ .

### 3.2. Elliptical Brownian motions, $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , and the Large- $N$ Limit

We summarize the constructions in Section 1.2 here, with further discussion of their large- $N$ limits.

#### Definition 3.10 (Elliptical Brownian motions).

Let $\varrho>0$ and let $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $0<|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ . Define

$$ \theta=\frac{1}{2}\arg\zeta\qquad a=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}(\varrho+|\zeta|)}\qquad b=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}(\varrho-|\zeta|)}. $$

Then $a^{2}+b^{2}=\varrho$ and $e^{2\mathbf{i}\theta}(a^{2}-b^{2})=\zeta$ , so that $(a,b,\theta)$ satisfy (1.11). This yields a bijective mapping

$$ \{(\varrho,\zeta)\colon 0<|\zeta|\leq\varrho\}\mapsto\{(a,b,\theta)\colon a>b\geq 0,\theta\in[0,\pi)\}. $$

We may extend the definitions of $a,b$ to allow $\zeta=0$ , in which case $a=b$ ; here $\theta$ is undefined.

Let $(X^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , $(Y^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$ . We define the general elliptical Brownian motion $(W^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ by

$$ W^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\left(aX^{N}(t)+\mathbf{i}bY^{N}(t)\right). $$

Similarly, if $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(y(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are freely independent free semicircular Brownian motion, the free elliptical Brownian motion $(w_{\varrho,\zeta}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is defined as

$$ w_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\left(ax(t)+\mathbf{i}by(t)\right). $$

In both cases, when $a=b$ (i.e. $\zeta=0$ ), all values of $\theta$ yield the same distribution for the right-hand-side, so we may take canonically $\theta=0$ in this case.

Note that the laws of $W^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ and $w_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ are invariant under $a\mapsto-a$ , $b\mapsto-b$ , and $(a,b,\theta)\mapsto(b,a,\theta+\frac{\pi}{2})$ . It then follows from (3.6) that $\varrho>0$ , $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ paramaterize the laws of all possible elliptical Brownian motions.

To lighten notation we will often drop the subscripts $\varrho,\zeta$ if there can be no confusion.

Of particular note is the case $(\varrho,\zeta)=(1,0)$ (corresponding to $a=b=1$ with $\theta$ undetermined); here $W^{N}$ is a Ginibre Brownian motion.

As we proceed to consider putative large- $N$ limits, it is useful to disambiguate the dimension of the Brownian motion processes.

#### Notation 3.11.

The processes above will be indexed by $N$ as needed. Moreover, the parameters $(\varrho,\zeta)$ will remain fixed throughout most of this paper. As such, for readability, we often suppress the explicit dependence of the notation for the Brownian motion processes on the parameters, and define

$$ \displaystyle W_{\varrho,\zeta}(t) \displaystyle=W_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(t)=W^{N}(t)=W(t)\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}) \displaystyle B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t) \displaystyle=B_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(t)=B(t)=B(t)\in\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C}). $$

#### Definition 3.12.

We define the $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motion $(B_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ as the solution of the SDE (1.12), restated here:

$$ B_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(t)=I_{N}+\int_{0}^{t}B_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(s)\,dW^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(s)\,ds. $$

We also define its free version $b_{\varrho,\zeta}$ by replacing the independent Hermitian Brownian motions in the SDE above by freely independent self-adjoint free Brownian motions. To lighten notation we will often drop the subscripts $\varrho,\zeta$ .

#### Remark 3.13 (Other Parametrizations in the Literature).

Our SDE in (1.12) and Definition 3.12 has a slight parametrization change from some papers in the literature dealing with the same Brownian motion processes.

- $\bullet$ In Biane’s original papers [19, 20] where the free multiplicative Brownian motion $\Lambda$ was introduced, the given SDE was $d\Lambda(t)=\mathbf{i}\,dZ(t)\Lambda(t)$ , where $Z$ was a circular Brownian motion (i.e. our $w_{1,0}$ ). Since $Z$ and $\mathbf{i}Z$ have the same law, and right vs left Brownian motions have the same law, Biane’s $\Lambda$ is the same as our $b_{0,1}$ .

- $\bullet$ In [76, 77, 31, 63, 62, 11], the processes $W_{\varrho,\zeta}$ and $B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ differ in parametrization from ours in two ways: $W\leftrightsquigarrow\mathbf{i}W$ , and the parameters $(\varrho,\zeta)$ are $(s,\tau)$ where $s=\varrho$ and $\tau=\varrho-\zeta$ ; in particular, the Brownian motions are indexed by $(s,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{C}$ with $|s-\tau|\leq s$ . This relates to the origin of the complex parameter in [47], where it arises in the complexification of time in the Segal–Bargmann transform.

- $\bullet$ The free elliptical Brownian motions $w_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ are discussed in [116], using the same parametrization as ours, with $\zeta$ renamed $\gamma$ .

The “flat” Brownian motions $W^{N}=W^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}$ are (by design) invariant under unitary conjugation, i.e. for a fixed $U\in\mathrm{U}(N)$ $(UW^{N}(t)U^{*})_{t\geq 0}$ has the same law (as a process) as $(W^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ . It follows that the same holds true for the process $(B^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ . A straightforward calculation with the SDE (Definition 3.12) shows that the Brownian motions $(B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are also $\mathrm{U}(N)$ -conjugation invariant:

$$ UB^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)U^{\ast}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)\qquad\forall\;t\geq 0,\,\varrho>0,\,|\zeta|\leq\varrho,\,U\in\mathrm{U}(N). $$

For any $t\geq 0$ , the free multiplicative Brownian motion $b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ is the large- $N$ limit in $\ast$ -distribution of the $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ Brownian motion $B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ ; this was proved for $\zeta\in(-\varrho,\varrho)$ in [76] and generalized to complex $\zeta$ with $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ (and strong convergence) in [11]. We need this convergence paired with an arbitrary initial condition, stated in Lemma 1.5; we now provide the proof.

#### Proof of Lemma 1.5.

Fix $t\geq 0$ . [32, 76, 11] proved that $B^{N}(t)\to b(t)$ in $\ast$ -distribution; by assumption of the Lemma, $B_{0}^{N}\to b_{0}$ in $\ast$ -distribution. Hence, by Proposition 3.5, $(B_{0}^{N},U^{N}B^{N}(t)U^{N\,\ast})$ converge a.s. in $\ast$ -distribution to $(b_{0},ub(t)u^{\ast})$ .

Now, let $f\in C_{b}(\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}))$ , and note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[f(B_{0}^{N},U^{N}B^{N}(t)U^{N\,\ast})\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{\mathrm{U}(N)}\mathrm{Haar}(dU)\int_{\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})}\mathrm{Law}_{B_{0}^{N}}(dB_{0})\int_{\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})}\mathrm{Law}_{B^{N}(t)}(dB_{1})\;f(B_{0},UB_{1}U^{\ast}) $$

where we have used the change-of-variables formula and the independence of $B_{0}^{N}$ and $B^{N}(t)$ . In the inside integral, $U$ is a fixed unitary matrix; hence, by (3.7), the law of $B^{N}(t)$ is invariant under conjugation by $U$ . Thus

$$ \int_{\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})}\mathrm{Law}_{B^{N}(t)}(dB_{1})\;f(B_{0},UB_{1}U^{\ast})=\int_{\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})}\mathrm{Law}_{B^{N}(t)}(dB_{1})\;f(B_{0},B_{1}) $$

and reassembling this establishes that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[f(B_{0}^{N},U^{N}B^{N}(t)U^{N\,\ast})\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[f(B_{0}^{N},B^{N}(t))\right]. $$

Since this holds for all $f\in C_{b}(\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}))$ , it follows that $(B_{0}^{N},U^{N}B^{N}(t)U^{N\,\ast})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}(B_{0}^{N},B^{N}(t))$ . Thus

$$ (B_{0}^{N},B^{N}(t))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}(B_{0}^{N},U^{N}B^{N}(t)U^{N\,\ast})\to(b_{0},ub(t)u^{\ast})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}(b_{0},b(t))\quad\text{a.s.} $$

where the last equality in $\ast$ -distribution comes from the fact that $ub(t)u^{\ast}$ has the same $\ast$ -distribution as $b(t)$ , and the pair $b_{0},b(t)$ is already freely independent. Thence, it follows that $B_{0}^{N}B^{N}(t)$ converges a.s. in $\ast$ -distribution to $b_{0}b(t)$ , as claimed. ∎

### 3.3. The Schwinger–Dyson Equations

One of the core computational toolsets we use are the Schwinger–Dyson equations, which (in our context) are free probability analogues of Gaussian integration by parts for matrix-valued functions. They are stated, for us, in terms of non-commutative polynomials (Notation 3.1) and non-commutative derivatives, discussed next.

#### Definition 3.14.

On the algebra $\mathcal{P}_{d}=\mathbb{C}\langle X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}\rangle$ , we define an involution $*$ by $X_{i}^{*}=X_{i}$ extended to $\mathcal{P}_{d}$ by real linearity and the product rule $(\alpha PQ)^{*}=\overline{\alpha}\,Q^{*}P^{*}$ for $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ and $P,Q\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ . A polynomial $P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ is called self-adjoint if $P=P^{\ast}$ .

The above $\ast$ -algebra structure on $\mathcal{P}_{d}$ is compatible with evaluation at self-adjoint random variables in a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space, which will be our focus for the constructions in the rest of this Section and the following one. Note: if $P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ is self-adjoint and $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{d})$ are all self-adjoint then the random variable $P(\boldsymbol{y})$ is also self-adjoint.

#### Definition 3.15.

If $1\leq j\leq d$ , the non-commutative derivatives $\partial_{j}:\mathcal{P}_{d}\to\mathcal{P}_{d}^{\otimes 2}$ are defined first on monomials $M$ by

$$ \partial_{j}M=\sum_{M=AX_{j}B}A\otimes B, $$

and then extended by linearity to all polynomials. We then define the cyclic derivatives $D_{j}=m\circ\partial_{j}$ with $m:A\otimes B\mapsto BA$ .

For proof of the next proposition see for instance [37, Proposition 2.10].

#### Proposition 3.16 (Schwinger–Dyson Equations).

Let $Q\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ and $1\leq j\leq d$ .

- (a) If $\boldsymbol{X}^{N}=(X^{N}_{1},\ldots,X^{N}_{d})$ is a $d$ -tuple of independent GUE random matrices in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , then

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}(X_{j}^{N}Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N}))\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\otimes\ts_{N}\left((\partial_{j}Q)(\boldsymbol{X}^{N})\right)\right], $$

(3.8) where we recall $\ts_{N}$ is the normalized trace.

- (b) If $\boldsymbol{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})$ is a $d$ -tuple of freely independent semicircular random variables,

$$ \tau(x_{j}Q(\boldsymbol{x}))=\tau\otimes\tau\left((\partial_{j}Q)(\boldsymbol{x})\right). $$

(3.9)

One of the core technical ingredients of this paper is a method for interpolating directly between random matrices and free variables that yields a powerful quantitative interpretation and extension of genus expansions for functions of GUEs. The method was introduced in [92, 94], and used in [11, 95, 96, 91] for various applications. A combinatorial approach was recently explored in [73], explaining more directly the connection to the classical genus expansion. We now briefly outline how the first $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{N^{2}})$ term in the expansion arises, yielding a fourth-order differential operator $L$ whose iteration underlies the full expansion.

Let $\boldsymbol{X}^{N}$ be a $d$ -tuple of independent GUE matrices in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , and let $\boldsymbol{x}$ be a $d$ -tuple of freely independent semicircular random variables; as in Lemma 3.9, we can realize $\boldsymbol{X}^{N}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}$ together in the same $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A}_{N},\tau_{N})$ , freely independent from each other. For any non-commutative polynomial $Q\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ , $\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N}))-\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{x}))\to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ . To get a handle on the rate of convergence, we introduce a smooth interpolation between $\boldsymbol{X}^{N}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}$ akin to the Mehler kernel for the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process:

$$ \boldsymbol{z}_{t}:=\sqrt{1-e^{-t}}\boldsymbol{x}+e^{-t/2}\boldsymbol{X}^{N}. $$

Note, then, that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N}))\right]-\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{x}))=-\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{d}{dt}\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}))\right]dt. $$

The expected derivative on the right-hand-side can then be expressed in terms of the generator $L_{1}$ of the process. With appropriate use of the Schwinger–Dyson equations (3.8) and (3.9), we can express

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{d}{dt}\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}))\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-t}\Big(\tau_{N}\otimes\tau_{N}-\tau_{N}\circ(\ts_{N}\otimes\ts_{N})\Big)(L_{1}Q(\boldsymbol{z}_{t}))\right]. $$

where $L_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}D_{i}$ . A key insight in [94] was to recognize the difference above as coming from a second Mehler-like interpolation. To see how, first note from Definition 3.15 that $L_{1}Q\in\mathcal{P}_{d}\otimes\mathcal{P}_{d}$ . Hence it is a finite linear combination of tensors $P_{1}\otimes P_{2}$ . When we evaluate such a tensor at a $d$ -tuple $\boldsymbol{z}$ , we mean $P_{1}(\boldsymbol{z})\otimes P_{2}(\boldsymbol{z})$ ; we could just as well evaluate the tensor factors at different $d$ -tuples $P_{1}(\boldsymbol{z}^{1})\otimes P_{2}(\boldsymbol{z}^{2})$ ; we denote such evaluation as $(L_{1}Q)(\boldsymbol{z}^{1},\boldsymbol{z}^{2})$ .

Let $\{\boldsymbol{z}^{\ell}\}_{1\leq\ell\leq 2}$ and $\{\boldsymbol{y}^{k}\}_{1\leq k\leq 4}$ be six families of $d$ -tuples of free semicircular variables freely independent from $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , and define

$$ \boldsymbol{z}^{k}_{s,t}=\sqrt{1-e^{-s}}\boldsymbol{y}^{k}+\sqrt{e^{-s}-e^{-t}}\boldsymbol{x}^{\lceil k/2\rceil}+e^{-t/2}\boldsymbol{X}^{N}. $$

Notice that $\boldsymbol{z}^{k}_{0,t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}\boldsymbol{z}^{k}_{t,t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}\boldsymbol{z}_{t}$ . Ergo, we may just as well express the right-hand-side of (3.11) as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-t}\Big(\tau_{N}\otimes\tau_{N}(L_{1}Q(\boldsymbol{z}^{1}_{t,t},\boldsymbol{z}^{2}_{t,t}))-\tau_{N}\circ(\ts_{N}\otimes\ts_{N})(L_{1}Q(\boldsymbol{z}^{1}_{0,t},\boldsymbol{z}^{2}_{0,t}))\Big)\right]. $$

The free independence of $\boldsymbol{z}^{1}_{s,t}$ and $\boldsymbol{z}^{2}_{s,t}$ allows the factoring of the $\tau_{N}$ on the right, putting the two terms on the same footing: expressed in terms of $\tau_{N}\otimes\tau_{N}$ . Combining this with (3.10) yields

$$ \displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N}))\right]-\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{x})) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\;-\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{d}{ds}\tau_{N}\left(\ts_{N}\otimes\ts_{N}(L_{1}Q(\boldsymbol{z}^{1}_{s,t},\boldsymbol{z}^{2}_{s,t}))\right)\right]\,ds\,dt $$

Since $\boldsymbol{z}^{1}_{s,t}$ and $\boldsymbol{z}^{2}_{s,t}$ are copies of another Ornstein–Uhlenbeck type process, the expected derivative in (3.12) will again be expressible in terms of the generator of this process, which is a second-order (non-commutative) differential operator $L_{2}$ . Hence, the difference we are estimating in (3.10) is expressed in term of the fourth order operator $L=L_{2}L_{1}$ . Indeed: again applying judicious use of the Schwinger–Dyson equations (3.8) and (3.9), (3.12) yields the explicit formula

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N}))\right]-\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{x}))=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-s-t}\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\left(\Theta_{s,t}\circ L_{2}L_{1}Q\right)\right]dsdt $$

where $L_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\partial_{j}\otimes\partial_{j}$ and $\Theta_{s,t}$ is a twisted evaluation map defined as follows. Noting that $L_{2}L_{1}\colon\mathcal{P}_{d}\to\mathcal{P}_{d}^{\otimes 4}$ , $\Theta_{s,t}$ is defined by linearity and

$$ \Theta_{s,t}(P_{1}\otimes P_{2}\otimes P_{3}\otimes P_{4}):=P_{2}(\boldsymbol{z}^{1}_{s,t})P_{1}(\boldsymbol{z}^{3}_{s,t})P_{4}(\boldsymbol{z}^{4}_{s,t})P_{3}(\boldsymbol{z}^{2}_{s,t}). $$

Crucially: the $\frac{1}{N^{2}}$ arises from (3.8) which employs $\partial_{j}$ to merge two normalized traces into one normalized trace, yielding an extra factor of $1/N$ . This happens twice because of a separate merging of free traces $\tau$ , which is where the extra interpolating processes $\boldsymbol{z}^{3}_{s,t}$ and $\boldsymbol{z}^{4}_{s,t}$ arise. See [93] for the full calculation.

Equation (3.13) gives an explicit $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{N^{2}})$ bound for the difference between the expected trace of $Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N})$ and its large- $N$ limit, in terms of the fourth-order non-commutative differential operator $L=L_{2}L_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}(\partial_{j}\otimes\partial_{j})\circ\partial_{i}D_{i}$ . The resultant polynomial $LQ$ is evaluated at interpolated processes $\boldsymbol{z}^{k}_{s,t}$ ; by comparing these to $\lim_{t\to\infty}\boldsymbol{z}^{k}_{0,t}=\boldsymbol{x}$ , the above calculations can be iterated, yielding an expansion in powers of $\frac{1}{N^{2}}$ for $\mathbb{E}[\tau_{N}(Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N}))]$ up to any integer order desired. This expansion coincides with the genus expansion in the case of monomial $Q$ (necessarily by uniqueness), but expresses the coefficients in terms of powers of the operator $L$ . We detail this expansion in (3.17) below.

The full details of the iterated expansion are notationally complicated. In order to minimize the amount of notation, we will not derive it fully here; the interested reader can find all the details in [94], or [73] for a more combinatorial approach. We present only the features of the expansion needed ultimately for our proof of Theorem 1.3, to be used as a black box as much as possible. We do however need to introduce the following three definitions, expanding on the constructions above.

#### Definition 3.17.

Let us assume that we are given

- $\bullet$ $\boldsymbol{X}^{N}=(X^{N}_{1},\dots,X^{N}_{d})$ a $d$ -tuple of independent GUE matrices,

- $\bullet$ $(x^{m}_{i})_{i\in[1,d],m\in\mathbb{N}}$ free semicircular variables,

- $\bullet$ $I=(I_{1},\dots,I_{2n})\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2n}$ a collection of $2n$ integers,

- $\bullet$ $T_{n}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{2n})$ a sequence of non-negative real numbers.

Then with $\widetilde{t}_{0}=0$ and $\widetilde{t}_{1}\leq\dots\leq\widetilde{t}_{2n}$ the elements of $T_{n}$ sorted in increasing order, we set

$$ X_{i,I}^{N,T_{n}}=\sum_{l=1}^{2n}(e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l-1}}-e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l}})^{1/2}x^{I_{l}}_{i}+e^{-\widetilde{t}_{2n}/2}X_{i}^{N},\qquad 1\leq i\leq d\,, $$

$$ x_{i,I}^{T_{n}}=\sum_{l=1}^{2n}(e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l-1}}-e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l}})^{1/2}x^{I_{l}}_{i}+e^{-\widetilde{t}_{2n}/2}x_{i}^{0}\,,\qquad 1\leq i\leq d. $$

Note that we used Lemma 3.9 to define $X^{N,T_{n}}_{i,I}$ .

Note that for $I,T_{n}$ fixed, the family $(x_{i,I}^{T_{n}})_{1\leq i\leq d}$ is a free semicircular system.

#### Definition 3.18 (Terms of the $m$ -th kind).

If $P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ , a “term of the $m$ -th kind associated to $P$ ” is a tuple $(P_{1},\dots,P_{m+1})\in\mathcal{P}_{d}^{m+1}$ defined inductively as follows:

- $\bullet$ For $m=0$ , it is either $P$ or $P^{*}$ .

- $\bullet$ For $m>0$ and any term of the $m-1$ -st kind $(P_{1},\dots,P_{m})$ , for every $i,j$ we fix choices of $A_{l}^{i,j},B_{l}^{i,j}\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ such that

$$ \partial_{i}P_{j}=\sum_{l}A_{l}^{i,j}\otimes B_{l}^{i,j}, $$

(3.14) and declare $(P_{1},\dots,P_{j-1},A_{l}^{i,j},B_{l}^{i,j},P_{j+1},\dots,P_{m})$ to be a term of the $m$ -th kind for each $i,j,l$ .

This allows us to define

$$ c(P)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\geq 0,\\
i\in[1,d]\end{subarray}}\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(P_{1},\dots,P_{m+1})\text{ is a}\\
\text{term of the $m$-th kind.}\end{subarray}}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}\kappa_{j}\ \middle|\ \forall j,\ \partial_{i}P_{j}=\sum_{l=1}^{\kappa_{j}}A_{l}^{i,j}\otimes B_{l}^{i,j}\right\}. $$

Heuristically, $c(P)$ measures the growth in the number of terms between the successive differentials of a polynomial: $\partial_{i}P$ will be a sum of at most $c(P)$ simple tensors and $\left(\partial_{j}\otimes\id\circ\partial_{i}+\id\otimes\partial_{j}\circ\partial_{i}\right)P$ will be a sum of at most $c(P)^{2}$ simple tensors. Besides, note that the definition of the terms of the $m$ -th kind is not unique since there is no canonical way of writing $\partial_{i}P_{j}$ as a sum of simple tensors, which is why we fix a way of doing so in the construction above.

#### Definition 3.19 ( $P$ -monomials).

With the notations of Definition 3.18, given $P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ , a $P$ -monomial is any non-commutative polynomial $M$ in variables $(X_{i,I})_{i\in[1,d],I\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2n}}$ , for some fixed $n\geq 0$ , obtained in the following way: For some finite set $\mathcal{C}$ of terms $\underline{P}^{j}=(P^{j}_{1},\dots,P^{j}_{m_{j}+1})$ , $j=1,\dots,q$ associated to $P$ , let

$$ M=\prod_{s=1}^{p}R_{s}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I^{s}}) $$

for some reordering $(R_{1},\dots,R_{p})\in\mathcal{P}_{d}^{p}$ of the concatenation $(\underline{P}^{1},\dots,\underline{P}^{q})\in\mathcal{P}_{d}^{p}$ , and some $I^{1},\dots,I^{p}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2n}$ (possibly with repetition), where $\boldsymbol{X}_{I^{s}}=(X_{i,I^{s}})_{i\in[1,d]}$ . Letting $r_{m}$ be the number of terms of the $m$ -th kind in $\mathcal{C}$ , we set

$$ p(M):=p=\sum_{i\geq 0}(i+1)r_{i},\quad q(M):=q=\sum_{i\geq 0}r_{i}. $$

#### Example 3.20.

With $P=(X_{2}+1)X_{1}X_{2}^{2}X_{1}+X_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}$ , we have

$$ \partial_{1}P=(X_{2}+1)\otimes X_{2}^{2}X_{1}+(X_{2}+1)X_{1}X_{2}^{2}\otimes 1+1\otimes 1, $$

$$ \partial_{2}P=1\otimes X_{1}X_{2}^{2}X_{1}+(X_{2}+1)X_{1}\otimes X_{2}X_{1}+(X_{2}+1)X_{1}X_{2}\otimes X_{1}, $$

so we may take the following six elements of $\mathcal{P}_{2}^{2}$ :

$$ \displaystyle(X_{2}+1,X_{2}^{2}X_{1}),((X_{2}+1)X_{1}X_{2}^{2},1),(1,1), \displaystyle(1,X_{1}X_{2}^{2}X_{1}),((X_{2}+1)X_{1},X_{2}X_{1}),((X_{2}+1)X_{1}X_{2},X_{1}), $$

to be the terms of the first kind associated to $P$ . Since we may alternatively express

$$ \partial_{1}P=X_{2}\otimes X_{2}^{2}X_{1}+1\otimes X_{2}^{2}X_{1}+(X_{2}+1)X_{1}X_{2}^{2}\otimes 1+1\otimes 1, $$

we could have taken the two terms

$$ (X_{2},X_{2}^{2}X_{1}),\;(1,X_{2}^{2}X_{1}) $$

in place of the first term in (3.15) to get a list of seven terms of the first kind.

Having fixed the list (3.15) of terms of the first kind, then by differentiating the second entry $X_{2}^{2}X_{1}$ of the first term in (3.15) with respect to $X_{2}$ as follows:

$$ \partial_{2}X_{2}^{2}X_{1}=1\otimes X_{2}X_{1}+X_{2}\otimes X_{1}, $$

we obtain the following two terms of the second kind:

$$ (X_{2}+1,1,X_{2}X_{1})\,,\qquad(X_{2}+1,X_{2},X_{1}). $$

From the collection $\mathcal{C}=\{\underline{P}^{1},\underline{P}^{2},\underline{P}^{3}\}$ of terms

$$ \underline{P}^{1}=P^{*}\,,\quad\underline{P}^{2}=(1,X_{1}X_{2}^{2}X_{1})\,,\quad\underline{P}^{3}=(X_{2}+1,X_{2},X_{1}) $$

and $I,I^{\prime}\in(\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\})^{2n}$ for some $n\geq 0$ , we can construct the following $P$ -monomial:

$$ \displaystyle M \displaystyle=P^{*}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I})P^{3}_{1}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I^{\prime}})P^{3}_{3}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I^{\prime}})P^{2}_{1}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I})P^{3}_{2}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I})P^{2}_{2}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I^{\prime}}) \displaystyle=P^{*}(\boldsymbol{X}_{I})(X_{2,I^{\prime}}+1)X_{1,I^{\prime}}X_{2,I}X_{1,I^{\prime}}X_{2,I^{\prime}}^{2}X_{1,I^{\prime}}. $$

For this $P$ -monomial (or any $P$ -monomial built from the selection (3.16)) we have $q(M)=3$ and $p(M)=1+2+3=6$ .

We can now state the lemma that we will use for estimating high order moments of the multiplicative Brownian motion.

#### Lemma 3.21.

There exist sequences $(A_{i})_{i},(J_{i})_{i},(\mathcal{L}_{i})_{i}$ with the following properties:

- (a) $A_{i}\subset\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2i}$ is a Borel set (in fact a polyhedron) with

$$ \int_{A_{i}}e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}}dt_{1}\dots dt_{2i}\leq\frac{1}{i!}\,. $$

- (b) $J_{i}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{2i}$ is an index set.

- (c) $\mathcal{L}_{i}$ is a mapping

$$ \mathcal{L}_{i}:\mathcal{P}_{d}\times A_{i}\to\mathbb{C}\langle X_{j,I}:j\in[1,d],I\in J_{i}\rangle $$

where $\bullet$ for each fixed $T\in A_{i}$ , $\mathcal{L}_{i}(\cdot,T)$ is a linear map, $\bullet$ for each fixed $Q\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ , the coefficients of $\mathcal{L}_{i}(Q,\cdot)$ are measurable (in fact simple) functions on $A_{i}$ , $\bullet$ given $M$ a monomial with coefficient $1$ , for each fixed $T\in A_{i}$ , $\mathcal{L}_{i}(M,T)$ is a sum of monomials with coefficient $1$ .

- (d) ( $\frac{1}{N^{2}}$ -Expansion). For any $Q\in\mathcal{P}_{d}$ and $s\geq 1$ , $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\Big(Q(\boldsymbol{X}^{N})\Big)\right]=\tau(Q(\boldsymbol{x}^{0}))+\sum_{i=1}^{s-1}\frac{\alpha_{i}(Q)}{N^{2i}}+\frac{\tilde{\alpha}^{N}_{s}(Q)}{N^{2s}}$ (3.17) with coefficients given by $\displaystyle\alpha_{i}(Q)$ $\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2^{i}}\int_{A_{i}}e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}}\tau\Big(\left[\mathcal{L}_{i}(Q,T_{i})\right](\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{i}})\Big)\ dt_{1}\dots dt_{2i}$ $\displaystyle\tilde{\alpha}_{s}^{N}(Q)$ $\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2^{s}}\int_{A_{s}}e^{-t_{2s}-\dots-t_{1}}\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\Big(\left[\mathcal{L}_{s}(Q,T_{s})\right](\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{s}})\Big)\right]\ dt_{1}\dots dt_{2s}\,$ (using the notation $T_{i}=(t_{1},\dots,t_{2i})$ of Definition (3.17)).

- (e) (Complexity). If $Q=(P^{*}P)^{k}$ , then for any $T\in A_{i}$ , $\mathcal{L}_{i}(Q,T)$ is the sum of at most $d^{2i}\times\left(2k\times c(P)\right)^{4i}$ $P$ -monomials $M$ (with $n=i$ ) such that $p(M)=2k+4i$ and $q(M)=2k$ .

We refer the interested reader to [94, Section 2.3] for the explicit definitions of the sets $J_{i}$ and mappings $\mathcal{L}_{i}$ ; their construction is quite lengthy and will not be used directly in this paper (the sets $A_{i}$ are recalled in the proof below). Lemma 3.21 distills all of the properties that we need for the proof of Theorem 1.3 in Section 4.

#### Proof.

This lemma, and notably the construction of $A_{i},J_{i},\mathcal{L}_{i}$ and the $\frac{1}{N^{2}}$ -expansion of part (d), is a direct corollary of Lemma 3.6 and Proposition 3.7 of [94]. To establish the esetimate in (a) we recall from [94] that

$$ A_{i}=\{t_{2i}\geq t_{2i-2}\geq\dots\geq t_{2}\geq 0\}\cap\{\forall g\in[1,i],t_{2g}\geq t_{2g-1}\geq 0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2i}. $$

Since for every $g$ , one has $\int_{0}^{t_{2g}}e^{-t_{2g-1}}dt_{2g-1}\leq 1,$ we get that

$$ \int_{A_{i}}e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}}dt_{1}\dots dt_{2i}\leq\int_{0\leq t_{1}\leq\dots\leq t_{i}}e^{-t_{i}-\dots-t_{1}}dt_{1}\dots dt_{i}=\frac{1}{i!}. $$

This yields (a).

For (c), one can set

$$ \mathcal{L}_{1}:(Q,T)\in\mathcal{P}_{d}\times A_{1}\mapsto\sum_{1\leq i,j\leq d}\Theta\circ\ev_{1}\circ\left(\partial_{j}\otimes\partial_{j}\right)\circ\left(\partial_{i}D_{i}\right)(Q), $$

where $\Theta(A\otimes B\otimes C\otimes D):=BADC$ and $\ev_{1}$ is a map which evaluates each tensorand in specific subsets of $(X_{j,I})_{1\leq j\leq d,I\in J_{1}}$ . Note that $\mathcal{L}_{1}(Q,T)$ does not depend on $T$ . Besides, $\mathcal{L}_{s+1}(Q,T_{s+1})$ is defined by induction by applying the operator

$$ \mathcal{K}_{l,J_{s}}:\mathbb{C}\langle(X_{i,I})_{1\leq i\leq d,I\in J_{s}}\rangle\ni R\mapsto\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i,j\leq d\\
I,K\in J_{s}\\
\text{such that }I_{l}=K_{l}\end{subarray}}\ev_{s+1}\circ\Theta\circ\left(\partial_{j,I}\otimes\partial_{j,K}\right)\circ\left(\partial_{i}D_{i}\right)R $$

to $\mathcal{L}_{s}(Q,T_{s})$ , for an integer $l=l(T_{s+1})$ determined by $T_{s+1}$ and $\ev_{s+1}$ a map which evaluates each tensorand in specific subsets of $(X_{j,I})_{1\leq j\leq d,I\in J_{s+1}}$ . In this context, given $M$ a monomial,

$$ \partial_{i,I}M=\sum_{M=AX_{i,I}B}A\otimes B, $$

$$ \partial_{i}M=\sum_{I\in J_{s}}\sum_{M=AX_{i,I}B}A\otimes B, $$

$$ D_{i}M=\sum_{I\in J_{s}}\sum_{M=AX_{i,I}B}BA. $$

In particular, when applied to a monomial with leading coefficient $1$ , the operator $\mathcal{K}_{l,J_{s}}$ returns a sum of monomial also with leading coefficient $1$ . Hence we get (c).

Now we prove assertion (e). Fix a list $\mathcal{T}_{P}$ of terms associated to $P$ as in Definition 3.18. Thus, whenever we take the non-commutative differential of a $P$ -monomial, we assume that the sum of simple tensors that appears is built with the help of the same equation (3.14) with which we built $\mathcal{T}_{P}$ by induction. Thus, if $M$ is a $P$ -monomial with $q(M)=2k$ , then by definition of $c(P)$ (computed with respect to $\mathcal{T}_{P}$ ), $\mathcal{K}_{l,J_{s}}(M)$ will be a sum of at most $d^{2}(2k\times c(P))^{4}$ simple tensors. By induction we obtain the claim on the number of $P$ -monomials. Besides, applying the operator $\mathcal{K}_{l,J_{s}}$ (which involves differentiating non-commutatively four times) to a $P$ -monomial $M$ with $q(M)=2k$ , then applying the operator $\Theta$ , yields a sum of $P$ -monomials, and given one such $P$ -monomial $L$ , the number of terms used to build it does not change, i.e. $q(L)=q(M)=2k$ . However, by performing this operation, we proceed to replace a term by a new term one kind higher four times in a row. Hence $p(L)=p(M)+4$ and the last part of (e) follows by induction on $i$ and the fact that $p(Q)=2k$ . ∎

Before concluding this subsection, let us prove the following proposition that allows us to control moments of semicircular variables and GUE matrices by the moments of certain jointly Gaussian random variables.

#### Proposition 3.22.

In the setting of Definition 3.17, for any monomial $M$ (with coefficient 1) in non-commutative variables $(X_{i,I})_{i\in[1,d],I\in J_{n}}$ we have

$$ 0\leq\tau\left(M(\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}})\right)\leq\mathbb{E}[M(g)], $$

$$ 0\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\left(M(\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{n}})\right)\right]\leq\mathbb{E}[M(g)], $$

where $g=(g_{i,I})_{i\in[1,d],I\in J_{n}}$ are centered real Gaussian random variables of variance $1$ such that $g_{i,I}$ and $g_{j,J}$ are independent if $i\neq j$ and equal otherwise.

In particular, given $c_{M}\in\mathbb{C}$ and $a_{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $|c_{M}|\leq a_{M}$ , then

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\left(\sum_{M\text{ monomial}}c_{M}M(\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{n}})\right)\right]\right|\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{M\text{ monomial}}a_{M}M(g)\right], $$

and similarly for $\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}}$ instead of $\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{n}}$ .

#### Proof.

Thanks to Proposition 3.16(b), assuming that $M=X_{i,I}R$ , we have that

$$ \tau\left(M(\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}})\right)=e^{-\widetilde{t}_{2n}}\tau\otimes\tau\left(\partial_{i,0}R(\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}})\right)+\sum_{l=1}^{2n}(e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l-1}}-e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l}})\tau\otimes\tau\left(\partial_{i,I_{l}}R(\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}})\right), $$

where $\partial_{i,I_{l}}$ is the non-commutative partial differential with respect to $x_{i,I_{l}}$ . Thus, by a straightforward induction, $\tau\left(M(\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}})\right)\geq 0$ .

Let us remark that the product of the $s$ -th and $r$ -th moment of a centered Gaussian random variable of variance $1$ is always bounded by its $s+r$ -th moment. Thus for any monomials $A$ and $B$ , $\mathbb{E}[A(g)]\mathbb{E}[B(g)]\leq\mathbb{E}[A(g)B(g)]$ . Hence if we assume that (3.18) is satisfied for monomials of degree strictly smaller than $k$ and that $M$ has degree $k$ , then

$$ \tau\left(M(\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{n}})\right)\leq\left(e^{-\widetilde{t}_{2n}}+\sum_{l=1}^{2n}(e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l-1}}-e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l}})\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial R(g)}{\partial g_{i}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial R(g)}{\partial g_{i}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[g_{i}R(g)\right], $$

where we used Gaussian integration by part in the last equality. The bound (3.18) now follows by induction.

Turning to (3.19), thanks to Lemma 3.21 (or more precisely [94, Lemma 3.6]),

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(M(\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{n}})\right)\right]=\sum_{i=0}^{k/4}\frac{\alpha_{i}}{N^{2i}}, $$

where the coefficients $\alpha_{i}$ are linear combinations with non-negative coefficients of traces of monomials in $x^{T_{l}}$ for $l\geq n$ . In particular, thanks to the first part of the proof, those coefficients are non-negative. Thus

$$ 0\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(M(\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{n}})\right)\right]=\sum_{i=0}^{k/4}\frac{\alpha_{i}}{N^{2i}}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{k/4}\alpha_{i}=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau\left(M(\boldsymbol{X}^{1,T_{n}})\right)\right]. $$

However, if we let $G=(G_{i,I}^{T_{n}})_{i\in[1,d],I\in J_{n}}$ be a family of Gaussian random variables, built exactly like $x_{i,I}^{T_{n}}$ in Definition 3.17 but with independent Gaussian random variables of variance $1$ instead of free semicircular variables, then by using Equation (3.18),

$$ 0\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(M(\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{n}})\right)\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[M(g)\right]. $$

Hence the conclusion by using the fact that if $g_{1},\dots,g_{l}$ are centered Gaussian random variables of variance $1$ , not necessarily independent but such that for all $i,j$ , $\cov(g_{i},g_{j})\geq 0$ , then $\mathbb{E}\left[g_{1}\dots g_{l}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}[g_{1}^{l}].$ ∎

## 4. Small-time Affine Approximation

### 4.1. Setup and overview

For the duration of this section we let $W^{N}=W^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}$ be an elliptical Brownian motion as in Definition 3.10, i.e.

$$ W^{N}(t)=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(aX^{N}(t)+\mathbf{i}bY^{N}(t))\,,\quad t\geq 0 $$

with $(X^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0},(Y^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ independent Hermitian Brownian motions. Given $W^{N}$ , we let $B^{N}$ be the multiplicative Brownian motion as in Definition (3.12), driven by $W^{N}$ , and for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we let $B^{N}_{n}$ be the discretized process

$$ B_{n}^{N}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\left(I_{N}+W^{N}\left(\frac{i}{2^{n}}\right)-W^{N}\left(\frac{i-1}{2^{n}}\right)+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}I_{N}\right). $$

Note that $B^{N}$ and $B^{N}_{n}$ are defined using the same driving process $W^{N}$ . We also fix realizations of the corresponding free non-commutative processes $x,y,w,b,b_{n}$ , defining the latter as in (4.1) with $W^{N}$ replaced by $w$ . We set

$$ t_{n}:=\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor/2^{n}\,. $$

Note that $B_{n}^{N}(t)=B_{n}^{N}(t_{n})$ for all $n,t$ .

We further let $(X_{i}^{N},Y_{i}^{N})_{i\geq 1}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of independent pairs of GUE matrices, independent of all other processes. For computations, and in particular for invoking Lemma 3.21, it will be convenient to reexpress joint moments of increments of the processes $B^{N},B_{n}^{N},W^{N}$ in terms of the $X_{i}^{N},Y_{i}^{N}$ . Indeed, note that

$$ W^{N}\bigg(\frac{i}{2^{n}}\bigg)-W^{N}\bigg(\frac{i-1}{2^{n}}\bigg)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\frac{e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}(aX_{i}^{N}+bY_{i}^{N})\,,\quad i\geq 1. $$

As in the previous section we use $X_{i},Y_{i}$ (without the superscript $N$ ) to denote generic arguments of non-commutative polynomials, which may be evaluated at the GUE matrices $X_{i}^{N},Y_{i}^{N}$ or semicircular variables.

In this section we use $L^{p}$ norms for the non-commutative probability space of random matrices equipped with $\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}$ as state, and also on a “large- $N$ limit” non-commutative probability space equipped with a tracial state $\tau$ . We use the same notation for both, which will always be clear from context: for an $N\times N$ random matrix $A$ and non-commutative random variable $a$ ,

$$ \left\|A\right\|_{p}:=\left(\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}(|A|^{p})\right)^{1/p}\quad\&\quad\left\|a\right\|_{p}:=\left(\tau(|a|^{p})\right)^{1/p} $$

recalling $|A|=(AA^{\ast})^{1/2}$ , $|a|=(a^{\ast}a)^{1/2}$ .

We prove Theorem 1.3 using the moment method. Thus, we need to bound

$$ \|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W_{N}(t)\|_{2k}^{2k}=\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W_{N}(t)|^{2k} $$

for large $k=k(N)$ . This is accomplished with Proposition 4.5.

Towards the proof of Proposition 4.5, in Section 4.2 we show $B_{n}^{N}\to B^{N}$ in $L^{2k}$ , uniformly on compact time intervals. This allows us to replace $B^{N}(t),W^{N}(t)$ in (4.4) with $B_{n}^{N}(t_{n}),W^{N}(t_{n})$ . From (4.1), (4.3) we can then view $|B_{n}^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W_{N}(t)|^{2k}$ as a non-commutative polynomial in independent GUE matrices, allowing for the application of Lemma 3.21. The proof of Proposition 4.5 is then concluded in Section 4.3 by bounding each term in the resulting expansion.

In Section 4.4 we deduce tail bounds on the norm of $B^{N}(t)$ that will also be useful in subsequent sections.

### 4.2. Random walk approximation

Recall the discretized processes $B_{n}^{N},b_{n}$ from (4.1). In this subsection we show these processes converge to $B,b$ in $L^{p}$ . The main results of this section are the following proposition and corollary.

#### Proposition 4.1.

For any $T\geq 0$ and $2\leq p<\infty$ , $B_{n}^{N}\to B^{N}$

in $L^{p}(\Omega\times[0,T],\ts_{N})$ . Moreover, there exists a constant $C_{\varrho,T,p}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|B^{N}(t)-B^{N}_{n}(t)\right\|_{p}\leq\frac{C_{\varrho,T,p}}{2^{n/2p}}\qquad\forall\,t\in[0,T]. $$

The same estimate holds in $L^{p}(\tau)$ with $B^{N}_{n},B^{N}$ replaced by their free counterparts.

#### Corollary 4.2.

For $t\geq 0$ and $2\leq p<\infty$ ,

$$ B^{N}_{n}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\text{ converges to }B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\text{ in }L^{p}\text{ as }n\to\infty. $$

The same holds with $B^{N}_{n},B^{N}$ replaced by their free counterparts $b_{n},b$ .

#### Proof of Corollary 4.2.

Note that the $L^{p}$ -norm of the difference is equal to

$$ \displaystyle\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)+W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right\|_{p} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{p}+\left\|W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right\|_{p}. $$

The first term tends to zero by Proposition 4.1. For the second term, note that $W^{N}(t)-W^{N}(s)$ has the same law as $\sqrt{t-s}W^{N}(1)$ , and so

$$ \left\|W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right\|_{p}=\sqrt{t-t_{n}}\left\|aX^{N}+\mathbf{i}bY^{N}\right\|_{p} $$

where $X^{N}$ and $Y^{N}$ are GUE matrices. This $L^{p}$ -norm is bounded independently of $N$ by a $\varrho$ -dependent constant times a $p$ th Gaussian moment. Since $t_{n}=\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor/2^{n}\to t$ , the result follows uniformly in $N$ . The argument for the free case is similar. ∎

The remainder of this subsection is dedicated to the proof of Proposition 4.1. We need the following:

#### Lemma 4.3.

For any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0\leq t\leq T$ there exists a constant $C_{k,T}$ such that

$$ \sup_{n,N\geq 1}\|B^{N}_{n}(t)\|_{2k}\leq C_{k,T}. $$

The same holds with $B^{N}_{n}(t)$ replaced by $b_{n}(t)$ .

#### Proof.

From (4.3),

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(|B^{N}_{n}(t)|^{2k}\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\Bigg|\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\left(\bigg(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\bigg)I_{N}+\frac{e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}\left(aX_{i}^{N}+\mathbf{i}bY_{i}^{N}\right)\right)\Bigg|^{2k}\right]. $$

Thanks to Proposition 3.22, with $g_{i},g_{i}^{\prime}$ i.i.d. standard Gaussians, the right hand side above is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\left(1+\frac{|a^{2}-b^{2}|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{1}{2^{n/2}}\left(|a|g_{i}+|b|g_{i}^{\prime}\right)\right)\right|^{2k}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\left(1+\frac{|a^{2}-b^{2}|}{2^{n+1}}+\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{2^{n}}}g_{i}\right)\right|^{2k}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(1+\frac{|a^{2}-b^{2}|}{2^{n+1}}+\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{2^{n}}}g_{1}\right)^{2k}\right]^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}. $$

One can write

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(1+\frac{|a^{2}-b^{2}|}{2^{n+1}}+\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{2^{n}}}g_{1}\right)^{2k}\right]=1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{c_{i,k}}{2^{in}}, $$

where the coefficients $c_{i,k}$ do not depend on $n$ . Thus

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(|B^{N}_{n}(t)|^{2k}\right)\right]\leq e^{t\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{c_{i,k}}{2^{(i-1)n}}}. $$

Hence the conclusion. The claim for $b_{n}$ follows by similar lines. ∎

Next we can show $B_{n}(t)$ and $b_{n}(t)$ are Cauchy in $L^{2}$ :

#### Lemma 4.4.

There are constants $C_{\varrho},K_{\varrho}<\infty$ so that, for any $n\geq 1$ , $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B_{n-1}^{N}(t)\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq C_{\varrho}\frac{t+1}{2^{n}}e^{K_{\varrho}t}. $$

The above inequality also stands if one replaces $B^{N}_{n}(t)$ by $b_{n}(t)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $(X_{i}^{N},Y_{i}^{N})_{i\geq 1}$ be a family of independent GUE matrices, and define

$$ \Upsilon_{i}^{n}\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)I_{N}+\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}X^{N}_{i}+\mathbf{i}\frac{be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}Y^{N}_{i}. $$

Then $B^{N}_{n}(t)$ has the same distribution as the product of the $\Upsilon_{i}^{n}$ for $1\leq i\leq\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor$ . We proceed inductively, peeling away the $i=1$ terms in the following product:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B^{N}_{n}(t))^{*}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\right)\right]\left|1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}X^{N}_{1}+\mathbf{i}be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}Y^{N}_{1}}{2^{n/2}}\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\right)\right]\left(1+\frac{\zeta^{*}}{2^{n+1}}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\frac{ae^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}X^{N}_{1}-\mathbf{i}be^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}Y^{N}_{1}}{2^{n/2}}\right)\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}X^{N}_{1}+\mathbf{i}be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}Y^{N}_{1}}{2^{n/2}}\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\frac{ae^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}X^{N}_{1}-\mathbf{i}be^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}Y^{N}_{1}}{2^{n/2}}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\right)\right]\left(\left|1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right|^{2}+\frac{\varrho}{2^{n}}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\right)\right]\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n}}+\frac{|\zeta|^{2}}{4^{n+1}}\right), $$

where we used Proposition 3.16 to go from the second to third equality, wherein the cross terms vanish (alternatively, this step follows from the fact that $(X_{i}^{N},Y_{i}^{N})_{i\geq 1}$ are independent standardized Wigner matrices). By induction we get that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B^{N}_{n}(t))^{*}\right)\right]=\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n}}+\frac{|\zeta|^{2}}{4^{n+1}}\right)^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}. $$

Now to compute $\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B_{n-1}^{N}(t))^{*}\right)\right]$ , we set

$$ \Gamma_{i}^{n}\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n}}\right)I_{N}+\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}(X^{N}_{2i-1}+X_{2i}^{N})+\mathbf{i}\frac{be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}(Y^{N}_{2i-1}+Y_{2i}^{N}) $$

and further note that $\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor=2\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor+\chi$ for $\chi\in\{0,1\}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B_{n-1}^{N}(t))^{*}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\ts_{N}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{2i-1}^{n}\Upsilon_{2i}^{n}\prod^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}_{i=2\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor+1}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}\times\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Gamma_{i}^{n}\Bigg)^{*}\Bigg)\Bigg] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\ts_{N}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{2i-1}^{n}\Upsilon_{2i}^{n}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Gamma_{i}^{n}\Bigg)^{*}\Bigg)\Bigg]\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)^{\chi} $$

where we used the fact that $\prod^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}_{i=2\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor+1}\Upsilon_{i}^{n}$ (which is either the identity or $\Upsilon_{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}^{n}$ , as $\chi\in\{0,1\}$ ) is independent of other random matrices. Now since

$$ \displaystyle\Upsilon_{2i-1}^{n}\Upsilon_{2i}^{n}= \displaystyle\ \left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)\left(\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}(X^{N}_{2i-1}+X^{N}_{2i})+\mathbf{i}\frac{be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}(Y^{N}_{2i-1}+Y^{N}_{2i})\right) \displaystyle+\left(\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}X^{N}_{2i-1}+\mathbf{i}\frac{be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}Y^{N}_{2i-1}\right)\left(\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}X^{N}_{2i}+\mathbf{i}\frac{be^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}Y^{N}_{2i}\right) \displaystyle+\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)^{2}I_{N}, $$

we can apply Proposition 3.16 once again (or alternatively that $(X_{i}^{N},Y_{i}^{N})_{i\geq 1}$ are independent standardized Wigner matrices), to get that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B_{n-1}^{N}(t))^{*}\right)\right]\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)^{-\chi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{2i-1}^{n}\Upsilon_{2i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Gamma_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\right)\right] \displaystyle\quad\quad\times\left(\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)^{2}\left(1+\frac{\overline{\zeta}}{2^{n}}\right)+\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)\frac{\varrho}{2^{n-1}}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Upsilon_{2i-1}^{n}\Upsilon_{2i}^{n}\left(\prod_{i=2}^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\Gamma_{i}^{n}\right)^{*}\right)\right]\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{C^{n,\varrho,\zeta}}{4^{n}}\right), $$

where $C^{n,\varrho,\zeta}$ is uniformly bounded by a constant that only depends on $\varrho$ (since $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ ). Hence, by induction, we get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B_{n-1}^{N}(t))^{*}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{C^{n,\varrho,\zeta}}{4^{n}}\right)^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)^{\chi}. $$

Thus we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B_{n-1}^{N}(t)\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(|B^{N}_{n}(t)|^{2}\right)\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(|B_{n-1}^{N}(t)|^{2}\right)\right]-2\Ree\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(B^{N}_{n}(t)(B_{n-1}^{N}(t))^{*}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n}}+\frac{|\zeta|^{2}}{4^{n+1}}\right)^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}+\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{|\zeta|^{2}}{4^{n}}\right)^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor} \displaystyle\quad-2\Ree\Bigg(\left(1+\frac{\varrho+\Ree\zeta}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{C^{n,\varrho,\zeta}}{4^{n}}\right)^{\lfloor t2^{n-1}\rfloor}\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\right)^{\chi}\Bigg). $$

Since $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ , the claimed bound for $B_{n}$ follows. The claim for $b_{n}$ follows from the same argument, using Proposition 3.16(b) in place of Proposition 3.16(a). ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.1.

We provide the proof for $B^{N}_{n}\to B^{N}$ ; the free version is essentially identical.

We first reduce to the case $p=2$ : we claim that for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , there exists a constant $C_{\varrho,T}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|B^{N}(t)-B^{N}_{n}(t)\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{C_{\varrho,T}}{2^{n/2}}\qquad\forall\,t\in[0,T]. $$

(Note the bound is stronger than the $p=2$ case of (4.5).) Before establishing (4.7) we use it to conclude the proof of the proposition. Note that, for $p\geq 1$ , and any random matrix $A$ ,

$$ |A|^{p}=(A^{\ast}A)^{\frac{p}{2}}=(A^{\ast}A)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}(A^{\ast}A)^{\frac{1}{2}}=|A|^{p-1}\cdot|A|, $$

and hence taking expected traces $\|A\|_{p}^{p}=\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}[|A|^{p-1}|A|]$ . Thus, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{p}^{p} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}[|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)|^{p-1}\cdot|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)|] \displaystyle\leq\left\||B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)|^{p-1}\right\|_{2}\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2} \displaystyle=\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}^{p-1}\cdot\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2}. $$

Now, $\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}\leq\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}+\left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}$ . By Lemma 4.3 (and the fact that $\|A\|_{p}\leq\|A\|_{\lceil p\rceil}$ ), there is a constant $C^{1}_{\varrho,T,p}$ with $\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}\leq C^{1}_{\varrho,T,p}$ for all $n,N$ and $t\in[0,T]$ .

Similarly, $\left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}\leq\left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2k}$ for $k=\lceil p-1\rceil$ . By [76, Theorem 5.1],

$$ \left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2k}^{2k}\leq\left\|b(t)\right\|_{2k}^{2k}+\frac{C(k,\varrho,\zeta,t)}{N^{2}} $$

where the constant $C(k,\varrho,\zeta,t)$ is continuous in all arguments; moreover, by [76, Proposition 1.8], $\|b(t)\|_{2k}^{2k}$ is continuous in $t$ . (These results are proved in [76] in the case $\zeta\in(-\varrho,\varrho)$ is real; tracking through the calculations shows they hold for general $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ complex, with formulas replacing $\zeta$ by $\mathrm{Re}\,\zeta$ .)

It follows by choosing $k$ with $2k>p$ that there is a constant $C^{2}_{\varrho,p,T}$ with $\sup_{N}\left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2(p-1)}\leq C^{2}_{\varrho,T,p}<\infty$ for $t\in[0,T]$ . Hence, from (4.8), we have

$$ \left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{p}^{p}\leq(C^{1}_{\varrho,T,p}+C^{2}_{\varrho,t,p})^{p-1}\cdot\left\|B^{N}_{n}(t)-B^{N}(t)\right\|_{2}. $$

Combining this with (4.7) and taking $p$ th roots, the proposition is thus proved with $C_{\varrho,T,p}:=(C_{\varrho,T})^{1/p}(C^{1}_{\varrho,T,p}+C^{2}_{\varrho,t,p})^{1-1/p}$ .

It remains to establish (4.7). Thanks to Lemma 4.4, $(B_{n}^{N})_{n\geq 0}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}))$ , and hence converges towards a stochastic process $\widetilde{B}^{N}$ . By construction, for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$

$$ \left\|\widetilde{B}^{N}(t)-B^{N}_{n}(t)\right\|_{2}\leq\sum_{s\geq n+1}\sqrt{C_{\varrho}\frac{t+1}{2^{s}}e^{K_{\varrho}t}}\leq\frac{\sqrt{C_{\varrho}(t+1)}e^{K_{\varrho}t/2}}{2^{n/2}(\sqrt{2}-1)}. $$

It only remains to show that $\widetilde{B}^{N}=B^{N}$ . By strong uniqueness for the SDE defining $B^{N}$ (see Definition 3.12) it suffices to show

$$ \widetilde{B}^{N}(t)=I_{N}+\int_{0}^{t}\widetilde{B}^{N}(s)dW^{N}(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\widetilde{B}^{N}(s)ds\qquad\forall t\geq 0. $$

We compute

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)dW^{N}(s) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\int_{\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}}^{\frac{j}{2^{n}}}B_{n}^{N}\left(\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}\right)dW^{N}(s)+\int_{t_{n}}^{t}B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)dW^{N}(s) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}B_{n}^{N}\left(\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}\right)\left(W^{N}\left(\frac{j}{2^{n}}\right)-W^{N}\left(\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}\right)\right)+B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\left(W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}\left(B_{n}^{N}\left(\frac{j}{2^{n}}\right)-B_{n}^{N}\left(\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}\right)\right)-\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor t2^{n}\rfloor}B_{n}^{N}\left(\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}\right) \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad+B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\left(W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right) \displaystyle=B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)-I_{N}-\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t_{n}}B_{n}^{N}(s)ds+B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\left(W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right) \displaystyle=B_{n}^{N}(t)-I_{N}-\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)ds+B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\left(W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\left(t-t_{n}\right)I_{N}\right). $$

Thanks to Lemma 4.3 and Hölder’s inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|B_{n}^{N}(t)-I_{N}-\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)dW^{N}(s)-\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)ds\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left\|B_{n}^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right\|_{4}^{2}\cdot\left\|W^{N}(t)-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\left(t-t_{n}\right)I_{N}\right\|_{4}^{2} \displaystyle\leq C_{2,t}\cdot\left\|W^{N}\left(t-t_{n}\right)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\left(t-t_{n}\right)I_{N}\right\|_{4}^{2} $$

wherein we used the fact that $C_{2,t}$ is nondecreasing in $t$ (and $t_{n}\leq t$ ) and that $W^{N}$ has stationary centered increments. Now, $e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}W^{N}(s)$ has the same distribution as $\sqrt{s}(aX^{N}+\mathbf{i}bY^{N})$ where $X^{N},Y^{N}$ are independent GUEs. The expected normalized trace moments of a GUE are well known from the genus expansion, see [75, Section 13.4]; in particular, $\left\|X^{N}\right\|_{4}^{4}=2+\frac{1}{N^{2}}\leq 3$ . By the triangle inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\leq C_{2,t}\cdot(t-t_{n})\cdot\left(|a|\left\|X^{N}\right\|_{4}+|b|\left\|Y^{N}\right\|_{4}+|\zeta|\right)^{2}=\mathcal{O}(2^{-n}) $$

so

$$ \left\|B_{n}^{N}(t)-I_{N}-\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)dW^{N}(s)-\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)ds\right\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(2^{-n/2}). $$

Now we also compare the above integrals of $B_{n}^{N}$ with the same integrals of $\widetilde{B}^{N}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\int_{0}^{t}B_{n}^{N}(s)dW^{N}(s)-\int_{0}^{t}\widetilde{B}^{N}(s)dW^{N}(s)\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=\left\|\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))dW^{N}(s)\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))dW^{N}(s)\left(\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))dW^{N}(s)\right)^{*}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{1\leq i,j,l,a,b,c\leq N}\ts_{N}\Bigg(\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))_{i,j}d(W^{N}(s))_{j,l}E_{i,l} \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\times\left(\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))_{a,b}d(W^{N}(s))_{b,c}E_{a,c}\right)^{*}\Bigg)\Bigg] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{1\leq i,j,l,b\leq N}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))_{i,j}d(W^{N}(s))_{j,l} \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\times\int_{0}^{t}\overline{(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))_{i,b}}\ d\overline{(W^{N}(s))_{b,l}}\Bigg] \displaystyle=\frac{2\varrho}{N^{2}}\sum_{1\leq i,j,l\leq N}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\left|(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))_{i,j}\right|^{2}ds\right] \displaystyle=2\varrho\int_{0}^{t}\left\|B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s)\right\|_{2}^{2}ds \displaystyle\leq\frac{\int_{0}^{t}C_{\varrho}(s+1)e^{K_{\varrho}s}ds}{2^{n}(\sqrt{2}-1)^{2}}, $$

where we used (4.9) in the last line. In combination with (4.12), and the fact that

$$ \left\|\int_{0}^{t}(B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s))ds\right\|_{2}\leq\int_{0}^{t}\left\|B_{n}^{N}(s)-\widetilde{B}^{N}(s)\right\|_{2}ds\,, $$

upon taking $n\to\infty$ we obtain (4.10) to complete the proof. ∎

### 4.3. Proof of Theorem 1.3

We now come to the main technical result of this section, from which Theorem 1.3 quickly follows.

#### Proposition 4.5.

Given a $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motion $B^{N}$ , driven by $W^{N}$ , there exists a constant $C_{\varrho,T}$ such that for all $k\geq 0$ and $t\leq T$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right)\right]\leq(tC_{\varrho,T})^{2k}e^{C_{\varrho,T}\frac{k^{4}}{N^{2}}}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Since the probability is trivially bounded by 1, by modifying the constant $C$ in the theorem statement we may assume $t\leq c\delta$ for any fixed $c=c(\varrho,T)>0$ . From Markov’s inequality and Proposition 4.5,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\right\|\geq\delta\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|\left|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right\|\geq\delta^{2k}\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\tr_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right)\geq\delta^{2k}\right) \displaystyle\leq N\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right)\right]}{\delta^{2k}} \displaystyle\leq N\left(\frac{tC_{\varrho,T}}{\delta}\right)^{2k}e^{C_{\varrho,T}\frac{k^{4}}{N^{2}}} \displaystyle=(e^{f(N,k)}t/\delta)^{2k} $$

for $f(N,x):=\log C_{\varrho,T}+\frac{1}{2x}\log N+\frac{1}{2}C_{\varrho,T}x^{3}/N^{2}$ . Now for any $x\in[N^{2/3},2N^{2/3}]$ ,

$$ f(N,x)\leq C_{0}:=\log C_{\varrho,T}+4C_{\varrho,T}+\sup_{N}N^{-2/3}\log N<\infty $$

so (4.13) is bounded by $(e^{C_{0}}t/\delta)^{2\lceil N^{2/3}\rceil},$ which in turn is at most $(e^{C_{0}}t/\delta)^{N^{2/3}}$ for $t\leq e^{-C_{0}}\delta$ . The claim follows. ∎

It remains to prove Proposition 4.5. We need the following:

#### Lemma 4.6.

Given $(b(t))_{t\geq 0}$ a $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -free Brownian motion driven by $(w(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , there exists constants $C_{\varrho},K_{\varrho}<\infty$ , such that

$$ \left\|b(t)\right\|\leq C_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t},\quad\left\|b(t)-1\right\|\leq\sqrt{t}\ C_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t},\quad\left\|b(t)-1-w(t)\right\|\leq t\ C_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t}. $$

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ b(t)=1+\int_{0}^{t}b(s)\ dw(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}b(s)ds, $$

$$ b(t)-1=\int_{0}^{t}b(s)\ dw(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}b(s)ds, $$

$$ b(t)-1-w(t)=\int_{0}^{t}(b(s)-1)\ dw(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}b(s)ds. $$

Besides $w=e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(ax+\mathbf{i}by)$ where $x,y$ are usual self-adjoint free Brownian motions. Thus by using the free Burkholder–Gundy inequality (see [18, Theorem 3.2.1]) coupled with the fact that

$$ \left\|\int_{0}^{t}b(s)ds\right\|\leq\left(\int_{0}^{t}\left\|b(s)\right\|^{2}ds\right)^{1/2}, $$

and $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ , we get that

$$ \left\|b(t)\right\|\leq 1+\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{t}\left\|b(s)\right\|^{2}ds\right)^{1/2}, $$

$$ \left\|b(t)-1\right\|\leq\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{t}\left\|b(s)\right\|^{2}ds\right)^{1/2}, $$

$$ \left\|b(t)-1-w(t)\right\|\leq\sqrt{32\varrho}\left(\sqrt{32\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{s}\left\|b(u)\right\|^{2}duds\right)^{1/2}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\left\|b(s)\right\|ds. $$

By squaring the first equation we get that

$$ \left\|b(t)\right\|^{2}\leq 2+2\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\left\|b(s)\right\|^{2}ds, $$

and by Gronwall’s inequality,

$$ \left\|b(t)\right\|^{2}\leq 2e^{2\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}t}. $$

Consequently, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|b(t)-1\right\| \displaystyle\leq\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{t}2e^{2\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}s}ds\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)\sqrt{2t}\ e^{\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}t}, $$

$$ \displaystyle\left\|b(t)-1-w(t)\right\| \displaystyle\leq 4\sqrt{2\varrho}\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{s}2e^{2\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}u}duds\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{\varrho}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\sqrt{2}e^{\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}s}ds \displaystyle\leq\left(8\sqrt{\varrho}\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)e^{\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}t}+\frac{\varrho}{\sqrt{2}}e^{\left(4\sqrt{2\varrho}+\frac{\varrho}{2}\right)^{2}t}\right)t. $$

Hence the conclusion. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.5.

To begin with, we define

$$ \displaystyle\boldsymbol{X}^{N}=\left(2^{n/2}\left(X^{N}\left(\textstyle{\frac{j}{2^{n}}}\right)-X^{N}\left(\textstyle{\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}}\right)\right)\right)_{1\leq j\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}, \displaystyle\boldsymbol{Y}^{N}=\left(2^{n/2}\left(Y^{N}\left(\textstyle{\frac{j}{2^{n}}}\right)-Y^{N}\left(\textstyle{\frac{j-1}{2^{n}}}\right)\right)\right)_{1\leq j\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}, $$

where $(X^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(Y^{N}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are the Hermitian Brownian motions used to define $W^{N}$ in Definition 3.10. In this proof, we work with $\mathcal{P}_{d}$ where $d=2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor$ . Besides, those $2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor$ indeterminates will be sorted in the following order: $X_{1},\dots,X_{\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor},$ $Y_{1},\dots,Y_{\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}$ . In particular, $\partial_{p}$ will be the non-commutative differential with respect to $X_{p}$ if $p\in[1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor]$ , and with respect to $Y_{p-\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}$ if $p\in[\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor+1,2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor]$ . $$ \displaystyle S_{n} \displaystyle:=\prod_{1\leq j\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}+e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\frac{aX_{j}+bY_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right), \displaystyle Q_{n} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\bigg|S_{n}-\sum_{1\leq j\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\frac{aX_{j}+\mathbf{i}bY_{j}}{2^{n/2}}-1\bigg|^{2k} $$

in non-commuting indeterminates $X_{j},Y_{j}$ . Note that $Q_{n}$ is such that $Q_{n}(\boldsymbol{X}^{N},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N})=\left|B^{N}_{n}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right|^{2k}$ . for any integer $s\geq 1$ , with the convention $\alpha_{0}(Q_{n})=\tau(Q_{n}(\boldsymbol{x}^{0},\boldsymbol{y}^{0}))$ . From there on, we will divide the proof in two steps where we upper bound each of the terms in the equation above, before eventually letting $s$ go to infinity.

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{s}^{N}(Q_{n})=\frac{1}{2^{s}}\int_{A_{s}}e^{-t_{2s}-\dots-t_{1}}\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\Big(\left[\mathcal{L}_{s}(Q_{n},T_{s})\right](\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{s}},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N,T_{s}})\Big)\right]\ dt_{1}\dots dt_{2s}\,. $$

This property of the polynomials $Q_{n}$ and $P_{n}$ is preserved under application of the operator $\mathcal{L}_{s}$ . Indeed, thanks to Lemma 3.21(c), we know that applying the operator $\mathcal{L}_{s}$ to a monomial $M$ yields a sum of monomials (with coefficients 1).
