$$ \displaystyle\int_{A_{s}}e^{-t_{2s}-\dots-t_{1}}\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\Big(\left[\mathcal{L}_{s}(Q_{n},T_{s})\right](\boldsymbol{X}^{N,T_{s}},\boldsymbol{Y}^{N,T_{s}})\Big)\right]\ dt_{1}\dots dt_{2s} \displaystyle\leq\int_{A_{s}}e^{-t_{2s}-\dots-t_{1}}dt_{1}\dots dt_{2s}\mathbb{E}\left[\left[\mathcal{L}_{s}(P_{n},T_{s})\right](g,\widetilde{g})\right]. $$

Besides, if $q_{1},q_{2}\in[1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor]$ and $p\in[l,m]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{p}\left(\prod_{q_{1}\leq j\leq q_{2}}\left(1+\frac{|\zeta|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{|a|X_{j}+|b|Y_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right)\right) \displaystyle=\frac{|a|}{2^{n/2}}\prod_{q_{1}\leq j<p}\left(1+\frac{|\zeta|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{|a|X_{j}+|b|Y_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right)\otimes\prod_{p<j\leq q_{2}}\left(1+\frac{|\zeta|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{|a|X_{j}+|b|Y_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right). $$

And we have the exact same formula for $\partial_{p+\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}$ but with $|a|$ replaced by $|b|$ in the first instance on the right hand side. Thus, a term of the $m$ -th kind associated to $U_{n}$ will be of the form

$$ \left(\frac{P_{1}}{2^{n/2}},\dots,\frac{P_{m}}{2^{n/2}},P_{m+1}\right), $$

where

$$ P_{l}=|c_{l}|\prod_{p_{l}\leq j<p_{l+1}}\left(1+\frac{|\zeta|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{|a|X_{j}+|b|Y_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right), $$

for $c_{m+1}=1$ , $c_{l}\in\{a,b\}$ else and $p_{l}\in[1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor]$ . Therefore, with the notations of Definition 3.18, we have $c(U_{n})=1$ . We also set $g_{j}:=g_{j,J}$ since this does not depend on $J$ . Then, thanks to Lemma 3.21 used with $d=2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor$ , for any $T_{s}\in A_{s}$ , we get that $\left[\mathcal{L}_{s}(P_{n},T_{s})\right](g,\widetilde{g})$ is a sum of at most $(2k)^{4s}(2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor)^{2s}$ $U_{n}$ -monomials evaluated in $(g,\widetilde{g})$ . Each of those quantities can then be upper bounded (since both $|a|$ and $|b|$ are smaller than $\sqrt{\varrho}$ ) by

$$ \left(\frac{\varrho}{2^{n}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{m\geq 0}mr_{m}}\prod_{j=1}^{\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\left|1+\frac{|\zeta|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{|a|g_{j}+|b|\widetilde{g}_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right|^{2k-z_{j}}, $$

where $z_{j}\in[0,2k]$ is such that $z_{1}+\dots+z_{\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}=4s$ , and $r_{m}$ is the number of terms of the $m$ -th kind used to build the $U_{n}$ -monomial. But thanks to Lemma 3.21(e),

$$ \sum_{m\geq 0}mr_{m}=\sum_{m\geq 0}(m+1)r_{m}-\sum_{m\geq 0}r_{m}=2k+4s-2k=4s. $$

Consequently, for some constant $C_{k,t,\varrho}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left[\mathcal{L}_{s}(P_{n},T_{s})\right](g,\widetilde{g})\right] \displaystyle\leq(2k)^{4s}(2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor)^{2s}\left(\frac{\varrho}{2^{n}}\right)^{2s}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|1+\frac{|\zeta|}{2^{n+1}}+\frac{|a|g_{j}+|b|\widetilde{g}_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right|^{2k}\right]^{\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor} \displaystyle\leq(2k)^{4s}(2\varrho t)^{2s}\ C_{k,t,\varrho}, $$

where for the last line we argue as in the proof of Lemma 4.3. Combining with Lemma 3.21(a), we conclude

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{n}\tilde{\alpha}_{s}^{N}(Q_{n}) \displaystyle\leq\frac{(2k)^{4s}(2\varrho t)^{2s}}{s!}\ C_{k,t,\varrho}. $$

Step 2: We turn to bound the coefficients $\alpha_{i}(Q_{n})$ in (4.14), where

$$ \alpha_{i}(Q_{n})=\frac{1}{2^{i}}\int_{A_{i}}e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}}\tau\Big(\left[\mathcal{L}_{i}(Q_{n},T_{i})\right](\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{i}},\boldsymbol{y}^{T_{i}})\Big)\ dt_{1}\dots dt_{2i}\,. $$

Note that if we set

$$ R_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\prod_{1\leq j\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}+e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\frac{aX_{j}+\mathbf{i}bY_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right)-\sum_{1\leq j\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\frac{aX_{j}+\mathbf{i}bY_{j}}{2^{n/2}}-1, $$

so that $Q_{n}=|R_{n}|^{2k}$ , as well as

$$ S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}=\prod_{q_{1}\leq j\leq q_{2}}\left(1+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}+e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\frac{aX_{j}+\mathbf{i}bY_{j}}{2^{n/2}}\right), $$

then for $p\in[1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{p}R_{n} \displaystyle=\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}\left(S_{n}^{1,p-1}\otimes S_{n}^{p+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}-1\otimes 1\right) \displaystyle=\frac{ae^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}\left(\left(S_{n}^{1,p-1}-1\right)\otimes S_{n}^{p+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}+1\otimes\left(S_{n}^{p+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}-1\right)\right). $$

And similarly for $p\in[q_{1},q_{2}]$ , we get that

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{p}S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}=\frac{e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}a}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{q_{1},p-1}\otimes S_{n}^{p+1,q_{2}}. $$

We also have similar formulas for $p\in[\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor+1,2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor]$ . Consequently, we have $c(R_{n})=2$ and terms of the first kind associated to $R_{n}$ are of the following form:

$$ \left(\frac{ce^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}\left(S_{n}^{1,p-1}-1\right),S_{n}^{p+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(\frac{ce^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}},S_{n}^{p+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}-1\right), $$

where $c\in\{a,b\}$ . Besides, terms of the $m$ -th kind for $m\geq 2$ are of the form

$$ \left(\frac{c_{1}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{1,p_{1}-1},\frac{c_{2}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{p_{1}+1,p_{2}-1},\dots,\frac{c_{m}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{p_{m-1}+1,p_{m}-1},S_{n}^{p_{m}+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\right), $$

$$ \text{or}\quad\left(\frac{c_{1}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}},\frac{c_{2}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{p_{1}+1,p_{2}-1},\dots,\frac{c_{m}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{p_{m-1}+1,p_{m}-1},S_{n}^{p_{m}+1,\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\right), $$

with $c_{l}\in\{a,b\}$ . Thus, thanks to Lemma 3.21, $\left[\mathcal{L}_{i}(Q_{n},T_{i})\right](\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{i}},y^{T_{i}})$ is a sum of at most $(4k)^{4i}(2\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor)^{2i}$ $R_{n}$ -monomials which are themselves products of $2k+4i$ polynomials of the following form (or of its adjoints):

$$ \displaystyle R_{n},\quad\frac{ce^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}\left(S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}-1\right),\quad\frac{ce^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}},\quad\frac{ce^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}, $$

each evaluated in a given free semicircular system and with $c\in\{a,b\}$ . Besides, since both $|a|$ and $|b|$ are smaller than $\sqrt{\varrho}$ , given $(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=(x_{i},y_{i})_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}$ a free semicircular system, thanks to Hölder inequality, one can upper bound the trace of such an expression by

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\varrho}{2^{n}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{m\geq 0}mr_{m}} \displaystyle\left\|R_{n}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\right\|_{2k+4i}^{r_{0}}\times\left(\sup_{q_{1},q_{2}}\left\|S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})-1\right\|_{2k+4i}\right)^{r_{1}} \displaystyle\times \displaystyle\left(\sup_{q_{1},q_{2}}\left\|S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\right\|_{2k+4i}\right)^{2k+4i-r_{1}-r_{0}}. $$

Let us now remark that thanks to Proposition 4.1 and Lemma 4.6, there exist constants $C_{\varrho,t,k,i}$ such that for $1\leq q_{1}\leq q_{2}\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor$ ,

$$ \left\|R_{n}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\right\|_{2k+4i}\leq tC_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t}+C_{\varrho,t,k,i}\ 2^{-\frac{n}{4k+8i}}, $$

$$ \displaystyle\left\|S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})-1\right\|_{2k+4i} \displaystyle=\left\|b_{n}\left(\frac{q_{2}-q_{1}+1}{2^{n}}\right)-1\right\|_{2k+4i}\leq\sqrt{t}C_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t}+\frac{C_{\varrho,t,k,i}}{2^{n/(4k+8i)}}, $$

$$ \left\|S_{n}^{q_{1},q_{2}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\right\|_{2k+4i}=\left\|b_{n}\left(\frac{l-m+1}{2^{n}}\right)\right\|_{2k+4i}\leq C_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t}+\frac{C_{\varrho,t,k,i}}{2^{n/(4k+8i)}}. $$

Thus, by using again Lemma 3.21(e) as in Equation (4.15), we get that (4.17) is upper bounded by

$$ \frac{\varrho^{2i}}{2^{2ni}}t^{r_{0}+\frac{r_{1}}{2}}\left(C_{\varrho}e^{K_{\varrho}t}\right)^{2k+4i}+K_{\varrho,t,k,i}2^{-\left(2i+c_{k,i}\right)n}, $$

for some constant $K_{\varrho,t,k,i}$ . Besides, thanks to Lemma 4.7 below coupled with Lemma 3.21(e), one can always lower bound $r_{1}+\frac{r_{2}}{2}$ by $2k-2i$ . Thus, one can upper bound $t^{r_{1}+\frac{r_{2}}{2}}$ by $t^{2k-2i}$ (up to a constant $T^{2i}$ if $t\geq 1$ ). Finally, we get that for some constant $C_{\varrho,T}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left|\int_{A_{i}}e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}}\tau\Big(\left[\mathcal{L}_{i}(Q_{n},T_{i})\right](\boldsymbol{x}^{T_{i}},\boldsymbol{y}^{T_{i}})\Big)\ dt_{1}\dots dt_{2i}\right| \displaystyle\leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_{A_{i}}e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}}dt_{1}\dots dt_{2i}\times k^{4i}\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor^{2i}\times\frac{1}{2^{2ni}}t^{2k-2i}(C_{\varrho,T})^{2k+i} \displaystyle\leq\frac{k^{4i}}{i!}t^{2k}(C_{\varrho,T})^{2k+i}, $$

where we used 3.21(a) in the last line.

From (4.14), (4.16) and Corollary 4.2, we have shown that for all integers $k,s\geq 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right)\right]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}_{n}(t)-I_{N}-W^{N}\left(t_{n}\right)\right|^{2k}\right)\right] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\leq\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}\frac{k^{4i}(C_{\varrho,T})^{i}}{N^{2i}i!}(tC_{\varrho,T})^{2k}+\frac{(2k)^{4s}(2\varrho t)^{2s}}{s!}\ C_{k,t,\varrho} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\leq(tC_{\varrho,T})^{2k}e^{C_{\varrho,T}\frac{k^{4}}{N^{2}}}+\frac{(2k)^{4s}(2\varrho t)^{2s}}{s!}\ C_{k,t,\varrho} $$

The result now follows by letting $s\to\infty$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.7.

If a sequence of non-negative integers $(r_{m})_{m\geq 0}$ satisfies

$$ \sum_{m\geq 0}(m+1)r_{m}=2k+4i,\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{m\geq 0}r_{m}=2k, $$

then $r_{0}+\frac{r_{1}}{2}\geq 2k-2i$ .

#### Proof.

We have

$$ \sum_{m\geq 0}(m+1)r_{m}=\sum_{m\geq 0}r_{m}+4i, $$

thus

$$ \frac{r_{1}}{2}+\sum_{m\geq 2}r_{m}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{m\geq 1}mr_{m}=2i. $$

Therefore,

$$ r_{0}+\frac{r_{1}}{2}=2k-\frac{r_{1}}{2}-\sum_{m\geq 2}r_{m}\geq 2k-2i.\qed $$

### 4.4. Tail bound for the norm

We will also need a concentration estimate on the norm of $B^{N}(t)$ . One could obtain it by using Proposition 4.5 coupled with an estimate on the norm of a GUE matrix and the triangle inequality. However, following the strategy developed in the proof of Proposition 4.5 yields the desired bound with no need for another reference. Hence, we have the following result.

#### Theorem 4.8.

There exists a constant $c_{\varrho,T}$ such that for any $t\in[0,T]$ and $K>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|\geq K\right)\leq\left(\frac{c_{\varrho,T}}{K}\right)^{N^{2/3}}. $$

#### Proof.

One has

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|B^{N}(t)\right\|\geq K\right)\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|\left|B^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right\|\geq K^{2k}\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\tr_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right)\geq K^{2k}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{N}{K^{2k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\left|B^{N}(t)\right|^{2k}\right)\right]. $$

The rest of the proof then follows exactly like those of Proposition 4.5 and 1.3. ∎

Letting $K>c_{\varrho,t}$ so that $r=c_{\varrho,t}/K\in(0,1)$ , an application of the Borel–Cantelli lemma yields the following:

#### Corollary 4.9.

There is some constant $K=K_{\varrho,t}<\infty$ so that

$$ \mathbb{P}\{\|B^{N}(t)\|\leq K\text{ for all large }N\}=1. $$

## 5. Estimates on Small Singular Values

To lighten notation, in this section we drop the superscript $N$ from matrices $B^{N}(t),Z^{N}$ , etc.

As discussed in Section 1.6, a key step in the Hermitization approach is to establish quantitative lower bounds on small singular value of shifts of $B(t)$ . Specifically, for an arbitrary fixed $N\times N$ matrix $A$ we seek bounds of the form

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N}(B(t)+A)\leq\delta)\lesssim N^{C}\delta^{c}\qquad\forall\delta\geq 0 $$

for the smallest singular value, and

$$ \sigma_{N-\ell}(B(t)+A)\geq c^{\prime}(\ell/N)^{C^{\prime}}\qquad\forall\,\ell\in[k,\kappa N] $$

holding with high probability for some $k=o(N)$ and $\kappa>0$ independent of $N$ . Such control is provided by the following two propositions.

#### Proposition 5.1 (Smallest singular value).

Let $(B(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be a $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motion. Let $A$ be an $N\times N$ matrix, deterministic or random and independent of $(B(t))_{t\geq 0}$ . Then the following hold for $0<t\leq T<\infty$ .

- (a) If $|\zeta|<\varrho$ , then for all $\alpha>0$ , (5.1) holds for all $N\geq(4/\alpha)^{3/2}+t^{-1/2}$ , with $C=2$ , $c=1-\alpha$ and the implicit constant depending only on $\alpha,\varrho,\zeta,T$ .

- (b) (Degenerate case). If $|\zeta|=\varrho$ , then (5.1) holds for universal constants $C,c\in(0,\infty)$ and all $N\geq t^{-c/C}$ , with the implicit constant in (5.1) depending only on $\varrho$ and $T$ .

#### Proposition 5.2 (Mesoscopic singular values).

In the setting of Proposition 5.1 (with no assumptions on $\zeta,\varrho$ ) there are universal constants $C,c\in(0,\infty)$ such that for any $k\geq C\log N$ , (5.2) holds with $C^{\prime}=2$ , $c^{\prime}=c^{\prime}(\varrho,\zeta,T)>0$ , $\kappa=\sqrt{t}$ with probability at least $1-\exp(-\min\{ck,N^{2/3}\})$ .

The key to the proof of both Propositions is Theorem 1.3, which enables a reduction to the study of shifted Gaussian matrices, for which we have the following two lemmas.

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $G$ be an $N\times N$ complex Ginibre or GUE matrix (having the distribution of $Z^{N}(1)$ or $X^{N}(1)$ in Definition 3.8), and let $A$ be an arbitrary complex $N\times N$ matrix, deterministic or random and independent of $G$ . Then

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N}(G+A)\leq\delta)\leq N^{C}\delta^{c}\qquad\forall\,\delta\geq 0 $$

for universal constants $C,c\in(0,\infty)$ .

For the Ginibre case see [10, Lemma 3.3], where it is established with optimal constants $C=c=2$ . (For a short argument with sub-optimal constants see [21, $\mathsection$ 4.4].) The GUE case appears to be new (note the perturbation $A$ is not assumed to be Hermitian). We defer the proof and a discussion of related literature to Appendix A.1.

#### Lemma 5.4.

There is a universal constant $c>0$ such that the following holds. Let $G$ be an $N\times N$ matrix with standard real Gaussian entries, and assume the $N(N+1)/2$ pairs $\{(G_{ij},G_{ji}):1\leq i\leq j\leq N\}$ are jointly independent. Then for any $N\times N$ complex matrix $A$ , deterministic or random and independent of $G$ , and any $k\geq c^{-1}\log N$ ,

$$ \sigma_{N-\ell}(G+A)\geq c\ell/N\qquad\forall\ell\,\geq k $$

with probability at least $1-e^{-ck}$ .

The proof of Lemma 5.4 is deferred to Appendix A.2.

We note that the unshifted matrix $B(t)$ is always well invertible with high probability:

#### Lemma 5.5.

For any $0<t\leq T<\infty$ and $\delta>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N}(B(t))\leq\delta)=\mathcal{O}_{\varrho,T}(\delta)^{N^{2/3}}. $$

#### Proof.

For any $t>0$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_{N}(B(t))\leq\delta\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\big(\big\|B(t)^{-1}\big\|\geq 1/\delta\big). $$

However, following (1.6), if we define $(\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ as the solution of the following stochastic differential equation:

$$ \rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)=I-\int_{0}^{t}dW(s)\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(s)+\frac{\zeta}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(s)ds $$

we get thanks to classical stochastic calculus that $B(t)\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)=I$ for all $t\geq 0$ (see [76, Section 4.2] for further details). In particular,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N}\left(B(t))\leq\delta\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)\right\|\geq 1/\delta\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$B$}(t)^{*}\right\|\geq 1/\delta\right). $$

But if ${B}^{\dagger}(t)=((B(t))^{-1})^{*}$ , and $W^{\dagger}(t)=-\left(W(t)\right)^{*}$ , we have that

$$ B^{\dagger}(t)=I+\int_{0}^{t}B^{\dagger}(s)d\widetilde{W}(s)+\frac{\overline{\zeta}}{2}\int_{0}^{t}B^{\dagger}(s)ds. $$

Since $(W^{\dagger}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ has the same law as $(W_{\varrho,\overline{\zeta}}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , we have that $(B^{\dagger}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is a $(\varrho,\overline{\zeta})$ -Brownian motion. Hence the conclusion follows thanks to Theorem 4.8. ∎

We turn to prove Propositions 5.1 and 5.2. We will first handle the case that $|\zeta|<\varrho$ and later note the modifications needed for the degenerate case.

With $|\zeta|<\varrho$ , and recalling the parametrization (3.5), we may assume without loss of generality that $0<b\leq|a|$ .

Given independent $(\varrho,\zeta)$ -Brownian motions $(B(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , $(\widetilde{B}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ driven respectively by $(W(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , $(\widetilde{W}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ , we have for any $0\leq\varepsilon\leq t$ the equality in law

$$ B(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny$d$}}}{{=}}B(t-\varepsilon)\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon). $$

Next we show that up to a small error we can replace $\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)$ with a shift $cG+M$ of a scaled Ginibre matrix $G$ for some $c=c(\varepsilon)>0$ , where $G$ and $M$ are independent. Indeed, note that if $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and $X,Y$ are independent GUE matrices of size $N$ , then $\alpha X+\beta Y$ has the same law as $\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}Z$ where $Z$ is also a GUE matrix. Furthermore, $\widetilde{W}(\varepsilon)$ has the same law as

$$ \sqrt{\varepsilon}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\left(aX+\mathbf{i}bY\right). $$

Thus, since $|a|\geq b\geq 0$ , we get that $\widetilde{W}(\varepsilon)$ has the same law as

$$ b\sqrt{\varepsilon}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\left(X+\mathbf{i}Y\right)+\sqrt{|\zeta|}\sqrt{\varepsilon}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\widetilde{X}, $$

where $\widetilde{X}$ is an independent copy of $X$ . Consequently,

$$ \widetilde{W}(\varepsilon)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny$d$}}}{{=}}b\sqrt{2\varepsilon}G+\sqrt{|\zeta|}\sqrt{\varepsilon}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\widetilde{X} $$

where $G$ is a Ginibre random matrix independent of $\widetilde{X}$ .

For $\varepsilon,\delta_{0},\delta_{1}\geq 0$ , denote the event

$$ \mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}(\delta_{0},\delta_{1},\varepsilon):=\big\{\,\sigma_{N}(B(t-\varepsilon))\geq\delta_{0},\,\|\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)-I-\widetilde{W}(\varepsilon)\|\leq\delta_{1}\,\big\}\,. $$

From Lemma 5.5 and Theorem 1.3,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}(\delta_{0},\delta_{1},\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{c}})\leq\mathcal{O}_{\varrho,T}(\delta_{0})^{N^{2/3}}+\mathcal{O}_{\varrho,T}(\varepsilon/\delta_{1})^{N^{2/3}}. $$

On $\mathcal{G}$ , for any $0\leq\ell\leq N-1$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{N-\ell}(B(t-\varepsilon)\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)+A) \displaystyle\geq\delta_{0}\,\sigma_{N-\ell}\big(\,\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)+B(t-\varepsilon)^{-1}A\,\big) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{N-\ell}\big(\,\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)+B(t-\varepsilon)^{-1}A\,\big) \displaystyle\geq\sigma_{N-\ell}\big(\,\widetilde{W}(\varepsilon)+I+B(t-\varepsilon)^{-1}A\,\big)-\delta_{1}\,. $$

Combining with (5.5) and (5.8) we have that for any $\delta\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\,\sigma_{N-\ell}(B(t)+A)\leq\delta\,,\,\mathcal{G}\,\Big) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\Big(\,\sigma_{N-\ell}(B(t-\varepsilon)\widetilde{B}(\varepsilon)+A)\leq\delta\,,\,\mathcal{G}\,\Big) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\,\sigma_{N-\ell}\big(b\sqrt{2\varepsilon}G+M\big)\leq\frac{\delta}{\delta_{0}}+\delta_{1}\bigg) $$

where

$$ M:=I+\sqrt{|\zeta|}\sqrt{\varepsilon}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}\widetilde{X}+B(t-\varepsilon)^{-1}A $$

is independent of the Ginibre matrix $G$ .

To conclude the proof of Proposition 5.1 for the case $|\zeta|<\varrho$ we use Lemma 5.3, along with (5.10) and (5.11) with $\ell=0$ and $\varepsilon,\delta_{0},\delta_{1}>0$ to be chosen, to get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\,\sigma_{N}(B(t)+A)\leq\delta\Big)\leq\frac{N^{2}}{2b^{2}\varepsilon}\bigg(\frac{\delta}{\delta_{0}}+\delta_{1}\bigg)^{2}+\mathcal{O}_{\varrho,T}(\delta_{0}+\varepsilon\delta_{1}^{-1})^{N^{2/3}}. $$

The claim follows upon taking $\varepsilon:=\delta$ , $\delta_{0}:=\delta^{\alpha/2}$ and $\delta_{1}:=\delta^{1-\alpha/2}$ . (Note that we may assume $\delta\leq N^{-2}$ as the claimed bound is trivial otherwise, so to ensure $\varepsilon=\delta\leq t$ it suffices to have $N\geq t^{-1/2}$ .)

Turning to conclude the proof of Proposition 5.2 for the case $|\zeta|<\varrho$ , from a union bound over the choices of $\ell$ , it suffices to show that for any fixed $\ell\geq C\log N$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N-\ell}(B(t)+A)\leq c(\ell/N)^{2})\leq e^{-c\ell}+\exp(-2N^{2/3}). $$

Taking $\delta_{0}=c$ , $\delta=\delta_{1}=c^{2}(\ell/N)^{2}$ , and $\varepsilon=c\delta$ for sufficiently small $c=c(T,\varrho,\zeta)>0$ , from (5.11) and (5.10) we can bound the left hand side above by

$$ \mathbb{P}\bigg(\sigma_{N-\ell}\Big(G+\frac{1}{b\sqrt{2\varepsilon}}M\Big)\leq\frac{2\sqrt{c}}{b}\frac{\ell}{N}\bigg)+\exp(-2N^{2/3}). $$

Taking $c$ smaller if necessary, Proposition 5.2 now follows from Lemma 5.4 after conditioning on the imaginary part of $G$ (rescaling by a factor $\sqrt{2}$ to standardize the real parts of the entries). From the constraint $\varepsilon\leq t$ , with this choice of parameters we can take $\ell$ as large as $C_{0}\sqrt{t}N$ for any fixed $C_{0}>0$ by shrinking $c$ .

We turn to the degenerate case $|\zeta|=\varrho$ . Now we may assume $b=0<a=\sqrt{\varrho}$ . Returning to (5.6), we see that $\widetilde{W}(\varepsilon)$ has the same law as

$$ \sqrt{a\varepsilon}e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}X, $$

where $X$ is a GUE matrix. Following the same lines we get that for any $\ell\geq 0$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\,\sigma_{N-\ell}(B(t)+A)\leq\delta\,,\,\mathcal{G}\,\Big) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\,\sigma_{N-\ell}\big(\sqrt{a\varepsilon}X+M^{\prime}\big)\leq\frac{\delta}{\delta_{0}}+\delta_{1}\bigg) $$

where now $M^{\prime}:=e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}(I+B(t-\varepsilon)^{-1}A)$ is independent of the GUE matrix $X$ . The proof now concludes along the same lines as for the case $|\zeta|<\varrho$ , using the GUE case of Lemma 5.3, and applying Lemma 5.4 to $\sqrt{2}$ times the real part of $X$ . ∎

## 6. An Analytic Approach for Mesoscopic Singular Values

In this section we provide an alternative argument for a lower bound on small singular values of $B_{0}^{N}B^{N}(t)-zI$ , as in Proposition 5.2. That proposition implies that the empirical cumulative distribution function of shifted singular values is essentially Hölder- $\frac{1}{2}$ continuous near $0$ , at shrinking scales, for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ . This is enough (in conjunction with the bound on polynomial decay of the smallest singular value in 5.1) to yield convergence of the empirical law of eigenvalues; in fact, it would be enough to have a Hölder continuity bound (of varying exponent) just at Lebesgue almost every $z\in\mathbb{C}$ .

In this section, we show that: at least for the Brownian motion $B^{N}(t)$ started at the identity (i.e. $B^{N}_{0}=I$ ), the expected empirical CDF of singular values $\sigma_{j}(B^{N}(t)-zI)$ is actually Lipschitz near $0$ , for Lebesgue almost all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ . In particular: the only $z$ where this may fail (and instead we get Hölder- $\frac{1}{2}$ continuity) are on the boundary of the the support set of the Brown measure of the limit free multiplicative Brownian motion.

To state and prove this precisely, we make the same parameter reduction as in Notation 2.2: Since $B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}B^{N}_{t\varrho,t\zeta}(1)$ , we henceforth consider the random matrices and operators

$$ B^{N}(t,\zeta)=B^{N}_{t,\zeta}(1)\quad\&\quad b(t,\zeta)=b_{t,\zeta}(1). $$

Recall that the Brown measure of $b(t,\zeta)$ was identified in [63]; in particular, its support set is a compact region $\overline{\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)}$ defined in Theorem 2.3. The boundary $\partial\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ is a simple smooth closed curve if $t<4$ , a smooth “figure-eight” curve if $t=4$ , and the union of two disjoint simple smooth closed curves if $t>4$ . In particular, the Lebesgue measure of $\partial\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ is $0$ for all $t>0$ and $|\zeta|\leq t$ .

#### Proposition 6.1.

Let $T>0$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq t$ . Let $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\partial\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ . Then there is a constant $\overline{C}_{z,T}$ so that, for all $N\in\mathbb{N}$ , all $t\in[0,T]$ , and all $\eta>N^{-2/11}$ ,

$$ \left|\mathrm{Im}\,\mathbb{E}\ts_{N}[(i\eta-|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|)^{-1}]\right|\leq\overline{C}_{z,T}. $$

Proposition 6.1 is a strong Wegner anti-concentration estimate (see [113]). The (conclusion of the) proof is in Section 6.3 below. It follows that the expected CDF of the empirical law of singular values of $B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)-zI$ is uniformly Lipschitz on mesoscopic-to-macroscopic scales.

#### Corollary 6.2.

For $0<t\leq T<\infty$ and $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\partial\Sigma(1,t\varrho,t\zeta)$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{E}\mu_{|B_{\varrho,\zeta}^{N}(t)-zI|}([0,\eta])=\mathcal{O}_{\varrho,z,T}(\eta) $$

uniformly for $\eta\in[N^{-2/11},1]$ .

#### Proof.

Since $B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lower 0.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}$}}}{{=}}B^{N}_{t\varrho,t\zeta}(1)=B^{N}(t\varrho,t\zeta)$ , it suffices to prove the corollary for $B^{N}(t,\zeta)$ ; i.e. for $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\partial\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}\mu_{|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|}([0,\eta])=\mathcal{O}_{z,T}(\eta). $$

Now since $\mathrm{Im}(i\eta-x)^{-1}=-\eta/(\eta^{2}+x^{2})$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , the claim follows from Proposition 6.1 and the pointwise bound $\eta/(\eta^{2}+x^{2})\geq(2\eta)^{-1}\mathbbm{1}_{x\in[0,\eta]}$ . ∎

Corollary 6.2 can be substituted for Proposition 5.2 in the proof of Theorem 1.2 in Section 7 (for the case $B_{0}^{N}=I$ ), following the argument from [58].

#### Remark 6.3.

It is worth noting that, for any matrix $A^{N}\in\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ , the spectral measure $\mu_{|A^{N}|}$ is exactly the empirical law of singular values $\sigma_{j}(A^{N})$ ; thus

$$ \mu_{|A^{N}|}([0,\eta])=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{\sigma_{j}(A^{N})}([0,\eta])=\frac{\#\{j\leq N\colon\sigma_{j}(A^{N})\leq\eta\}}{N}. $$

This is indeed the empirical CDF of singular values. Hence, Corollary 6.2 says that the expected empirical CDF of singular values of $B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)-zI$ is Lipschitz near $0$ , with a Lipschitz constant that is is locally uniform in $t$ , for all $z$ except possibly on the boundary of the domain $\Sigma(1,t\varrho,t\zeta)$ .

The quantity on the left-hand-side of (6.2) is the (imaginary part of the) expected Cauchy transform $G_{|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|}(i\eta)$ . Our approach to prove Proposition 6.1 is to compare this to the Cauchy transform of the large- $N$ limit operator, $G_{|b(t,\zeta)-z|}(i\eta)$ . As shown in Section 6.1 below, this difference is $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{N^{2}})$ with constants that depend polynomially on $1/\eta$ ; then by choosing $\eta>N^{-\alpha}$ for an appropriate power $\alpha>0$ , the bound (6.2) reduces to a similar bound on the free multiplicative Brownian motion; i.e. it reduces to showing $G_{|b(t,\zeta)-z|}(i\eta)$ is bounded for $\eta>0$ . This is accomplished in Section 6.2, primarily using analytic results derived from the PDE methods in [48, 63] together with spectral bounds from [62].

### 6.1. Smooth Functional Comparison to the Large- $N$ Limit

Throughout this section, our estimates will be formulated in terms of the overparametrized $B^{N}(t)=B^{N}_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ ; they will be converted to the reduced parametrization $B^{N}(t,\zeta)$ when needed in Section 6.3. Additionally, the tools in this section apply equally well for a deterministic initial condition $B_{0}^{N}$ , so we prove them in that level of generality for potential future use.

We begin with the following lemma.

#### Lemma 6.4.

Let $B_{0}^{N}$ be a deterministic matrix. There exists a constant $C_{\varrho,t}$ such that, for any $y\in\mathbb{R}$ , we have that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}y\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right|^{2}}\right)\right]-\tau_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}y|B^{N}_{0}b(t)-z|^{2}}\right)\right| \displaystyle\leq C_{\varrho,t}\frac{(1+y^{4})(1+|z|^{4})(1+\left\|B^{N}_{0}\right\|^{4})}{N^{2}}, $$

where we used the construction of the space $\mathscr{A}_{N}$ of Lemma 3.9 to define the product of $B^{N}_{0}$ and $b(t)$ .

#### Proof.

Given two operators $A$ and $B$ , one has that

$$ e^{A}-e^{B}=\int_{0}^{1}e^{\alpha A}(A-B)e^{(1-\alpha)B}d\alpha. $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}y\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right|^{2}}\right)\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}y\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}_{n}(t)-z\right|^{2}}\right)\right]\right| \displaystyle=\Bigg|y\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\ts_{N}\Big(e^{\mathbf{i}\alpha y\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right|^{2}}\Big(\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right|^{2} \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad-\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}_{n}(t)-z\right|^{2}\Big)e^{\mathbf{i}y(1-\alpha)\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}_{n}(t)-z\right|^{2}}\Big)\Big]d\alpha\Bigg| \displaystyle\leq\left|y\right|\left\|B^{N}_{0}\right\|\left(\left\|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right\|_{2}+\left\|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}_{n}(t)-z\right\|_{2}\right)\left\|B^{N}(t)-B^{N}_{n}(t)\right\|_{2}, $$

where we used that for any self-adjoint operator $X$ , the operator norm of $e^{\mathbf{i}yX}$ is equal to $1$ . Thus, thanks to Lemma 4.3 and Proposition 4.1,

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}yB^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)}\right)\right]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}yB^{N}_{0}B^{N}_{n}(t)}\right)\right] $$

and similarly,

$$ \tau_{N}(e^{\mathbf{i}yB^{N}_{0}b(t)})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau_{N}(e^{\mathbf{i}yB^{N}_{0}b_{n}(t)}). $$

Finally, thanks to [94, Lemma 3.6], one has that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}y\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right|^{2}}\right)\right]-\tau_{N}\left(e^{\mathbf{i}y|B^{N}_{0}b(t)-z|^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{u}e^{-v-u}\int_{[0,1]^{4}}\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\left(R_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},\alpha_{4},}^{n,N,y}\right)\right]\ d\alpha_{1}d\alpha_{2}d\alpha_{3}d\alpha_{4}dvdu, $$

where

$$ \frac{\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{N}\left(R_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},\alpha_{4},}^{n,N,y}\right)\right]\right|}{(1+y^{4})(1+|z|^{4})(1+\left\|B^{N}_{0}\right\|^{4})} $$

can, up to a universal constant, be upper bounded by

$$ \sup_{1\leq l\leq m\leq\lfloor 2^{n}t\rfloor}\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(\left|\prod_{i=l}^{m}\left(I_{N}+\frac{e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{2^{n/2}}\left(aX_{i,\{1,2\}}^{N,\{v,u\}}+\mathbf{i}bY_{i,\{1,2\}}^{N,\{v,u\}}\right)+\frac{\zeta}{2^{n+1}}I_{N}\right)\right|^{12}\right)\right], $$

where the variables $X_{i,\{1,2\}}^{N,\{v,u\}}$ and $Y_{i,\{1,2\}}^{N,\{v,u\}}$ are defined as in Lemma 3.21. Besides, by the same proof as in Lemma 4.3, the quantity above is bounded by a constant which only depends on $t$ and $\varrho$ since $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ . Hence the conclusion. ∎

The following corollary is the main tool to handle the global regime.

#### Corollary 6.5.

There exists a constant $C_{\varrho,t}$ such that, for any functions $f\in\mathcal{C}^{5}(\mathbb{R})$ with compact support bounded by $K$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(f\left(\left|B^{N}_{0}B^{N}(t)-z\right|^{2}\right)\right)\right]-\tau_{N}\left(f\left(|B^{N}_{0}b(t)-z|^{2}\right)\right)\right| \displaystyle\leq C_{\varrho,t}\sqrt{K}\frac{(1+|z|^{4})(1+\left\|B^{N}_{0}\right\|^{4})\left\|f\right\|_{\mathcal{C}^{5}(\mathbb{R})}}{N^{2}}, $$

where $\left\|f\right\|_{\mathcal{C}^{5}(\mathbb{R})}=\sum_{k=0}^{5}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f^{(k)}(x)|$ .

#### Proof.

Let $f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ , and set

$$ \widehat{f}(y)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\mathbf{i}yx}f(x)dx. $$

Then if $\widehat{f}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ , by Fourier inversion theorem,

$$ f(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\mathbf{i}xy}\widehat{f}(y)dy. $$

Besides, if $f$ is sufficiently smooth, then $\left|y^{k}\widehat{f}(y)\right|=\left|\widehat{f^{(k)}}(y)\right|$ , where $f^{(k)}$ is the $k$ -th derivative of $f$ . Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|y^{k}|\left|\widehat{f}(y)\right|dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{(|y^{k}|+|y^{k+1}|)\left|\widehat{f}(y)\right|}{1+|y|}dy\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\left|\widehat{f^{(k)}}(y)\right|+\left|\widehat{f^{(k+1)}}(y)\right|}{1+|y|}dy \displaystyle\leq\left(\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\widehat{f^{(k)}}(y)\right|^{2}dy\right)^{1/2}+\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\widehat{f^{(k+1)}}(y)\right|^{2}dy\right)^{1/2}\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{(1+|y|)^{2}}dy\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left(\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|f^{(k)}(y)\right|^{2}dy\right)^{1/2}+\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|f^{(k+1)}(y)\right|^{2}dy\right)^{1/2}\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{(1+|y|)^{2}}dy\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{K}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{(1+|y|)^{2}}dy\right)^{1/2}\left(\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left|f^{(k)}(y)\right|+\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left|f^{(k+1)}(y)\right|\right), $$

where we used Plancherel theorem on the second line. Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+y^{4})\left|\widehat{f}(y)\right|dy \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{K}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{(1+|y|)^{2}}dy\right)^{1/2}\left\|f\right\|_{\mathcal{C}^{5}(\mathbb{R})}. $$

Hence the conclusion by using Lemma 6.4. ∎

### 6.2. Free Wegner Estimate

Here we prove a version of the desired Wegner estimate in Proposition 6.1 but for the free multiplicative Brownian motion already in the large- $N$ limit. The reader may wish to review Section 2 for the definitions of the regions $\Sigma(1,t)=\Sigma(1,t,0)$ and more generally $\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ ; here the $1$ is the initial condition $b_{0}=u_{0}=1$ for the Brownian motion.

#### Lemma 6.6.

Let $T>0$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq t$ . Let $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\partial\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ . Then there is a constant $\overline{C}_{z,T}$ so that, for all $t\in[0,T]$ , and all $\eta>0$ ,

$$ \left|\mathrm{Im}\,\tau[(i\eta-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]\right|\leq\overline{C}_{z,T}. $$

#### Proof.

The potentially bad set $\partial\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ , which is of Lebesgue measure $0$ , separates $\mathbb{C}$ into two regions. We treat separately the two cases: where $z\in\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ , and where $z\notin\overline{\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)}$ . We begin with the latter.

In [62, Theorem 3.7], it was shown that $\overline{\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)}$ is precisely equal to the spectrum of $b(t,\zeta)$ . Hence, for $z\notin\overline{\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)}$ , $b(t,\zeta)-z$ has a bounded inverse, and therefore so does $|b(t,\zeta)-z|$ (by the spectral theorem). For readability, set $x=|b(t,\zeta)-z|$ . We can therefore compute that

$$ \displaystyle(i\eta-x)^{-1}=-x^{-1}(1-i\eta x^{-1})^{-1}=-x^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(ix^{-1})^{k}\eta^{k} $$

which converges in $\mathscr{A}$ provided $|\eta|<\|x^{-1}\|^{-1}$ . Thus

$$ \tau[(i\eta-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]=-\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}i^{k}\tau[(x^{-1})^{k+1}]\eta^{k} $$

has a convergent power series expansion for $|\eta|<\||b(t,\zeta)-z|^{-1}\|^{-1}$ , and hence it is bounded for $0<\eta<\||b(t,\zeta)-\lambda|^{-1}\|^{-1}$ . Since this norm is continuous in $t$ , the bound is locally uniform in $T$ , as stated.

Now, consider the case that $z\in\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ . Define

$$ S(t,z,\zeta,\eta)=\tau[\log(|b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2}+\eta^{2})]. $$

(Then $\lim_{\eta\downarrow 0}S(t,z,\zeta,\eta)=4\pi U_{b(t,\zeta)}(z)$ where $U_{b(t,\zeta)}$ is the log potential and the Brown measure of $b(t,\zeta)$ is the Laplacian of this limit, see Definition 1.6.)

$$ \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}S(t,z,\zeta,\eta)\right|_{\eta=\eta_{0}}=2\eta_{0}\,\tau[(|b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2}+\eta_{0}^{2})^{-1}]=-2\mathrm{Im}\,\tau[(i\eta_{0}-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}] $$

where the second equality follows just as in Corollary 6.2 from the identity $\mathrm{Im}(i\eta-x)^{-1}=-\eta/(\eta^{2}+x^{2})$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ .

Now, [63, Theorem 8.2] (or more precisely its proof) showed that there is a diffeomorphism $\Phi_{\zeta}\colon\Sigma(1,t)\to\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ such that

$$ S(t,z,\zeta,\eta)=S(t,\Phi_{\zeta}^{-1}(z),0,\eta). $$

Moreover, the diffeomorphism does not depend on $t$ or $\eta$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\,\tau[(i\eta_{0}-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]=-\frac{1}{2}\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}S(t,z,\zeta,\eta)\right|_{\eta=\eta_{0}}=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}S(t,\Phi_{\zeta}^{-1}(z),0,\eta)\right|_{\eta=\eta_{0}} $$

By [48, Theorem 6.4], for $z^{\prime}\in\Sigma(1,t)$ the function $(t,\eta)\mapsto S(t,z^{\prime},0,\eta)$ has real analytic continuation to $\mathbb{R}_{+}\times(-\delta,\delta)$ where $\delta$ may depend on $z$ , but not $t$ . (The statement of that theorem suggests the analytic continuation is only local in $t$ as well; however, in the proof, the actual extension implicitly computed in [48, Eq. (6.20)], is analytic on $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ and continuous on $[0,\infty)$ .) Since $z^{\prime}=\Phi_{\zeta}^{-1}(z)\in\Sigma(1,t)$ precisely when $z\in\Sigma(1,t,\zeta)$ , it therefore follows that the $\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}$ derivative above is continuous and bounded, locally uniformly in $t$ , for $0<\eta_{0}<\delta/2$ (where $\delta$ may depend on $z$ ).

Hence, for such $z$ , the derivative $\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}S(t,z,\zeta,\eta)$ is continuous and bounded for $0<\eta<\delta/2$ . What’s more, the Cauchy transform $|[(i\eta-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]|$ is $\leq 2/\delta$ for all $\eta\geq\delta/2$ . This proves the bound for all $\eta>0$ , concluding the proof. ∎

### 6.3. Proof of Proposition 6.1

We now combine Corollary 6.5 with Lemma 6.6 to prove Proposition 6.1.

Taking $B_{0}^{N}=I$ and reparametrizing per (6.1), (6.4) yields

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\ts_{N}\left(f(|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|^{2})\right)\right]-\tau\left(f(|b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2})\right)\right| \displaystyle\leq 2C_{t\varrho,t}\sqrt{K}\frac{(1+|z|^{4})\|f\|_{\mathcal{C}^{5}(\mathbb{R})}}{N^{2}} $$

for any function $f\in\mathcal{C}^{5}(\mathbb{R})$ that is compactly supported with support of diameter $\leq K$ . Let $M=M(t,z,\zeta)<\infty$ be a constant large enough that $\||B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|^{2}\|\leq M$ a.s. for all large $N$ (see Corollary 4.9) and $\||b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2}\|\leq M$ . For given $\eta\in(0,1]$ , let $f_{\eta}$ be a smooth, compactly supported function satisfying

- $\bullet$ $f_{\eta}(x)=-\frac{\eta}{\eta^{2}+x}$ for $x\in[0,M]$

- $\bullet$ For each $k\leq 5$ , the maximum derivative $\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f_{\eta}^{(k)}(x)|$ does not exceed the maximum derivative $\max_{x\in[0,M]}|f_{\eta}^{(k)}(x)|=|f_{\eta}^{(k)}(0)|=\frac{k!\eta}{(\eta^{2})^{k+1}}=k!\eta^{-2k-1}$ .

This can be accomplished with a smooth function $f_{\eta}$ whose support diameter $K$ is uniform in $\eta\in(0,1]$ : the smaller $\eta>0$ is, the larger the maximum derivative of the approximation is allowed to be. Hence, $K=K(M)$ can be taken to depend on $M$ independent of $\eta$ .

Then, since the spectra of $|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|^{2}$ and $|b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2}$ are contained in the interval $[0,M]$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\ts_{N}\left(f(|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|^{2})\right) \displaystyle=-\lambda\ts_{N}\left((\eta^{2}+|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|^{2})^{-1}\right) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Im}\,\ts_{N}[(i\eta-|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|)^{-1}] \displaystyle\&\qquad\tau\left(f(|b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2})\right) \displaystyle=-\lambda\tau\left((\eta^{2}+|b(t,\zeta)-z|^{2})^{-1}\right) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Im}\,\tau[(i\eta-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]. $$

What’s more, the second condition on $f_{\eta}$ shows that

$$ \|f_{\eta}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{5}}=\sum_{k=0}^{5}k!\eta^{-2k-1}\leq 154\eta^{-11}. $$

Hence, (6.6) shows that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{Im}\,\ts_{N}[(i\eta-|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|)^{-1}]\right)-\mathrm{Im}\,\tau[(i\eta-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]\right| \displaystyle\leq 2C_{t\varrho,t}\sqrt{K(M)}\frac{(1+|z|^{4})\cdot 154\eta^{-11}}{N^{2}}. $$

That is to say: for all $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $\eta\in(0,1]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{Im}\,\ts_{N}[(i\eta-|B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|)^{-1}]\right)\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\left|\mathrm{Im}\,\tau[(i\eta-|b(t,\zeta)-z|)^{-1}]\right|+308C_{t\varrho,t}\sqrt{K(M)}(1+|z|^{4})\frac{\eta^{-11}}{N^{2}}. $$

By Lemma 6.6, the first term is bounded above by a constant $\overline{C}_{z,T}$ for all $\eta>0$ and for all $t\in[0,T]$ . For the second term, if we take $\eta\geq N^{-2/11}$ then $\eta^{-11}/N^{2}\leq 1$ . This proves boundedness.

Lastly, we consider the dependence of the bound on $t$ . The constant $K(M)$ depends on $z,\zeta,t$ only through the uniform upper bound on $\||B^{N}(t,\zeta)-zI|^{2}\|\leq\|B^{N}(t,\zeta)\|^{2}+2|z|\|B^{N}(t,\zeta)\|+|z|^{2}$ . The strong convergence result of [11] shows that $\|B^{N}(t,\zeta)\|$ is bounded uniformly in $N$ by a smooth exponential function of $t$ . Finally, the constant $C_{t\varrho,t}$ is increasing in $t$ , as is clear from the last display equation in the proof of Lemma 6.4 defining it. This shows, therefore, that the bound in Proposition 6.1 is indeed locally uniform in $t$ , concluding the proof.

## 7. Convergence of Eigenvalues

In this final section, we briefly outline again the Hermitization procedure for proving convergence of empirical eigenvalue distributions, and put it together with the estimates bounding the decay rates of shifted singular values we proved in Sections 5 and 6 to prove our main Theorem 1.2. We then prove one more result: combined with the established strong convergence of the processes $B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ , and recent results on the spectrum of the free limit $b_{\varrho,\zeta}$ , we prove that the (random) spectrum of $B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ converges a.s. in Hausdorff metric to the spectrum of $b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ as $N\to\infty$ .

### 7.1. Proof of Theorem 1.2: Convergence of the Empirical Law

We begin by recalling the following lemma encapsulating the Hermitization procedure outlined in Section 1.6.

#### Lemma 7.1 ([21, Lemma 4.3]).

Let $(A^{N})_{N\geq 1}$ be a sequence of random matrices where $A^{N}$ is $N\times N$ . Suppose there exists a family of non-random probability measures $(\nu_{z})_{z\in\mathbb{C}}$ on $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ such that for a.e. $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , almost surely:

- (a) $\mu_{|A^{N}-zI_{N}|}\to\nu_{z}$ , and

- (b) $\log$ is uniformly integrable for $(\mu_{|A^{N}-zI_{N}|})_{N\geq 1}$ .

Then there exists a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{C}$ such that

- (a’) $\mu_{A^{N}}\to\mu$ weakly almost surely, and

- (b’) for a.e. $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , we have

$$ \int_{\mathbb{C}}\log|\lambda-z|d\mu(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\log(s)d\nu_{z}(s). $$

We proceed to prove Theorem 1.2. Fix $t>0$ . Lemma 1.5 verifies condition (a) of the above lemma for $A^{N}=B_{0}B(t)=B_{0}^{N}B^{N}(t)$ , with $\nu_{z}=\nu_{b_{0}b(t)-z}$ as in Definition 1.6, i.e. $\nu_{z}$ is the spectral measure of $|b_{0}b(t)-z|$ . By definition, these measures satisfy (b’) with $\mu=\mu_{b_{0},t}$ .

It only remains to verify condition (b) of the lemma. From the Borel–Cantelli lemma it suffices to show that, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and a.e. $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , there exists $H=H(\varepsilon,z)<\infty$ such that

$$ \mathbb{P}\bigg(\int_{\{|\log s|>H\}}|\log s|d\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-z|}(s)>\varepsilon\bigg)\leq N^{-2} $$

for all $N$ sufficiently large. We show this holds for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ .

Fix $z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ arbitrary. We henceforth suppress from the notation the dependence of constants on the fixed parameters $\varrho,\zeta,t,z$ , and we assume without comment that $N$ is sufficiently large. From Theorem 4.8, we have with probability at least $1-\exp(-N^{2/3})$ that $\|B(t)\|\leq K$ for some constant $K$ , and hence that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\{\log s>H\}}|\log s|d\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-z|}(s) \displaystyle\leq e^{-H}\int_{\{s>\exp(L)\}}s^{2}d\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-z|}(s) \displaystyle\leq e^{-H} \displaystyle\ts_{N}\left(|B_{0}B(t)-z|^{2}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-H} \displaystyle\left(K^{2}\ts_{N}\left(|B_{0}|^{2}\right)+2K|z|\ts_{N}\left(|B_{0}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}+|z|^{2}\right). $$

Since we assumed that $B_{0}$ converges in $*$ -distribution, in particular $\ts_{N}\left(|B_{0}|^{2}\right)$ converges when $N$ goes to infinity and therefore its supremum over $N$ is bounded. Thus, with probability at least $1-\exp(-N^{2/3})$ , we have that

$$ \int_{\{\log s>H\}}|\log s|d\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-z|}(s)=\mathcal{O}(e^{-H}). $$

It thus suffices to show that, with sufficiently high probability,

$$ \int_{0}^{\delta}|\log s|d\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-z|}(s)\lesssim o(1)+f(\delta) $$

for some function $f(\delta)=o_{\delta\to 0}(1)$ . Note that for any $\varepsilon>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_{N}(B_{0}B(t)-z)\leq\varepsilon\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_{N}\left((B_{0}-z(B(t))^{-1})\cdot B(t)\right)\leq\varepsilon\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P} \displaystyle\left(\sigma_{N}(B(t))\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_{N}(B_{0}-zB(t)^{-1})\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\right), $$

where we used in the last line that for any matrices $X,Y$ , $\sigma_{N}(XY)\geq\sigma_{N}(X)\sigma_{N}(Y)$ . Since we know that $\widetilde{B}^{N}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=((B(t))^{-1})^{*}$ is a solution of the SDE (5.4), $(B(t))^{-1}$ is also a multiplicative Brownian motion. Thus, since we assumed $z\neq 0$ , we can apply Proposition 5.1 to $B(t)$ and $(B(t))^{-1}$ along with the union bound to conclude

$$ \sigma_{N}(B_{0}B(t)-z)\geq N^{-\mathcal{O}(1)} $$

with probability at least $1-N^{-10}$ , say. Similarly, from Proposition 5.2 we have that with probability at least $1-N^{-10}$ ,

$$ \min\Big\{\sigma_{N-k}(B(t))\,,\;\sigma_{N-k}(B_{0}-z(B(t))^{-1})\Big\}\gtrsim(k/N)^{2}\quad\forall\,C\log N\leq k\leq\sqrt{t}N $$

for a sufficiently large constant $C$ . Then from the fact that for any matrices $X,Y$ , $\sigma_{N-2k}(XY)\geq\sigma_{N-k}(X)\sigma_{N-k}(Y)$ , we conclude that

$$ \sigma_{N-k}(B_{0}B(t)-z)\gtrsim\min\{(k/N)^{4},t^{2}\}\qquad\forall\;k\geq 2C\log N $$

with probability at least $1-2N^{-10}$ .

For brevity we denote the singular values of $B_{0}B(t)-z$ by $\sigma_{i}:=\sigma_{i}(B_{0}B(t)-z)$ . For any $\delta\in(0,1)$ , on the probability $1-\mathcal{O}(N^{-10})$ event $\mathcal{G}$ that (7.3), (7.4) hold,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\delta}\log(1/s)d\mu_{|B_{0}B(t)-z|}(s) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\log\frac{1}{\sigma_{N-k}}1_{\sigma_{N-k}\leq\delta} \displaystyle\leq 2C\frac{\log N}{N}\log\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\geq 2C\log N}\log\frac{1}{\sigma_{N-k}}1_{\sigma_{N-k}\leq\delta} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{\log^{2}N}{N}+\Big((\delta/c)^{1/4}-\sqrt{t}\Big)_{+}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq(\delta/c)^{1/4}N}\log\frac{N}{k} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{\log^{2}N}{N}+\Big((\delta/c)^{1/4}-\sqrt{t}\Big)_{+}+\int_{0}^{(\delta/c)^{1/4}}\log(1/x)dx $$

where in the final line we recognized the sum over $k$ as a Riemann sum for the integral of $\log$ near the origin. Since $\log$ is locally integrable under the Lebsegue measure, we hence obtain (7.2) to conclude the proof of Theorem 1.2.

### 7.2. Convergence of the Spectrum

In this final section, we prove that the spectrum of the Brownian motion, with a unitary initial condition, converges a.s. as $N\to\infty$ in Hausdorff distance. Precisely: for any subset $H\subset\mathbb{C}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , we denote by $H+\varepsilon$ the Euclidean $\varepsilon$ -neighborhood of $H$ ,

$$ H+\varepsilon\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\ |\ \exists z\in H\colon|z-\lambda|<\varepsilon\}. $$

The Hausdorff distance between two compact sets $H,K$ is

$$ \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{Haus}}(H,K)=\inf\{\varepsilon>0\colon H\subset K+\varepsilon\;\&\;K\subset H+\varepsilon\}. $$

Ergo, given compact sets $\Sigma,\Sigma^{N}$ , to stay $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{Haus}}(\Sigma^{N},\Sigma)\to 0$ is precisely to say that, for any $\varepsilon>0$ , for all sufficiently large $N$ it holds true that $\Sigma\subset\Sigma^{N}+\varepsilon$ and $\Sigma^{N}\subset\Sigma+\varepsilon$ .

Our main result in Theorem 1.2, weak convergence of Brown(ian) measures, is not enough on its own to prove convergence of the support of the measures, i.e. the spectrum. But coupled with strong convergence and some limit spectral results, we prove the following.

#### Theorem 7.2.

Let $\varrho>0$ and $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\zeta|\leq\varrho$ . Let $B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ be a Brownian motion on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$ , and let $b_{\varrho,\zeta}$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion. Let $u_{0}$ be a unitary operator freely independent from $b_{\varrho,\zeta}$ , and suppose that for each $N$ $U_{0}\in\mathrm{U}(N)$ is a random unitary matrix independent from $B_{\varrho,\zeta}$ with the property that, a.s., $U_{0}$ converges strongly to $u_{0}$ as $N\to\infty$ .

Then for any fixed $t\geq 0$ the spectrum of $U_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ converges a.s. in Hausdorff distance to the spectrum of $u_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ , which coincides with the support $\overline{\Sigma(u_{0},t\varrho,t\zeta)}$ of the Brown measure of $u_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ .

We prove Theorem 7.2 as a consequence of the following more general result which may be of independent interest. We state it here for fixed (deterministic) matrices; in its application to prove Theorem 7.2, all almost sure statements refer to single probability $1$ events on which they hold true, and so we may treat all matrices as fixed for this purpose.

#### Proposition 7.3.

Let $a$ be an operator in a $W^{\ast}$ -probability space $(\mathscr{A},\tau)$ , and for each $N\in\mathbb{N}$ let $A^{N}$ be a matrix in $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ .

- (1) If $A^{N}$ converges strongly to $a$ , then for each $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N\in\mathbb{N}$ the spectrum of $A^{N}$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$ -neighborhood of the spectrum of $a$ : $\sigma(A^{N})\subset\sigma(a)+\varepsilon$ .

- (2) If the ESD $\mu_{A^{N}}$ of $A^{N}$ converges weakly to the Brown measure $\mu_{a}$ of $a$ , then for each $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N\in\mathbb{N}$ the support of $\mu_{a}$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$ -neighborhood of the spectrum of $A^{N}$ : $\supp\mu_{a}\subset\sigma(A^{N})+\varepsilon$ .

- (3) Ergo: if $A^{N}\to a$ strongly and $\mu_{A^{N}}\to\mu_{a}$ weakly, and in addition $\supp\mu_{a}=\sigma(a)$ , then $\sigma(A^{N})\to\sigma(A)$ in Hausdorff distance.

In the case that $A^{N}$ and $a$ are selfadjoint, (1) was proved in [35, Prop. 2.1(3)]; the non-selfadjoint setting has not been covered in any literature known to us.

#### Proof.

We begin with (2). Fix $\varepsilon>0$ . Since $\supp\mu_{a}\subseteq\sigma(a)$ it is compact, there are finitely many points $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\in\supp\mu_{a}$ so that the union of the open balls $\{B(z_{j},\varepsilon/2)\}_{1\leq j\leq m}$ covers $\supp\mu_{a}$ . For each $j$ , let $\psi_{j}$ be a $C_{c}(\mathbb{C})$ function which is strictly positive on $B(z_{j},\varepsilon/2)$ and $0$ elsewhere. By assumption in (2),

$$ \int_{\mathbb{C}}\psi_{j}\,d\mu_{A^{N}}\to\int_{\mathbb{C}}\psi_{j}\,d\mu_{a}\quad a.s. $$

Since $\psi_{j}>0$ on a neighborhood of $z_{j}\in\supp\mu_{a}$ , $\int_{\mathbb{C}}\psi_{j}\,d\mu_{a}>0$ ; hence it follows that $\int_{\mathbb{C}}\psi_{j}\,d\mu_{A^{N}}>0$ for all large $N$ . This implies that there is an element $\lambda_{j}^{N}\in\sigma(A^{N})$ in $B(z_{j},\varepsilon/2)$ for all large $N$ . Now, if $\zeta\in B(z_{j},\epsilon/2)$ , it follows that $|\zeta-\lambda_{j}^{N}|\leq|\zeta-z_{j}|+|z_{j}-\lambda_{j}^{N}|<\varepsilon$ and so $\zeta\in\sigma(A^{N})+\varepsilon$ for all large $N$ . As $\supp\mu_{a}$ is contained in the union of the $B(z_{j},\varepsilon/2)$ , it follows that $\supp\mu_{a}\subset\sigma(A^{N})+\varepsilon$ for all large $N$ , as claimed.

We now turn to (1). If $\lambda\notin\sigma(a)$ , then $a-\lambda$ is invertible, and thus so is $|a-\lambda|^{2}$ . In particular, since the spectrum of $|a-\lambda|^{2}$ is compact, $c_{\lambda}:=\inf\sigma(|a-\lambda|^{2})>0$ . Since $A^{N}$ converges strongly to $a$ , it follows that $|A^{N}-\lambda I|^{2}$ converges strongly to $|a-\lambda|^{2}$ . As $|A^{N}-\lambda I|^{2}$ and $|a-\lambda|^{2}$ are selfadjoint, it thence follows from [35, Prop. 2.1(3)] that $\sigma(|A^{N}-\lambda I|^{2})$ converges to $\sigma(|a-\lambda|^{2})$ in Hausdorff distance. In particular $\inf\sigma(|A^{N}-\lambda I|^{2})>\frac{1}{2}\inf\sigma(|a-\lambda|^{2})=c_{\lambda}/2$ for all sufficiently large $N$ , say $N\geq N_{\lambda}$ . Note that $\inf\sigma(|A^{N}-\lambda|^{2})=(\sigma_{N}(A^{N}-\lambda I))^{2}$ is the square of the smallest singular value of $A^{N}-\lambda I$ .

Now, for any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ ,

$$ A^{N}-zI=A^{N}-\lambda I+(\lambda-z)I=(A^{N}-\lambda I)\left(I+(\lambda-z)(A-\lambda I)^{-1}\right). $$

Since the smallest singular value $\sigma_{N}$ is a supermultiplicative function on $\mathbb{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ ,

$$ \sigma_{N}(A^{N}-zI)\geq\sigma_{N}(A^{N}-\lambda I)\cdot\sigma_{N}\left(I+(\lambda-z)(A-\lambda I)^{-1}\right). $$

If $|\lambda-z|<\sqrt{c_{\lambda}/2}$ , then for $N\geq N_{\lambda}$ , $\sigma_{N}(A^{N}-\lambda I)>\sqrt{c_{\lambda}/2}>|\lambda-z|$ . But then

$$ |\lambda-z|\|(A^{N}-\lambda I)^{-1}\|=|\lambda-z|\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}(A^{N}-\lambda I)}<1 $$

and it follows that $I+(\lambda-z)(A-\lambda I)^{-1}$ is invertible. Combined with (7.5), this shows that $A^{N}-zI$ is invertible whenever $|z-\lambda|<\sqrt{c_{\lambda}/2}$ , for $N\geq N_{\lambda}$ . In summary: for any $\lambda\notin\sigma(a)$ , the open ball $B(\lambda,\sqrt{c_{\lambda}/2})$ is disjoint from $\sigma(A^{N})$ for all $N\geq N_{\lambda}$ .

Now, since $A^{N}$ converges strongly to $a$ , $R=\sup_{N}\left\|A^{N}\right\|$ is finite, and so $\sigma(A^{N})$ is contained in the closed ball $\overline{B(0,R)}$ for all $N$ . For any $\varepsilon>0$ , $\overline{B(0,R)}\setminus(\sigma(a)+\varepsilon)$ is compact; hence, there is a finite subset $\Lambda$ of $\lambda$ in this set so that

$$ \overline{B(0,R)}\setminus(\sigma(a)+\varepsilon)\subset\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}B(\lambda,\sqrt{c_{\lambda}/2}). $$

Thus, for $N\geq\max\{N_{\lambda}\colon\lambda\in\Lambda\}$ , $A^{N}-zI$ is invertible for any $z\in\overline{B(0,R)}\setminus(\sigma(a)+\varepsilon)$ . In other words: for all large $N$ , $\overline{B(0,R)}\setminus(\sigma(a)+\varepsilon)$ is contained in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\sigma(A^{N})$ . As $\sigma(A^{N})\subset\overline{B(0,R)}$ , it therefore follows taking complements that $\sigma(A^{N})\subseteq\sigma(a)+\varepsilon$ as claimed.

Finally, (3) follows immediately from (1) and (2) together with the stated assumption that $\supp\mu_{a}$ is equal to the full spectrum $\sigma(a)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 7.2.

From [11, Corollary 1.2], it follows that $B_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ converges strongly to $b_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ a.s. for any sequence of initial conditions $B_{0}$ converging strongly to $b_{0}$ ; hence from Proposition 7.3(1) we have $\sigma(B_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t))$ eventually contained in any neighborhood of $\sigma(b_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t))$ a.s. Conversely, from our Theorem 1.2, the ESD of $B_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ converges weakly a.s. to the Brown measure of $b_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ ; hence, from Proposition 7.3(2) it follows that the support of the Brown measure of $b_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ is eventually contained in any neighborhood of the spectrum of $B_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ .

Now restricting to the case that $B_{0}=U_{0}$ and $b_{0}=u_{0}$ are unitary as in the theorem statement, we have that the support of the Brown measure of $u_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ is equal to $\overline{\Sigma(u_{0},t\varrho,t\zeta)}$ (see our Theorem 2.3). Moreover, [62, Theorem 3.7] proves that the Brown measure support is exactly equal to the spectrum $\sigma(u_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t))$ ; hence, we conclude the statement of the theorem. ∎

As a final remark: we expect it to hold true in full generality that the spectrum of $B_{0}B_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ converges in Hausdorff distance to the spectrum of $b_{0}b_{\varrho,\zeta}(t)$ a.s., for any initial conditions $B_{0}$ converging strongly to $b_{0}$ a.s. The only technical obstacle to this is extending the results of [62] beyond the unitary initial condition case.

## Appendix A Small Singular Values of Shifted Gaussian Matrices

### A.1. Proof of Lemma 5.3

In this section we prove the GUE case of Lemma 5.3, restated below. As we noted, the Ginibre case was established in [10, Lemma 3.3].

It will be convenient to work with a GUE matrix $G$ scaled to have entries of unit variance. Thus, letting $G$ have the distribution of $\sqrt{N}X^{N}(1)$ , with $X^{N}$ as in Definition 3.7, it suffices to prove the following:

#### Lemma A.1 (Non-normal shift of a GUE matrix).

Let $G$ be a scaled $N\times N$ GUE matrix as above, and let $A$ be an arbitrary complex $N\times N$ matrix, deterministic or random and independent of $G$ . For any $\delta\geq 0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N}(G+A)\leq\delta)\leq CN^{2}\delta^{1/8}\,. $$

for a universal constant $C$ .

Previous works have controlled the smallest singular value for Hermitian shifts $H+A$ of Hermitian random matrices $H$ with independent centered entries on and above the diagonal satisfying some tail or anti-concentration assumptions. The first results of this type were by Nguyen [86] and Vershynin [109]. An optimal bound on the lower tail for unshifted Hermitian random matrices $H$ was recently obtained in [30]; we refer to that work for a detailed review of the literature for unshifted Hermitian random matrices.

For matrices with Gaussian entries, it is common to obtain bounds that are completely uniform in $A$ , with no constraint on the norm. This was done in the non-normal case of shifted Ginibre matrices in the well-known work of Shankar–Spielman–Teng on the smoothed analysis of Gaussian elimination [100]. Sharp bounds for the case that $H$ is GOE were obtained by Bourgain in [23]; another argument that also covers GUE matrices was found in [1].

In the present work we need to allow the deterministic shift $A$ to be non-normal. Hence the matrix is generically non-normal, and the above-mentioned sharp results for Hermitian $A$ do not apply.

For the proof we follow the approach from [109] reducing the problem to bounding the lower tail for the distance of a column to the span of remaining columns, which can be expressed in terms of entries of the first row and column of $G+A$ and the inverse of the complementary $N-1$ -dimensional principal submatrix – see (A.4). The difference here from [109] is that there is some additional case analysis due to the fact that the first row and column of $A$ are completely arbitrary (and may be very large). On the other hand, we do not need hard results from the Littlewood–Offord theory for anticoncentration of random walks as in [109], due to the Gaussianity of entries of $G$ .

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality we take $A$ to be deterministic. We may also assume $\delta\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Let $S_{i}\subset S^{N-1}$ be the set of complex unit vectors $x$ such that $|x_{i}|\geq 1/\sqrt{N}$ . Then $S^{N-1}\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}$ , so by the union bound,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\sigma_{N}(G+A)\leq\delta)=\mathbb{P}\bigg(\inf_{x\in S^{N-1}}\|(G+A)x\|_{2}\leq\delta\bigg)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{P}\bigg(\inf_{x\in S_{i}}\|(G+A)x\|_{2}\leq\delta\bigg). $$

By permuting coordinates we see it suffices to show

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})\lesssim N\delta^{1/8}\,,\qquad\mathcal{E}:=\bigg\{\inf_{x\in S_{1}}\|(G+A)x\|_{2}\leq\delta\bigg\}. $$

Let $Y\in\mathbb{C}^{N-1}$ be the first column of $G$ with first entry removed, and let $B,\widetilde{B}^{\mathsf{T}}$ be respectively the first column and row of $A$ with first entry removed. Thus,

$$ G+A=\begin{pmatrix}G_{1,1}+A_{1,1}&Y^{*}+\widetilde{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\\
Y+B&M^{\mathsf{T}}\end{pmatrix} $$

for an $(N-1)\times(N-1)$ matrix $M$ that is independent of $G_{1,1},Y$ . We will only use that $M$ is invertible almost surely. ( $M$ is a.s. invertible because its distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C}^{N^{2}}$ , and the collection of non-invertible matrices viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{C}^{N^{2}}$ has measure 0. The latter property is a consequence of the fact that the zero set of a polynomial has Lebesgue measure 0.)

From [98, Lemma 3.2] (see also [109, Proposition 5.1]) we have

$$ \mathcal{E}\subset\big\{Q\leq\delta\sqrt{N}\big\} $$

where

$$ Q:=\frac{|G_{1,1}+A_{1,1}-(Y+B)^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}(\overline{Y}+\widetilde{B})|}{\sqrt{1+\|M^{-1}(\overline{Y}+\widetilde{B})\|_{2}^{2}}}\,. $$

(This is the distance of the first column of $G+A$ to the span of the other $N-1$ columns.) Letting $K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}>0$ to be chosen later, define events

$$ \mathcal{E}_{1}:=\big\{\|M^{-1}(\overline{Y}+\widetilde{B})\|_{2}\leq K_{1}\big\}\,,\quad\mathcal{E}_{2}:=\big\{\|M^{-1}\|\geq K_{2}\big\}\,,\quad\mathcal{E}_{3}:=\big\{\|Y\|_{2}\geq K_{3}\sqrt{N}\big\}. $$

The rest of the proof divides into four claims:

#### Claim A.2.

$\mathbb{P}(\{Q\leq\delta\sqrt{N}\}\cap\mathcal{E}_{1})\lesssim\delta(1+K_{1}^{2})^{1/2}\sqrt{N}$ .

#### Claim A.3.

$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2})\lesssim(\delta^{2}+K_{2}^{-2})N$ .

#### Claim A.4.

$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{3})\leq K_{3}^{-2}$ .

#### Claim A.5.

With $K_{1}=\delta^{-1/2}$ , $K_{2}=K_{3}\sqrt{N}=\delta^{-1/8}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\{Q\leq\delta\sqrt{N}\}\cap\mathcal{E}_{1}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}^{c})\lesssim\delta^{1/8}N. $$

Combining the claims with (A.3) we obtain (A.1) as desired. It only remains to prove the four claims.

#### Proof of Claim A.2.

For this claim we use the randomness of $G_{1,1}$ . On $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ we have

$$ Q\geq(1+K_{1}^{2})^{-1/2}|G_{1,1}+R| $$

where $R:=A_{1,1}-(Y+B)^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}(\overline{Y}+\widetilde{B})$ is independent of $G_{1,1}$ . Conditioning on $R$ , the claim follows from the fact that the standard real Gaussian variable $G_{1,1}$ has bounded density. ∎

#### Proof of Claim A.3.

For this claim we use the randomness of $Y$ . Condition on a realization of $M$ satisfying $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ . Let $u\in S^{N-2}$ such that $\|M^{-1}u\|_{2}\geq K_{2}$ . We may select such a vector $u$ deterministically under the conditioning on $M$ . On $\mathcal{E}$ , fix $x=(x_{1},\tilde{x})\in S_{1}$ such that $\|(G+A)x\|_{2}\leq\delta$ . With $v:=M^{-1}u/\|M^{-1}u\|_{2}$ , on $\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2}$ we thus have

$$ \displaystyle\delta\geq\|(G+A)x\|_{2} \displaystyle\geq|(0\;v^{\mathsf{T}})(G+A)x| \displaystyle=|x_{1}v^{\mathsf{T}}(Y+B)+v^{\mathsf{T}}M^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{x}| \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}|v^{\mathsf{T}}(Y+B)|-\|Mv\|_{2} \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}|v^{\mathsf{T}}(Y+B)|-\frac{1}{K_{2}}\,. $$

Since $v$ is a fixed unit vector and $Y\in\mathbb{C}^{N-1}$ is standard Gaussian, $g:=v^{\mathsf{T}}Y$ is standard Gaussian in $\mathbb{C}$ and in particular has bounded density. Hence,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2})\leq\mathbb{P}\big(|g+v^{\mathsf{T}}B|\leq\sqrt{N}(\delta+K_{2}^{-1})\big)\lesssim(\delta^{2}+K_{2}^{-2})N\,.\qed $$

#### Proof of Claim A.4.

Since $Y$ is standard Gaussian in $\mathbb{C}^{N-1}$ , the claim is immediate from Markov’s inequality. ∎

#### Proof of Claim A.5.

Note that on $\mathcal{E}_{1}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}^{c}$ ,

$$ K_{1}<\|M^{-1}(\overline{Y}+\widetilde{B})\|_{2}<K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}+\|M^{-1}\widetilde{B}\|_{2}\,. $$

Combining these bounds, we get that the denominator in (A.4) is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle 1+\|M^{-1}(\overline{Y}+\widetilde{B})\|_{2} \displaystyle<\|M^{-1}\widetilde{B}\|_{2}\bigg(1+\frac{1+K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}{\|M^{-1}\widetilde{B}\|_{2}}\bigg) \displaystyle\leq\|M^{-1}\widetilde{B}\|_{2}\bigg(1+\frac{1+K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}{K_{1}-K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}\bigg)\,. $$

On $\mathcal{E}_{2}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}^{c}$ the numerator in (A.4) is bounded below by

$$ \displaystyle|Y^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}\widetilde{B}+B^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}\overline{Y}+R^{\prime}|-K_{2}K_{3}^{2}N $$

where $R^{\prime}:=B^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}\widetilde{B}-G_{1,1}-A_{1,1}$ is independent of $Y$ . Decomposing the standard Gaussian vector $Y\in\mathbb{C}^{N-1}$ as $Y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(U+iV)$ for $U,V$ standard real Gaussian vectors, we have

$$ Y^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}\widetilde{B}+B^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}\overline{Y}=\sqrt{2}(a+b)U+i\sqrt{2}(a-b)V $$

where we denote the deterministic row vectors

$$ a:=(M^{-1}\widetilde{B})^{\mathsf{T}}\,,\quad b:=B^{\mathsf{T}}M^{-1}\,. $$

Combining with (A.6), (A.7), we have that on $\{Q\leq\delta\sqrt{N}\}\cap\mathcal{E}_{1}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2}^{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{3}^{c}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\delta\sqrt{N}\geq Q \displaystyle\geq\frac{|\sqrt{2}(a+b)U+i\sqrt{2}(a-b)V+R^{\prime}|-K_{2}K_{3}^{2}N}{\|a\|_{2}\Big(1+\frac{1+K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}{K_{1}-K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}\Big)}\,. $$

Rearranging and substituting the bound $\|a\|_{2}\leq\|a+b\|_{2}+\|a-b\|_{2}$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle\big|z\cdot(U,V)+ \displaystyle R^{\prime}/\sqrt{2}(\|a+b\|_{2}+\|a-b\|_{2})\big| \displaystyle\leq\delta\sqrt{N}\Big(1+\frac{1+K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}{K_{1}-K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}}\Big)+\frac{K_{2}K_{3}^{2}N}{K_{1}-K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}} $$

where for the second term on the right hand side we again used (A.5) to bound $\|a\|_{2}\geq K_{1}-K_{2}K_{3}\sqrt{N}$ , and we set

$$ z:=\bigg(\frac{a+b}{\|a+b\|_{2}+\|a-b\|_{2}},\frac{i(a-b)}{\|a+b\|_{2}+\|a-b\|_{2}}\bigg)\in\mathbb{C}^{2N-2}. $$

With $K_{1}=\delta^{-1/2}$ , $K_{2}=K_{3}\sqrt{N}=\delta^{-1/8}$ , (A.8) becomes

$$ \big|z\cdot(U,V)+R^{\prime}/\sqrt{2}(\|a+b\|_{2}+\|a-b\|_{2})\big|\lesssim\delta^{1/8}N $$

Clearly $\|z\|_{2}\gtrsim 1$ , so at least one of its real or imaginary parts has norm $\gtrsim 1$ . It follows that at least one of the real or imaginary parts of $z\cdot(U,V)$ is Gaussian of variance $\gtrsim 1$ , since $(U,V)$ is standard Gaussian in $\mathbb{R}^{2N-2}$ . Hence,

$$ \sup_{w\in\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{P}(|z\cdot(U,V)+w|\leq\varepsilon)\lesssim\varepsilon $$

for any $\varepsilon\geq 0$ . Together with (A.9) this yields the claim. ∎

The proof of Lemma A.1 is complete. ∎

### A.2. Proof of Lemma 5.4

In this appendix we prove Lemma 5.4, restated below.

#### Lemma A.6.

There is a universal constant $c>0$ such that the following holds. Let $G$ be an $N\times N$ matrix with standard real Gaussian entries, and assume the $N(N+1)/2$ pairs $\{(G_{ij},G_{ji}):1\leq i\leq j\leq N\}$ are jointly independent. Then for any $N\times N$ complex matrix $A$ , deterministic or random and independent of $G$ , and any $k\geq c^{-1}\log N$ , the event that

$$ \sigma_{N-\ell}(G+A)\geq c\ell/N\qquad\text{for all $k\leq\ell\leq N-1$} $$

holds with probability at least $1-e^{-ck}$ .

We prove Lemma A.6 via the geometric argument of Tao and Vu [104], with a small modification to allow dependency between entries $G_{ij}$ and $G_{ji}$ . The first step in this approach is to establish the following lower bound for $\sigma_{N-j}(A)$ for an arbitrary $N\times N$ matrix $A$ . Informally, the lemma below provides a lower bound on $\sigma_{N-j}(A)$ in terms of the extent to which the rows of $A$ are linearly independent.

#### Lemma A.7.

For any $N\times N$ matrix $A$ with complex entries, we have that

$$ \sigma_{N-j}(A)\gtrsim\sqrt{\frac{j}{N}}\min_{i\in[m]}\text{\emph{dist}}(R_{i},V_{i}) $$

where $m=N-\lceil j/2\rceil$ , $R_{i}$ denotes the $i$ th row of $A$ , and $V_{i}=\text{\emph{span}}(R_{\ell}:\ell\neq i,\ell\leq m)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $M$ denote the matrix consisting of the top $m$ rows of $A$ . We may assume the the right hand side of (A.10) is positive, i.e. the rows of $M$ are linearly independent, as otherwise the claim holds trivially. By Cauchy interlacing, we have that

$$ \sigma_{N-j}(A)\geq\sigma_{N-j}(M). $$

Combining with the inverse second moment identity (see [104, Lemma A.4]):11 1 Proof: By projecting the rows to their span we reduce to the case that $M$ is square and invertible. Then one sees that the expressions in (A.12) are two ways of writing the Frobenius norm of $M^{-1}$ .

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\text{dist}(R_{i},V_{i})^{-2}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sigma_{i}(M)^{-2}, $$

we get that

$$ \displaystyle N\max_{i\in[m]}\text{dist}(R_{i},V_{i})^{-2}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sigma_{i}(M)^{-2}\geq\sum_{i=N-j}^{m}\sigma_{i}(M)^{-2}\geq \displaystyle\frac{j-1}{2}\sigma_{N-j}(M)^{-2}\,. $$

Combining with (A.11) and rearranging, we obtain the desired conclusion. ∎

With Lemma A.7 in hand, we complete the proof of Lemma A.6 using concentration of measure.

#### Proof of Lemma A.6.

We begin by noting that it suffices to show that, by union bound, there exists a constant $c>0$ (possibly different from the one in the lemma statement) such that for every $j\geq k$

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_{N-j}(X)\leq cj/\sqrt{N}\right)\leq e^{-cj}. $$

Moreover, applying Lemma A.7 with $A=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}X$ , we see it suffices to show there exists a universal constant $c$ , possibly different from the one in (A.13), such that

$$ \mathbb{P}(\text{dist}(R_{i},V_{i})\leq c\sqrt{j})\leq e^{-cj}. $$

For an $N$ -dimensional row vector $y$ we write $y^{(i)}$ for the $(N-1)$ -dimensional vector obtained by removing the $i$ th entry of $y$ . Set

$$ \displaystyle V_{i}^{\prime}=\text{span}\left(R_{\ell}^{(i)}:\ell\neq i,\ell\leq m\right)\,,\qquad V_{i}^{\prime\prime}=\text{span}\left(V_{i}^{\prime},Y^{(i)}_{i}\right) $$

which are subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^{N-1}$ . Then,

$$ \text{dist}(R_{i},V_{i})\geq\text{dist}\left(R_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime}\right)\geq\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right). $$

By our assumptions, $G_{i}^{(i)}$ is a standard Gaussian vector and $V_{i}^{\prime\prime}$ is an independent subspace of dimension $\leq N-\lceil\frac{j}{2}\rceil+1$ . Additionally, notice that $x\mapsto\text{dist}(x,V_{i}^{\prime\prime})$ is a 1-Lipshitz function of $x$ . Thus, we can apply Gaussian concentration, conditional on $V_{i}^{\prime\prime}$ , to obtain

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\,\Big|\,V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right]-\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\geq t\,\Big|\,V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\leq e^{-t^{2}/2}. $$

It remains to estimate $\mathbb{E}\left[\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\big|V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right]$ . First, observe that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)^{2}\,\Big|\,V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right]=N-1-\dim(V_{i}^{\prime\prime}). $$

By the Gaussian Poincaré inequality,

$$ \text{Var}\left(\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\,\Big|\,V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\leq 1. $$

(One also sees the variance is $\mathcal{O}(1)$ from integrating the tail bound (A.15), along with the same bound for the lower tail.) Therefore,

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\text{dist}\left(G_{i}^{(i)},V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right)\,\Big|\,V_{i}^{\prime\prime}\right]\geq(N-2-\dim(V_{i}^{\prime\prime}))^{1/2}\gtrsim\sqrt{j}. $$

Combining the above lower bound with (A.15), we can see that (A.14) holds and the desired conclusion follows. ∎
